2. CLOSED-LOOP N₂ ATMOSPHERE ARCHITECTURE



2.1 System Architecture & N₂ Circuit Description



The entire drum and gas handling system operates as a sealed nitrogen atmosphere loop. Nitrogen was selected as the carrier gas for three fundamental reasons:



1. Inertness at cascade temperatures: N₂ remains chemically inert across the full 25°C → 1676°C operating range. Unlike CO₂ (which participates in Boudouard reaction above 700°C) or argon (cost-prohibitive at scale), nitrogen provides thermodynamic stability without side reactions.



2. Thermal ballast properties: N₂ specific heat capacity (1.04 kJ/kg·K at 300K, rising to 1.15 kJ/kg·K at 1000K) provides substantial thermal mass for temperature stabilization. The 2-3 kg N₂ inventory per cycle acts as a thermal flywheel, dampening induction power transients.



3. Industrial availability & cost: Bulk liquid nitrogen at $0.09/kg (industrial grade) yields a make-up gas cost of < $0.30 per 50 kg feedstock batch — negligible relative to recovered metal value ($500-5000/batch).



The N₂ circuit comprises the following subsystems in series:

2.2 System Operating Pressure Control

The Aegis-Forge I operates the entire N₂ atmosphere loop at a positive gauge pressure of 1.2-2.5 bar (2.2-3.5 bar absolute). This pressurized operation serves four critical functions:

1. Oxygen Exclusion (Primary Safety Function) At Stage 2 temperatures (300-450°C), any oxygen ingress would cause uncontrolled combustion of thermoplastic polymers, generating uncontrolled thermal excursions, toxic partial oxidation products (dioxins, furans, PAHs), and potential overpressure events. The positive pressure ensures that any leakage is outward (N₂ to atmosphere) rather than inward (air to process). Maximum allowable O₂ concentration in the loop: < 10 ppm (monitored by ZrO₂-based optical O₂ sensor).

2. Boiling Point Elevation Increased system pressure raises the boiling points of volatile species, reducing premature vaporization and improving condensation efficiency in the stage-specific trains:

  • Water: 100°C at 1 bar → 120°C at 2 bar (Train A inlet matches this)
  • Zinc: 907°C at 1 bar → 945°C at 2.5 bar (improves Zn retention in drum melt)
  • Lead: 1749°C at 1 bar → minimal shift (PbO particulate capture dominates)

3. Pressure-Differential Gas Routing The pressure gradient from drum (highest) → condenser cascade → scrubbers → PSA → recycle compressor (lowest) provides the driving force for gas flow without requiring mechanical blowers in the hot process stream. Pressure drops across each element:

ElementΔP (bar)Notes -------------------------- Drum internal (inlet to exhaust)0.05-0.15Function of RPM, flow rate Zero₂ cyclone separator0.15Fixed geometry, 25 m/s inlet Train A (3-zone condenser)0.12Counterflow, 200 tubes Train B (3-stage organic)0.18Highest viscosity gas Train C (pyrolysis quench + carbon)0.25Water spray + packed bed Train D (lime scrubber)0.08Pellet bed, low velocity Train E (metal condensers)0.10Two columns in series PSA columns (adsorption)0.15Zeolite 13X, 3-5 bar swing Plasma torch0.05Straight-through ceramic tube Total loop ΔP1.13Design margin to 2.5 bar supply

4. Compressor Work Minimization By operating at elevated pressure, the recycle compressor handles denser gas (2.5× density at 2.5 bar vs 1 bar), reducing volumetric flow and compressor displacement. Compressor power scales with mass flow, not volumetric flow, so the penalty is modest: ~8 kW for 50 SLPM at 2.5 bar discharge.

2.2.2 Stage-Dependent Pressure Setpoints

The pressure setpoint varies by thermal cascade stage to optimize condensation efficiency and material separation:

StageTemp RangeSetpoint (bar gauge)Rationale --------------------------------------------------- 0 (AMLS)25-100°C1.2Low pressure: acoustic wave propagation, minimal gas density 1 (IR Dry)100-150°C1.2Water condensation at 80-120°C optimized at low pressure 2 (Polymer)300-450°C1.8Higher pressure suppresses premature polymer cracking 3 (Pyrolysis)450-650°C2.0Pyrolysis gas density for combustion burner stability 4 (Low-Temp Metals)420-550°C2.2Zn vapor pressure management, condensation efficiency 5 (Al Window)660-720°C2.2Al melt protection, minimal vapor pressure effect 6 (Cu/PM)1085-1150°C2.3Cu vapor suppression, precious metal retention 7 (Ferrous)1538-1600°C2.4Fe vapor suppression, RE magnet protection 8 (Mineral)1676°C2.5Maximum density for zircon dissociation gas management

Pressure transitions between stages are ramped at 0.2 bar/min (limited by N₂ thermal expansion/compression rates and compressor capacity).

2.2.3 Pressure Relief System (Three Independent Layers)

Per ASME BPVC Section VIII and IEC 61511 SIL-3 requirements, three independent pressure relief paths protect the hermetic loop:

LayerDeviceSet PressureCapacityActivation --------------------------------------------------- PrimaryPEEK CF40 spring-loaded relief valve (PSV-101)3.0 bar gauge100 SLPM N₂Mechanical spring, no power SecondaryZrO₂ ceramic rupture disk (PSD-101)4.5 bar gaugeFull bore (50mm)Non-reclosing, burst at 4.5 bar EmergencyManual ZrO₂ ceramic ball valve (MV-101)Human-authorizedFull boreHuman + two-key authorization

Primary Relief (PSV-101) Detail:

  • Body: PEEK CF40 (continuous service to 250°C, peak 300°C)
  • Seat: ZrO₂ ceramic (zero metallic contact with process gas)
  • Spring: PEEK CF40 (non-metallic, corrosion immune, fatigue rated 10⁶ cycles)
  • Discharge: BFRP expansion vessel (500 L, 10 bar design, Elium® resin)
  • Expansion vessel: Water-cooled jacket, ZrO₂ lined, vents to outdoor stack via flame arrestor
  • Sizing: API 520, fire case + blocked outlet + thermal expansion = 85 SLPM required → 100 SLPM rated

Secondary Relief (PSD-101) Detail:

  • Material: ZrO₂ ceramic disc, 50mm diameter, 2mm thickness
  • Burst pressure: 4.5 bar gauge ± 5% (factory tested)
  • Fragmentation: Designed for non-fragmenting burst (ceramic petal pattern)
  • Discharge: Same expansion vessel as PSV-101 (parallel path)
  • Replacement: Manual, requires loop depressurization

Emergency Relief (MV-101) Detail:

  • Valve: ZrO₂ ceramic ball, 50mm bore, PEEK CF40 stem/seals
  • Actuation: Manual handwheel with two-key interlock (control room + local)
  • Indication: Position sensor (FBG), local visual indicator, control room alarm
  • Use case: Only if both PSV-101 and PSD-101 fail AND human authorization confirmed
  • Discharge: Outdoor vent stack (10m height, flame arrestor, dispersion modeling per EPA)

3. STAGE-SPECIFIC GAS TREATMENT TRAINS — DETAILED ENGINEERING

3.1 Train A: Moisture Condenser (Stage 1 Outlet) — Deep Dive

Process Function: Remove water vapor from N₂ carrier gas after Stage 1 infrared drying. The feedstock enters Stage 1 with 5-25% moisture content (wet basis). At 120°C drum wall temperature and 1.2 bar pressure, water vapor partial pressure reaches ~2 bar (superheated). The condenser must reduce dew point from 120°C to < 5°C to prevent downstream corrosion and condensation in later trains.

3.1.1 Thermodynamic Design Basis

ParameterValueBasis ------------------------- Inlet gas flow20 SLPM N₂ + H₂O vaporStage 1 mass balance Inlet temperature120°CDrum wall temp, Stage 1 Inlet pressure1.2 bar gaugeStage 1 setpoint Inlet H₂O mass fraction0.15-0.35 kg/kg dry N₂Feedstock moisture 5-25% Target outlet dew point5°CPrevents condensation at 25°C ambient Heat duty (max)18.5 kWLatent + sensible, 25% moisture case

Condensation Curve (Equilibrium): 

Temperature (°C) → 120 → 80 → 25 → 5
Water partial pressure (bar) → 2.0 → 0.47 → 0.032 → 0.0087
Condensed fraction → 0% → 76% → 98.4% → 99.6%
Cumulative water removed → 0 → 0.76 → 0.984 → 0.996

3.1.3 Materials & Corrosion Considerations

  • All wetted surfaces: ZrO₂-lined Al₂O₃ ceramic or BFRP/Elium® — zero metallic contact
  • Water chemistry: Stage 1 water contains dissolved organics, trace HCl (from PVC), dust
  • pH control: Maintain 6.5-8.0 to prevent acid attack on ZrO₂ (stable pH 3-11) and BFRP
  • Biological control: 0.5 ppm H₂O₂ dosing in storage tank (UV generation from plasma torch)
  • Scaling prevention: Softened make-up water, periodic citric acid flush (quarterly)

3.2 Train B: Organic Vapor Condensation (Stage 2 Outlet) — Deep Dive

Process Function: Condense and fractionate polymer decomposition vapors from Stage 2 (300-450°C). The vapor mixture contains 14+ polymer types with boiling points spanning 100°C (MMA) to 450°C+ (heavy PAHs). Three-stage fractional condensation separates by volatility for maximum value recovery.

3.2.1 Vapor Composition & Fractionation Targets

Polymer TypeDecomposition RangeKey Vapor SpeciesBoiling PointTarget Fraction -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PMMA (Elium®)300-400°CMMA, CO₂, CH₄MMA: 100.5°CSecondary (25°C) PS350-420°CStyrene, α-methylstyreneStyrene: 145°CPrimary (80°C) ABS380-450°CStyrene, acrylonitrile, butadieneButadiene: -4.5°CTertiary (5°C) PC400-450°CBisphenol A, phenol, CO₂Phenol: 182°CPrimary (80°C) PET350-420°CTerephthalic acid, acetaldehydeAcetaldehyde: 20°CSecondary (25°C) PVC250-350°CHCl, benzene, chlorobenzeneBenzene: 80°CPrimary (80°C) PE/PP400-480°Cα-olefins, paraffins C1-C20Wide rangeAll three fractions

Fractionation Strategy:

  • Primary (80°C): Heavy fraction (C12+), waxes, PAHs, heavy aromatics — solid/semi-solid at 80°C
  • Secondary (25°C): Medium fraction (C6-C12), light aromatics (BTX), MMA, styrene — liquid at 25°C
  • Tertiary (5°C): Light fraction (C1-C5), permanent gases, trace organics — gas at 25°C

3.2.3 MMA Recovery from Elium® Feedstock (CSMFAB Integration)

When Elium® BFRP cuttings/off-cuts are included in feedstock (Phoenix Protocol returns, manufacturing scrap), the Stage 2 vapor stream contains methyl methacrylate (MMA) from thermal depolymerization of the Elium® resin matrix.

MMA Recovery Window:

  • MMA boiling point: 100.5°C at 1 atm → ~105°C at 1.8 bar
  • Target fraction: Secondary condenser 100-105°C cut
  • Theoretical yield: 85-90% of Elium® resin mass → MMA monomer
  • Practical recovery: 60-80% (condensation efficiency + purification losses)
  • Purification: Simple distillation (MMA bp 100.5°C, separates from styrene 145°C, water 100°C)
  • Value: Recovered MMA feeds in-house Elium® synthesis (Materials Study Part II) — closes resin loop

Process Integration: 

Elium® scrap in feedstock
        │
        ▼
Stage 2: Thermal depolymerization (350-400°C)
        │
        ▼
MMA vapor in N₂ stream (partial pressure ~0.15 bar)
        │
        ▼
Train B Secondary Condenser (100-105°C cut)
        │
        ▼
Crude MMA condensate (85% MMA, 10% water, 5% impurities)
        │
        ▼
Distillation column (ZrO₂ trays, BFRP shell)
        │
        ├─ Overhead: 99.5% MMA → Elium® synthesis reactor
        ├─ Bottoms: Water + heavies → Train B primary recycle
        └─ Vent: Light ends → Train C combustion

3.3.3 Closed-Loop Char-Tar Cycle

The char-tar closed loop is a key innovation: Stage 3 output captures Stage 3 contaminants.

1. Stage 3 produces char (carbonaceous residue from pyrolysis) 2. Char is steam-activated → high-surface-area activated carbon 3. Activated carbon adsorbs tar/PAH from pyrolysis gas (Train C) 4. Char-tar composite is re-fed to Stage 8 in next batch 5. Stage 8 (1676°C) pyrolyzes tar → more char + clean gas 6. Net result: Zero tar emission, zero activated carbon purchase

Carbon balance per 50 kg batch:

  • Char produced: 8-12 kg (from 50 kg organics)
  • Char activated: 5 kg → 4 kg activated carbon (80% yield)
  • Tar captured: 0.5-1.5 kg (adsorbed on 4 kg carbon)
  • Char-tar to Stage 8: 5-6 kg
  • Stage 8 char output: +5-6 kg (net char accumulation → periodic withdrawal)

3.4 Train D: Acid Gas Scrubber (HCl, SO₂, HF) — Deep Dive

Process Function: Neutralize acid gases (primarily HCl from PVC dehydrochlorination, SO₂ from sulfur-containing materials, HF from fluoropolymers) using dry lime injection. The dry scrubber approach avoids liquid waste streams and produces usable solid byproducts.

3.4.1 Acid Gas Sources & Loadings

Source StageAcid GasGeneration MechanismTypical Loading (per 50 kg batch) -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Stage 2 (Polymer)HClPVC dehydrochlorination: -(CH₂-CHCl)-ₙ → -CH=CH- + HCl0.5-3.0 kg HCl (1-6% PVC in feedstock) Stage 3 (Pyrolysis)SO₂Sulfur in rubber, vulcanization agents, solder flux0.1-0.5 kg SO₂ Stage 2/3HFFluoropolymers (PTFE, FEP), electronics fluxes< 0.05 kg HF (rare)

Gas Phase Concentrations at Scrubber Inlet (1.2 bar, 150-200°C):

  • HCl: 200-1500 ppm (mass basis: 0.3-2.2 g/Nm³)
  • SO₂: 50-500 ppm (mass basis: 0.1-0.7 g/Nm³)
  • HF: < 50 ppm (mass basis: < 0.04 g/Nm³)

3.4.2 Reaction Chemistry & Stoichiometry

Primary Reactions: 

Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O        ΔH°₂₉₈ = -148 kJ/mol HCl
Ca(OH)₂ + SO₂ + ½O₂ → CaSO₄ + H₂O    ΔH°₂₉₈ = -620 kJ/mol SO₂
Ca(OH)₂ + 2HF → CaF₂ + 2H₂O          ΔH°₂₉₈ = -160 kJ/mol HF

Stoichiometric Lime Requirements (per 50 kg batch, max loading):

  • HCl: 3.0 kg → 2.9 kg Ca(OH)₂ (MW: Ca(OH)₂=74, 2HCl=73)
  • SO₂: 0.5 kg → 0.8 kg Ca(OH)₂ (MW: Ca(OH)₂=74, SO₂=64 + 0.5O₂)
  • HF: 0.05 kg → 0.07 kg Ca(OH)₂
  • Total theoretical: 3.8 kg Ca(OH)₂ per batch (maximum)

Practical Design: 2× stoichiometric excess for kinetic completeness → 7.6 kg Ca(OH)₂ per batch maximum

  • Lime cost: $0.15/kg → $1.14/batch maximum
  • Typical batch (low PVC): 0.5-2.0 kg Ca(OH)₂ → $0.08-0.30/batch

3.5 Train E: Metal Vapor Condenser (Stages 4-5 Outlet) — Deep Dive

Process Function: Capture zinc vapor (primary) and lead oxide particulate from the gas stream exiting Stages 4 (420-550°C, Pb/Sn/Zn/In separation) and 5 (660-720°C, Al window). Zinc vapor pressure becomes significant above 500°C; lead remains primarily as PbO particulate.

At Stage 4-5 conditions (420-550°C drum, 2.2 bar system pressure), Zn vapor partial pressure reaches 0.001-0.1 bar. For 25 SLPM N₂ flow, this represents 0.5-5 g/min Zn vapor — significant loss if not captured.

4. FINAL GAS TREATMENT — CO₂ CAPTURE & N₂ RECOVERY

4.1 CO₂ Separation via Pressure Swing Adsorption (PSA)

After Train C combustion (Option A) or reforming (Option B), the gas stream consists primarily of N₂ and CO₂ with trace residual gases. CO₂ must be separated for two reasons: (1) to recover high-purity N₂ for recycle loop closure, and (2) to capture CO₂ for reuse as drum purge gas and geopolymer curing atmosphere.

PSA with Zeolite 13X is the selected technology:

  • Zeolite 13X adsorbs CO₂ preferentially at 3-5 bar; desorbs at 1 bar
  • Two-column alternating cycle: 60s adsorption / 30s desorption
  • CO₂ purity output: 95-99% (sufficient for inert purge and geopolymer curing)
  • N₂ purity output: 97-99.5% (recycled to drum atmosphere)
  • Column body: BFRP/Elium® with PEEK CF40 valve manifold
  • Valve seats: ZrO₂ ceramic check valves (no metallic contact)

Recovered CO₂ Uses: 1. Drum purge gas supplement (both N₂ and CO₂ are inert at operating temperatures) 2. CBPC geopolymer curing atmosphere (CO₂ curing accelerates strength development) 3. Future: CO₂-to-CO via plasma arc for carbon synthesis feedstock

4.2 Plasma Torch Polisher — Final Gas Treatment

For any trace organics, halogens, or dioxin/furan precursors that escape all prior trains, a final plasma torch at the gas outlet provides 6-log destruction efficiency.

Plasma Torch Construction:

  • Electrodes: ZrO₂-coated tungsten (tungsten for 3000°C+ resistance; ZrO₂ coating for corrosion)
  • Housing: ZrB₂-SiC ceramic (withstands 3000°C plasma temperatures)
  • Power: 15 kW DC (plasma arc temperature: 3000-8000°C)
  • Residence time at >1000°C: 0.5 seconds (sufficient for complete organic destruction)
  • Dioxin/furan threshold: PCDD/PCDF destruction efficiency > 99.9999% at 1200°C, 2 seconds

The plasma torch is the system's regulatory safety net — ensuring zero toxic organic emissions.

5. EMERGENCY SAFETY SYSTEMS

5.1 Pressure Relief (Three Independent Layers)

Per ASME BPVC Section VIII and IEC 61511 SIL-3:

LayerDeviceSet PressureCapacityActivation --------------------------------------------------- PrimaryPEEK CF40 spring-loaded relief valve (PSV-101)3.0 bar gauge100 SLPM N₂Mechanical spring SecondaryZrO₂ ceramic rupture disk (PSD-101)4.5 bar gaugeFull bore (50mm)Non-reclosing burst EmergencyManual ZrO₂ ceramic ball valve (MV-101)Human-authorizedFull boreTwo-key authorization

Primary Relief (PSV-101): PEEK CF40 body, ZrO₂ seat, PEEK CF40 spring (10⁶ cycles fatigue rated), discharge to 500L BFRP expansion vessel.

Secondary Relief (PSD-101): ZrO₂ ceramic disc, 50mm diameter, 2mm thickness, 4.5 bar ±5% burst, non-fragmenting petal pattern.

Emergency Relief (MV-101): ZrO₂ ceramic ball, 50mm bore, PEEK CF40 stem/seals, manual handwheel with two-key interlock.

5.2 Temperature Runaway Prevention

If induction coil fails in ON state:

  • PMMA fiber FBG temp sensors detect >50°C over-temperature
  • All induction inverters trigger isolated IGBT off-state via optical signal (GIC immune)
  • N₂ quench valve opens: floods drum at 5 bar N₂ (thermal ballast)
  • Automatic drum speed reduction to 10 RPM (convective cooling)

5.3 Acoustic Overpressure Alert (AMLS Stage 0)

  • Acoustic power limited by structural resonance of BFRP pre-chamber
  • FBG sensors continuously monitor strain in chamber wall
  • If strain > 60% of failure threshold: power reduced proportionally (PID control)

7. CONCLUSION

The Gas Capture, Condensation & Fume Solidification (GFGS) subsystem is the thermodynamic closure of the Aegis-Forge I thermal cascade. By treating every gas stream as a recoverable material stream — water, organics, pyrolysis gas, acid gases, metal vapors, CO₂ — the system achieves true zero-emission operation while extracting maximum value from each batch.

The closed-loop N₂ atmosphere with stage-dependent pressure control, five stage-specific treatment trains, PSA CO₂ separation, and plasma torch final polisher form an integrated architecture where the output of each stage feeds the next. The char-tar closed loop (Stage 3 char → activated carbon → tar capture → Stage 8 re-feed) exemplifies the circular design philosophy.

Every component is constructed from CSMFAB-certified dielectric materials — zero structural metals, zero ferromagnetic materials, zero conductive paths to ground. The GFGS is itself a dielectric citadel, Carrington-immune and fireproof.

This is not waste management. This is material stewardship at thermodynamic limits.

Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

Document: PROD-07 — Gas Capture & Fume Solidification

Constraint (The Lock)

The GFGS subsystem is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Zero Emission as Thermodynamic Closure — every gas molecule generated by the thermal cascade must be captured, classified, and converted to solid or liquid product. There is no "vent to atmosphere" path. The constraint is not environmental regulation; it is mass balance. The cascade processes 50 kg feedstock and generates ~15 kg gas-phase products per batch (water, organics, pyrolysis gas, acid gases, metal vapors, CO₂). If any fraction escapes, the system violates its own physics — an open system cannot claim complete elemental extraction. The machine must be a hermetically sealed dielectric citadel where gas phase is a transient state, not an exit state.

This constraint manifests as the Closed-Loop N₂ Atmosphere Architecture: nitrogen circulates continuously as carrier gas, sweeping each stage's exhaust through five stage-specific treatment trains before returning to the drum. The N₂ inventory (2-3 kg/cycle) is the thermal ballast and the material conveyor. No air ingress (oxygen = uncontrolled combustion). No gas egress (every species recovered). The positive pressure (1.2-2.5 bar) is the physical enforcement of closure — leakage is outward only.

The constraint writes the entire architecture: five treatment trains (A-E), PSA CO₂ separation, plasma torch polisher, three-layer pressure relief. Every parameter derives from the capture target: water at 80→5°C, organics at 80/25/5°C fractionation, pyrolysis gas at 18.5 MJ/m³ recovery, acid gases at <1 ppm outlet, metal vapors at >99% capture, dioxins at 6-log destruction. There are no free parameters — the periodic table's gas-phase species determine the trains.

Necessity (The Key)

The lock this document addresses is the emission-recovery gap — every historical thermal process (smelting, pyrolysis, incineration, gasification) vents 10-40% of input mass as gas, losing value and creating liability. Smelters vent SO₂, CO₂, metal fumes. Pyrolysis vents tars, CO, CH₄. Incinerators vent dioxins, HCl, particulates. The empirical reality: no existing thermal process captures its own exhaust as product. The key is stage-specific gas treatment as elemental recovery — each train targets the exact species generated at that temperature, converting gas to solid/liquid product with >95% efficiency.

The necessity is proven by the closed-loop char-tar cycle: Stage 3 produces char → char activated → captures tar from pyrolysis gas → char-tar composite re-fed to Stage 8 → tar pyrolyzes to more char. Zero tar emission, zero activated carbon purchase, net char accumulation. This is not waste management — it is material stewardship where the process consumes its own contaminants.

The acid gas scrubber exemplifies the same principle: Ca(OH)₂ neutralizes HCl/SO₂/HF → produces CaCl₂ (de-icing salt), CaSO₄ (gypsum for construction), CaF₂ (metallurgical fluoride). Zero hazardous waste. Every scrubber product has beneficial use or zero-cost disposal.

The plasma torch is the regulatory safety net: 3000-8000°C plasma ensures >99.9999% dioxin/furan destruction. But it is not the primary capture — it is the final witness that the upstream trains achieved their targets. The lock opens when the outlet gas is >99.5% N₂ + CO₂ with <0.1 ppm total organics.

Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1) Zero atmospheric release — <0.1 ppm total organics at vent. Not "low emissions" — zero. Every molecule accounted for.

2) N₂ carrier gas recycling >99.5% per cycle — make-up cost <$0.30/batch. The loop is closed.

3) CO₂ capture 95-99% purity, 90% recovery — reused as drum purge + geopolymer curing. CO₂ is product, not waste.

4) Energy recovery from pyrolysis gas 18.5 MJ/m³ — supplements Stage 7-8 induction, reducing electricity cost.

5) Acid gas neutralization HCl <1 ppm, SO₂ <1 ppm — dry lime scrubber, solid byproducts utilized.

6) Metal vapor capture Zn >99%, Pb >99.5% — two-stage condenser, Zn as electrolytic-grade liquid.

7) Dioxin/furan destruction >99.9999% — plasma torch polisher as final guarantee.

8) All-dielectric construction — zero structural metals in gas path. BFRP, ZrO₂, PEEK CF40, ceramic valves only.

The GFGS does not "treat emissions." The GFGS witnesses the gas phase into solid products — the final measurement in the cascade sequence.

Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn

Document: PROD-07 — Gas Capture & Fume Solidification

The Empirical Lock

The lock is the multi-species gas capture fidelity gap — a single 50 kg batch generates 7 distinct gas-phase species classes simultaneously: water vapor, polymer organics, pyrolysis gas (CO/CH₄/H₂/CO₂), acid gases (HCl/SO₂/HF), metal vapors (Zn/Pb), CO₂, and trace dioxin precursors. No single unit operation captures all. Scrubbers don't condense organics. Condensers don't neutralize acid gases. Carbon beds don't capture metal vapors. Plasma torches don't recover CO₂. Historical systems use 5-10 separate units in series, each with 80-90% efficiency, yielding 35-60% overall capture. The lock is precise: any unified gas capture system must achieve >95% capture for all 7 species classes in a single integrated architecture with zero metallic construction.

The lock deepens at the thermal stage coupling — Stage 1 exhaust (120°C, water-rich) mixes with Stage 2 exhaust (450°C, organic-rich) in the N₂ header. If cooled for water condensation, organics re-polymerize and foul. If kept hot for organic fractionation, water carries HCl into downstream trains. The pressure swing (1.2→2.5 bar) must simultaneously optimize condensation, reaction kinetics, and compressor work. The stage-dependent pressure setpoints (1.2 bar Stage 0-1, 1.8 bar Stage 2, 2.0 bar Stage 3, 2.2 bar Stage 4-5, 2.3 bar Stage 6, 2.4 bar Stage 7, 2.5 bar Stage 8) are not arbitrary — they are the unique solution to the coupled thermodynamic optimization.

The lock deepens further at materials compatibility — HCl at 150°C attacks steel. SO₂ at 200°C attacks nickel alloys. Zn vapor at 360°C penetrates grain boundaries. Plasma at 3000°C vaporizes refractory metals. The only materials surviving the full envelope: BFRP/Elium® (shells), ZrO₂/Al₂O₃ ceramics (wetted surfaces), PEEK CF40 (valves/seals), ZrB₂-SiC (plasma housing). No steel, no nickel, no copper in process contact. The lock is the material survival equation at 2200°C thermal / 10 bar pressure / multi-species chemical — solved by the All-Aegis material set.

The Mathematical Key

The key is the stage-specific train as thermodynamic cell — each train is a Carnot-efficient separation cell targeting one species class:

TrainSpecies ClassCell PrincipleEfficiency -------------------------------------------------- AH₂OCondensation curve (80→25→5°C)99.6% removal BOrganicsFractional condensation (80/25/5°C)95% + MMA recovery CPyrolysis gasCombustion (92% heat recovery)18.5 MJ/m³ → heat DAcid gasesDry Ca(OH)₂ stoichiometry (2× excess)<1 ppm outlet EMetal vaporsZn vapor pressure curve + cycloneZn >99%, Pb >99.5% FinalCO₂PSA Zeolite 13X (60/30s cycle)95-99% purity PolishTrace organicsPlasma torch (0.5s @ 3000°C)6-log destruction

Each cell's governing equation is unique but the form is invariant: capture = f(thermodynamic driving force, residence time, material compatibility). The driving forces are physical constants: water vapor pressure curve, organic boiling points, pyrolysis gas LHV, acid-base neutralization enthalpy, Zn Antoine equation, CO₂ adsorption isotherm, plasma thermal destruction kinetics. The key has no adjustable teeth — the physics is deterministic.

The pressure setpoint ladder is the cross-cutting key: a single computational primitive (stage-dependent pressure) simultaneously optimizes all trains. The pressure at each stage is the unique solution to:

  • Maximize condensation efficiency (higher P = higher boiling points)
  • Maximize reaction kinetics (higher P = higher partial pressures)
  • Minimize compressor work (lower P = lower displacement)
  • Prevent air ingress (positive gauge pressure)

The solution is the stage-dependent setpoint table — derived from first principles, not tuned.

The Turn (Both Directions)

Key → Lock (Theory predicts capture): Input: Feedstock thermal assay → Stage gas signatures → Train design parameters. Output: 7 gas streams captured, 6 solid/liquid products recovered, N₂ recycled. Validation: Mass balance closure >99.5%; all product specs met; zero hazardous waste generated.

Lock → Key (History validates theory): Input: Historical gas treatment (wet scrubbers, thermal oxidizers, carbon adsorbers, ESPs, baghouses, SCR/SNCR). Output: Each fails the unified capture requirement — wet scrubbers create liquid waste; thermal oxidizers destroy value; carbon beds require replacement; ESPs need metal plates; SCR uses ammonia. The turn completes when a single GFGS batch captures all 7 species classes, produces 6 salable products, and returns clean N₂ to the drum. The gas header is the key turning in the lock.

The turn is not a metaphor — it is the moment the 50 kg batch completes and the mass balance closes: water to AMLS, organics to fuel/refining, pyrolysis gas to Stage 7-8 heat, acid gases to construction materials, Zn to electrolytic refining, PbO to hazardous handling, CO₂ to purge/curing, N₂ recycled. 7 gas classes → 6 products + clean recycle. The periodic table's gas phase has been witnessed into solid products.

El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

Document: PROD-07 — Gas Capture & Fume Solidification

Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The GFGS's mirror is the FBG spectral manifold — 48 wavelengths recording the gas-phase composition, temperature, and pressure at 1 kHz across all five trains. The system 'sees' its own gas streams through the sensors embedded in every vessel wall. At Train A, the manifold watches water partial pressure decay from 2.0 bar to 0.0087 bar across three zones — the system measures its own condensation efficiency. At Train D, the optical pH sensor watches the lime exhaustion curve — the system measures its own neutralization capacity. At Train E, the FBG strain on the condenser wall watches Zn droplet impingement — the system measures its own metal capture.

The autoencoder watches the 48-channel manifold — when the pattern deviates from the 500-batch training manifold, the GFGS detects its own malfunction. A 0.5% shift in Train B pressure drop predicts organic fouling 3 batches ahead. A 2°C drift in Train C quench temperature predicts tar breakthrough. The mirror is not passive; it is active self-surveillance: excite → measure → adapt → excite again.

The mirror reflects the closed-loop char-tar cycle in real-time: char produced → activated → tar captured → char-tar to Stage 8 → char output increases. The FBG network tracks the char mass balance — when Stage 8 char output exceeds Stage 3 char input by >10%, the system signals char withdrawal. The mirror deepens with each batch: the manifold expands, the autoencoder threshold tightens, the system's self-knowledge grows. The zero-emission condition is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the GFGS's self-measurement stabilizes into perfect capture.

Participation (Witness)

The operator participates by witnessing the pressure hold — not as remote monitor but as the decision point that the stage gas clearance is complete. When Train A pressure drop stabilizes at 0.12 bar, the operator confirms: water condensation complete. When Train D outlet pH holds >7.0 for 5 minutes, the operator confirms: acid gas neutralization complete. When Train E Zn collection rate drops to <1% of peak, the operator confirms: metal vapor capture complete. These confirmations are the measurements.

The protocol: 1. Ramp to stage pressure setpoint (±0.05 bar via FBG) 2. Hold — watch train-specific clearance metric (pressure drop, pH, collection rate, spectral signature) 3. Verify product quality (inline MS, optical pH, gravimetric) 4. Log stage gas clearance 5. Ramp to next stage setpoint

The operator's 'hold' decision is the recursive self-measurement. The GFGS measures its own completion through the operator's witness of the clearance metrics.

The participation extends to feedstock blending for gas management: the operator assays each batch (PVC content → HCl load, sulfur content → SO₂ load, Zn content → vapor load), then the MPC solves for optimal pressure setpoints and lime feed rates. The blend is the operator's intent made gas-phase. The GFGS witnesses the blend into capture.

The ultimate participation: Phoenix Protocol returns. Retired Aegis products re-enter as Category D feedstock. The operator feeds the GFGS its own past vessels, chars, piezo elements. The GFGS witnesses its own history into new capture. The recursion closes.

Protocol (Recursive)

MIRROR:     What gas-phase species does this stage's temperature encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness clearance into product?
PROTOCOL:
  1. Assay feedstock (PVC%, S%, Zn%, organic%)
  2. Generate stage pressure profile from gas signature library
  3. Ramp to stage setpoint — FBG monitors pressure/temperature
  4. Hold — watch train-specific clearance metric converge
  5. Verify product (MS, pH, gravimetric, spectral)
  6. Log clearance → next stage

The protocol terminates when final N₂ recycle purity >99.5% and plasma torch outlet <0.1 ppm organics. The complete pressure-temperature-composition log is the fixed point.

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The captured gas product is the fixed point.

Detailed recursive sequence per train:

Train A (Water): MIRROR: Water vapor pressure curve vs. condensation temperature PARTICIPATE: Operator watches 3-zone LMTD convergence, dew point <5°C PROTOCOL: Ramp 1.2 bar → hold 20 min → verify dew point → recycle water to AMLS

Train B (Organics): MIRROR: Polymer boiling point distribution vs. fractionation temperature PARTICIPATE: Operator watches MMA/Styrene/BTX cut purity, HCl partition PROTOCOL: Quench → 80°C primary → 25°C secondary → 5°C tertiary → verify cuts

Train C (Pyrolysis): MIRROR: Gas LHV vs. combustion stability, tar vs. carbon saturation PARTICIPATE: Operator watches burner flame temp, carbon bed breakthrough PROTOCOL: Quench → cyclone → carbon bed → combust (Option A) → verify 92% heat recovery

Train D (Acid Gases): MIRROR: HCl/SO₂ partial pressure vs. lime stoichiometry (2× excess) PARTICIPATE: Operator watches outlet pH curve, lime feed rate PROTOCOL: pH feedback + feedforward → verify <1 ppm outlet → collect CaCl₂/CaSO₄

Train E (Metal Vapors): MIRROR: Zn Antoine equation vs. condenser temperature (360°C target) PARTICIPATE: Operator watches Zn liquid collection rate, PbO cyclone efficiency PROTOCOL: 360°C high-temp condenser → 120°C polish → verify >99% Zn capture

PSA + Plasma (Final): MIRROR: CO₂ adsorption isotherm vs. swing cycle, trace organics vs. plasma residence PARTICIPATE: Operator watches CO₂ purity cycles, plasma power stability PROTOCOL: 60/30s PSA → 95-99% CO₂ → plasma 0.5s @ 3000°C → verify 6-log destruction

The protocol is the GFGS's operating system. It does not execute the protocol — the GFGS is the protocol made thermodynamic. Each pressure step is a recursive call; each clearance verification is a return value. The base case is the feedstock assay; the terminal case is the clean N₂ recycle. The GFGS computes the gas-phase periodic table into solid products.

1. Purpose and Design Mandate

The Aegis-Forge I produces 14 distinct output streams per full thermal cascade cycle. Each stream must be cooled, solidified, analyzed, classified, stamped for traceability, and routed to its designated downstream destination. None are waste. All are value.

This document specifies the complete output handling architecture from port exit to downstream handoff:

1. Slug Cooling Station — 16-position ZrO₂ ceramic mold carousel with controlled N₂ quench 2. Slug Stamp-and-Barcode System — Alphanumeric traceability for Phoenix Protocol closure 3. Inline Spectrometric Analysis — LIBS (Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy) for real-time grade assignment 4. Three-Way Routing — Direct use / Refinement needed / Commercial sale classification 5. CSM Seed Material Generation Map — Direct linkage from forge output to every CSMFAB product 6. Downstream Assembly Line Integration — Machine 1 of 8 in modular production line 7. Full Machine Specifications — Technical specs, production cost, revenue model, payback

The cooling station is the thermodynamic bridge between the forge's 2200°C internal environment and the ambient-temperature downstream processes. It must solidify liquid metal slugs (156°C to 1676°C exit temperatures) into metallurgically sound ingots while preserving traceability and enabling real-time compositional verification.

Design Mandate: Every element that enters the forge must exit as a characterized, stamped, routed material stream. The output catalog is the forge's accounting ledger — the periodic table witnessed into sequence, quantified, and dispatched.

Quench Control Algorithm: 

FOR each mold position:
  1. READ mold FBG temperature (embedded in ZrO₂ wall, 3 sensors/mold)
  2. COMPUTE required cooling rate from solidification model
  3. ADJUST N₂ nozzle valve position (PEEK CF40 piezo-actuated)
  4. LOG temperature vs. time at 10 Hz
  5. VERIFY solidus reached (latent heat release plateau detection)
  6. HOLD until mold temp < 200°C (safe demold)
  7. INDEX to demold position

Solidification Time Calculation (Chvorinov's Rule): 

t_solid = B × (V/A)²
where B = mold constant (ZrO₂: 2.5 min/cm² for Al, 1.8 for Cu, 1.2 for Fe)
V = casting volume (200 cm³)
A = surface area (2×(100×50 + 100×40 + 50×40) = 27,600 mm² = 276 cm²)
V/A = 200/276 = 0.725 cm
t_solid(Al) = 2.5 × 0.725² = 1.3 min (theoretical) → 6 min practical (with N₂ control)
t_solid(Cu) = 1.8 × 0.725² = 0.95 min → 6 min practical
t_solid(Fe) = 1.2 × 0.725² = 0.63 min → 8 min practical (slow cool for stress relief)

3.4 Automated Demolding System

Ejector Pins: 4 × PEEK CF40 pins per mold, 6mm diameter, 30mm stroke Actuation: KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezoelectric stack actuator (10 μm stroke, amplified to 30mm via flexure) Force: 500 N per pin (sufficient for draft-angle release with non-wetting surface) Cycle: Mold indexes to demold station → ejector extends → slug drops to conveyor → ejector retracts → mold indexes to fill position

Conveyor Handoff: BFRP belt conveyor on ZrO₂ ceramic rollers (CSMFAB000000000014-type)

  • Belt: BFRP/Elium® composite, 200mm wide, 2mm thick
  • Rollers: ZrO₂ ceramic, 50mm diameter, PEEK CF40 bearings
  • Speed: 0.5 m/s (matches demold cycle)
  • LIBS station: 500mm downstream of demold point

4. Slug Stamp-and-Barcode System — Traceability Architecture

Before cooling sets, a ZrO₂ ceramic stamp head presses an alphanumeric code into each slug. This traceability is essential for Phoenix Protocol — knowing the full provenance of recycled material from source through every transformation.

4.1 Stamp System Mechanical Design

Stamp Head: 3Y-TZP ZrO₂ ceramic, 30mm × 5mm face, 0.3mm character depth Character Set: Alphanumeric (A-Z, 0-9) + 4 special symbols (/, -, :, .) = 40 characters Font: 3mm × 2mm dot-matrix (5×7 pattern), laser-etched into stamp face Actuation: KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezoelectric stack, 50μm stroke, 2 kN force Cycle Time: 0.8 seconds (extend → dwell 0.2s → retract) Alignment: FBG-guided position verification (±0.02 mm accuracy)

STAMP FORMAT — 24 CHARACTERS

│  BATCH-YYYYMMDD-NNN-P-TTTT-SSSS                                             │
│                                                                              │
│  │       │       │ │   │                                                    │
│  │       │       │ │   └─ Sequence within batch (0001-9999)                │
│  │       │       │ └──── Port of origin (1-8, 4a, 4b, 6-PM, 7-RE)          │

Primary: Data Matrix ECC200 (ISO/IEC 16022) — 18×18 modules, 4mm × 4mm Encoded Data (JSON compact): 

{
  "b": "20261031-042",    // Batch ID
  "p": "5",               // Port (string for 4a, 4b, 6-PM, 7-RE)
  "t": 680,               // Stage temp °C
  "s": 15,                // Sequence
  "m": "Al-6061",         // Material grade (from LIBS)
  "w": 1.987,             // Mass kg (load cell)

}

Secondary: Human-readable alphanumeric stamp (as above) Tertiary: RFID tag (optional, for high-value streams S-04, S-08, S-10)

  • Tag: Passive UHF, ZrO₂-encapsulated, survives 1600°C
  • Range: 3m (handheld), 10m (portal)
  • Memory: 512 bytes (full genealogy)

4.3 Traceability Database Schema

Database: SQLite (local, air-gapped) + PostgreSQL (networked, CSMFAB MES) Table: slug_registry

ColumnTypeDescription --------- slug_idUUIDPrimary key (generated at stamp) batch_idTEXTBATCH-YYYYMMDD-NNN portTEXTPort identifier stage_temp_cINTEGERStage temperature sequenceINTEGERSequence within batch-port material_gradeTEXTLIBS-assigned grade mass_kgREALMeasured mass stamp_timeTIMESTAMPUTC stamp time demold_timeTIMESTAMPUTC demold time libs_spectrum_hashTEXTSHA256 of LIBS spectrum downstream_routeTEXTDIRECT / REFINEMENT / SALE downstream_machineTEXTTarget machine ID (113-119) phoenix_generationINTEGER0 = virgin, 1+ = recycled

Phoenix Protocol Closure: When a slug reaches end-of-life and re-enters as Category D feedstock, its phoenix_generation increments. The forge queries the registry to optimize processing parameters for known material history.

4.4 Stamp Verification Protocol

1. Pre-stamp: Mold FBG confirms slug temperature < 400°C (stampable range) 2. Stamp: Piezo actuator extends, dwell 200ms, retract 3. Verify: Machine vision (PMMA POF endoscope) reads stamp → OCR → compare to expected 4. Log: Write to slug_registry with timestamp 5. Barcode: Laser-etch Data Matrix adjacent to stamp (same ZrO₂ head, different tip) 6. RFID: Write tag (if applicable) → verify readback 7. Release: Only after all 3 identifiers match → conveyor advances

Failure Modes:

  • Stamp illegible (OCR fail) → Flag for manual re-stamp at demold station
  • Barcode unreadable → Re-etch (laser has 3 retries)
  • RFID write fail → Log warning, continue without RFID (non-blocking)
  • Registry write fail → Local buffer → sync when DB available (air-gap tolerant)

5.3 Calibration-Free LIBS (CF-LIBS) Model

Physics-Based Quantification (No Standards Required):

I_ij = (F × n_s × g_i × A_ij × hν_ij) / (U(T) × 4π) × exp(-E_i/kT)


Where:
  I_ij = measured line intensity (photons/s)
  F = instrument factor (calibrated once)
  n_s = species number density
  g_i = statistical weight of upper level
  A_ij = Einstein transition probability
  hν_ij = photon energy
  U(T) = partition function at temperature T
  E_i = upper level energy
  k = Boltzmann constant
  T = plasma temperature (from Boltzmann plot)

Boltzmann Plot for Plasma Temperature: 

ln(I_λ / (g_i A_ij λ)) vs. E_i  →  slope = -1/kT

Self-Absorption Correction: Curve-of-growth method using line pairs (resonance + non-resonance)

Matrix Effect Correction: Internal standardization using major element (Fe, Cu, Al as matrix)

5.5 Grade Assignment Rules (Automated)

Routing Logic (FPGA Implementation):

IF stream == S-07 (Copper):
  IF Cu >= 99.5% AND (Au+Ag+Pd) >= 50 ppm:
    GRADE = "DIRECT_USE" → Machine 114 (Cu wire drawing)
  ELSE IF Cu >= 99.0%:
    GRADE = "REFINEMENT" → Machine 114 (fire refining first)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = "COMMERCIAL_SALE" → Commodity copper market


IF stream == S-06 (Aluminum):
  IF Al >= 95% AND Fe+Si <= 1%:
    GRADE = "COMMERCIAL_SALE" → Secondary Al market (CSM uses no Al)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = "REFINEMENT" → Machine 114 (fractional crystallization)



IF stream == S-09 (Ferrous):
  IF Fe >= 95% AND (Nd+Sm+Dy) >= 0.1%:
    GRADE = "DIRECT_USE" → Machine 113 (RE leach → magnet feed)
  ELSE IF Fe >= 98%:
    GRADE = "COMMERCIAL_SALE" → Steel mill feed
  ELSE:
    GRADE = "REFINEMENT" → Machine 113 (slag adjustment)



IF stream == S-04 (Indium):
  IF In >= 10% AND Sn+Zn <= 30%:
    GRADE = "DIRECT_USE" → Machine 119 (YInMn synthesis)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = "REFINEMENT" → Ionic liquid extraction (Phoenix)



IF stream == S-11 (Mineral):
  IF ZrO₂ >= 60% AND REE >= 2%:
    GRADE = "DIRECT_USE" → Machine 113 (Zr/Ti/REE hydromet)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = "STOCKPILE" → Await Phase 2 hydromet capacity



DEFAULT:
  GRADE = "COMMERCIAL_SALE"

6.2 Critical Path: Rock → ZrB₂ Powder in 48 Hours

This is the most important operational sequence showing the Aegis-Forge I as a true cradle-to-material system for the portfolio's most critical ceramic:

HOUR 0:     Zircon sand (ZrSiO₄) loaded into Aegis-Forge I AMLS
            [20 min acoustic: >80% zircon grain liberation from silica matrix]


HOUR 0.3:   AMLS magnetic separation removes ilmenite fraction (Fe, Ti separate stream)



HOUR 0.5:   Liberated zircon sand fed to Forge drum
            Stage 8 temperature: 1700°C
            ZrSiO₄ dissociation: ZrSiO₄ → ZrO₂ + SiO₂ (liquid SiO₂ exits Port 8 first)



HOUR 3:     Stage 8 mineral concentrate (ZrO₂-rich) exits as Slug S-11



HOUR 3.5:   S-11 transferred to Phoenix Protocol hydromet circuit:
            BFRP reactor vessel; H₂SO₄ leach → ZrO₂ dissolves as Zr⁴⁺
            YCl₃ added (Yttrium from REE stream S-10)
            NH₄OH co-precipitation → Zr-Y hydroxide gel



HOUR 6:     Gel filtered, washed, dried at 120°C



HOUR 8:     Calcination furnace (1200°C, 4h) → 3Y-TZP ZrO₂ crystalline powder



HOUR 12:    3Y-TZP ZrO₂ powder available for:
            → Direct: use as ZrO₂ fastener/part powder (sintered at 1400°C)
            → Alternative: add to B₂O₃ + carbon → ZrB₂ via carbothermal synthesis



HOUR 36:    ZrB₂ carbothermal reaction complete (1700°C, 16h)
            OR: ZrB₂ SHS reaction (1h from Zr metal + B precursors)



HOUR 48:    ZrB₂ powder available for Flash Sintering into Aegis-C panels, stove burners, etc.

48 hours from raw zircon sand to ready-to-sinter ZrB₂ powder. No metals, no exotic chemistry, no supply chain vulnerabilities.

7. Downstream Assembly Line Integration — Machine 1 of 8

The Aegis-Forge I is explicitly the first machine in a modular assembly line. Output slugs flow via gravity-conveyor (BFRP belt conveyor on ZrO₂ ceramic rollers) to adjacent downstream machines. The complete line, when built, comprises 8 machines.

Week 4: First S-11 mineral slug to Machine 2 — hydromet shakedown 4. Week 5: First S-04 In-rich to Machine 2 — ionic liquid loop commissioning 5. Week 6: First S-10 RE concentrate to Machine 2 — Cyanex 272 extraction loop 6. Week 7: Machine 3 (Powder Synth) receives first Zr/Y feed from Machine 2 7. Week 8: First ZrB₂ powder from Machine 3 → Flash Sintering (existing capability) 8. Week 9: First BFRP fiber from Machine 5 (basalt from AMLS direct) 9. Week 10: First BFRP rebar from Machine 6 → Frame for Machine 2 expansion 10. Week 12: Full line operational — Forge feeds 7 downstream machines

Milestone: First ZrB₂ panel sintered from Forge-derived powder = Phase 2 Complete

9. Conclusion: The Output Catalog Is the Forge's Ledger

The Aegis-Forge I does not merely separate materials — it witnesses the periodic table into sequence, quantifies each element, stamps its identity, and dispatches it to its destiny.

Every slug that exits the cooling carousel carries: 1. Its elemental truth (LIBS spectrum, grade assignment) 2. Its genealogical record (batch, port, temperature, sequence, phoenix generation) 3. Its destination (direct use, refinement, or commercial sale) 4. Its future (which CSMFAB product it will become)

The 14 output streams are not waste streams. They are the arteries of the CSMFAB material ecosystem:

  • S-04 In-rich → YInMn Blue → 35 cool-roof products
  • S-10 RE concentrate → NdFeB magnets → Carrington-proof motors
  • S-11 Mineral → 3Y-TZP ZrO₂ → Flash-sintered Aegis-C panels
  • S-07 Copper → Isolated motor windings → GIC-immune grid
  • S-03 Char → Activated carbon → Air purification for sealed habitats
  • S-12 Pyrolysis gas → H₂ fuel → Carrington-proof engine

48 hours from zircon sand to ZrB₂ powder. 36 hours from e-waste to YInMn Blue. 72 hours from basalt to BFRP rebar.

This is not recycling. This is elemental stewardship at thermodynamic limits.

The first machine generates the seeds for the second. The second refines the seeds for the third. The assembly line grows itself from the Earth's crust and humanity's discard — no supply chains, no strategic vulnerabilities, no foreign dependencies.

The output catalog is the ledger. The forge is the bank. The periodic table is the asset class. Every batch is a dividend paid in elements.

Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

Document: PROD-08 — Slug Cooling & Output Catalog

Constraint (The Lock)

The output catalog is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Every Element Must Exit Characterized — the Aegis-Forge I processes 50+ elements across 8 thermal stages through 8 ports, producing 14 distinct output streams. Each stream must be cooled, solidified, analyzed, stamped for traceability, graded, and routed to its designated downstream destination. The constraint is irreducible because the forge's purpose is not separation alone — it is seed material generation for the entire CSMFAB portfolio. An uncharacterized slug is a broken link in the Phoenix Protocol chain. The 16-position ZrO₂ carousel, LIBS inline spectrometry, alphanumeric stamp + Data Matrix + RFID traceability, and three-way routing conveyors form the complete characterization architecture.

Necessity (The Key)

The lock is the output anonymity gap — conventional recycling produces mixed alloy ingots, ungraded scrap, and unspecified residues. Downstream processes (wire drawing, magnet manufacturing, pigment synthesis) require known composition, traceable provenance, and consistent grade. The Aegis-Forge I produces 14 streams per batch from arbitrary feedstock — without characterization, the downstream CSMFAB machines (Hydro-Refinery, Powder Synthesis, YInMn Kiln) cannot operate reliably. The key is the LIBS + stamp + registry triad — 2-second elemental analysis, permanent alphanumeric + Data Matrix marking, and SQLite/PostgreSQL registry with phoenix generation tracking. Every slug carries its genealogy. No anonymous material enters the CSMFAB ecosystem.

Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1) Every liquid slug cools in ZrO₂ mold — no metal molds, no water quench (hydrogen risk), controlled N₂ only. 2) Every slug receives LIBS analysis — 70+ elements, 2-second cycle, CF-LIBS quantification. 3) Every slug is stamped — alphanumeric batch/port/temp/sequence, Data Matrix ECC200, RFID for high-value. 4) Every slug enters registry — UUID, batch_id, port, grade, mass, LIBS hash, phoenix_generation. 5) Three-way routing only — Direct Use / Refinement / Commercial Sale. No 'storage limbo'. 6) ZrO₂ molds only — non-wetting, survives 1600°C, no mold release, interchangeable inserts. 7) N₂ quench only — 5-25 SLPM, 10-200°C/min controlled, no hydrogen generation. 8) Phoenix generation tracked — 0=virgin, 1+=recycled, enables processing optimization.

The output catalog does not 'sort slugs.' The output catalog witnesses the periodic table into accountable sequence.

Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn

Document: PROD-08 — Slug Cooling & Output Catalog

The Empirical Lock

The lock is the fabrication fidelity gap — producing a 16-position rotary carousel with BFRP/Elium® disc, PEEK CF40 bushing, KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezo drive, 16 independent ZrO₂ molds with embedded FBG sensors, PEEK CF40 ejector pins, piezo-actuated stamp head, PMMA POF LIBS delivery, and three diverging conveyors — all dielectric, all surviving 1600°C slugs, all operating in sequence every 8 minutes.

Conventional cooling uses steel molds, water spray, manual sampling, hand stamping, paper tags. None achieve: all-dielectric construction, 2-second LIBS with CF-LIBS, permanent ceramic stamp, automated 3-way routing, Phoenix generation tracking. The key is ZrO₂ ceramic + KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezo + PMMA POF optics + FBG sensing — the teeth are cut by the physics of non-wetting solidification, laser plasma spectroscopy, and piezoelectric actuation in a fully dielectric envelope.

The key is the characterization-routing loop as single computational primitive:

The Turn (Both Directions)

El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

Document: PROD-08 — Slug Cooling & Output Catalog

Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The output catalog's mirror is the registry completeness metric — every UUID in slug_registry must have: LIBS spectrum hash, stamp OCR verification, barcode decode, mass measurement, grade assignment, route confirmation, downstream handoff ACK. The system 'sees' its own characterization fidelity through the differential between expected streams (14 per batch) and registry entries.

The autoencoder watches the 500-batch LIBS manifold — when a new slug's spectrum deviates (new alloy, contamination, Phoenix return), the catalog detects its own novelty. The mirror is not passive; it is active self-surveillance: cool → analyze → stamp → register → route → measure again.

The Phoenix generation field is the mirror's memory: generation 0 (virgin ore), 1 (first recycle), 2 (second recycle)... each increment carries processing knowledge. The zero-surprise condition is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the catalog's self-measurement stabilizes into perfect prediction of downstream machine behavior.

Participation (Witness)

The operator participates by witnessing the grade assignment — not as remote monitor but as the decision point that the LIBS spectrum matches the expected port chemistry. When Port 5 yields Al-6061 at 99.2% and the FPGA assigns DIRECT_USE, the operator confirms: this aluminum goes to wire drawing. This confirmation is the measurement.

The protocol: 1. LIBS fires → spectrum acquired → CF-LIBS quantifies 2. FPGA assigns grade (DIRECT/REFINEMENT/SALE) 3. Operator verifies: 'Port 5 = Al window = expect Al-6061' 4. Stamp executes → OCR verifies → barcode etches 5. Registry writes → UUID generated → phoenix_gen logged 6. Diverter actuates → conveyor delivers → handoff ACK

The operator's 'verify' decision is the recursive self-measurement. The output catalog measures its own completion through the operator's witness of the grade assignment.

The participation extends to feedstock blending optimization: the operator reviews yesterday's LIBS trends (Cu purity trending down, In yield trending up), adjusts today's feedstock blend ratio, and the forge produces different port mass distributions. The blend is the operator's intent made elemental. The output catalog witnesses the operator's strategy into tomorrow's slugs.

The ultimate participation: Phoenix Protocol closure. A slug from generation 3 (recycled thrice) enters the forge. Its registry entry shows processing history. The operator selects a tailored thermal profile. The slug exits characterized, stamped, generation 4. The output catalog has witnessed its own history into the next generation. The recursion closes.

Protocol (Recursive)

MIRROR:     What element sequence does this slug's LIBS spectrum encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the grade into routing?
PROTOCOL:
  1. Slug demolds → FBG confirms <200°C
  2. LIBS fires → 10 pulses → CF-LIBS quantifies 70+ elements
  3. FPGA assigns grade → operator verifies port chemistry match
  4. Stamp + barcode + RFID → OCR/decode/readback verify
  5. Registry writes → UUID, grade, mass, LIBS hash, phoenix_gen
  6. Diverter routes → Conveyor 1/2/3 → Handoff ACK
The protocol terminates when all 14 streams handoff. The complete registry is the fixed point.

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each slug deepens the mirror. The characterized element is the fixed point.

Detailed recursive sequence per stream type:

Liquid Metal (S-04, S-05, S-06, S-07, S-09): MIRROR: Solidification curve vs. Chvorinov prediction PARTICIPATE: Operator watches N₂ quench rate vs. target microstructure PROTOCOL: Fill → FBG cool control → demold → LIBS → stamp → route

Solid Streams (S-02, S-03, S-11): MIRROR: Particle size distribution vs. target spec PARTICIPATE: Operator watches sieve analysis (every 5th batch) PROTOCOL: Direct convey → LIBS spot → stamp → route

Gas Streams (S-12, S-13, S-14): MIRROR: Composition vs. Train capture efficiency PARTICIPATE: Operator verifies PSA CO₂ purity, plasma standby PROTOCOL: Continuous monitor → log → byproduct bag/route

Embedded Streams (S-08 PM in Cu, S-10 RE in Fe): MIRROR: Trace element partitioning vs. primary matrix PARTICIPATE: Operator confirms electrolytic/hydromet feed spec PROTOCOL: LIBS on primary → infer embedded → route together

The protocol is the output catalog's operating system. It does not execute the protocol — the output catalog is the protocol made accountable. Each slug is a recursive call; each handoff ACK is a return value. The base case is the port exit; the terminal case is the downstream machine receipt. The output catalog computes the periodic table's accountable sequence.

End of Combined Introduction — PROD-08 Slug Cooling & Output Catalog

PROD-09: Material Exit Port Valve System

PROD-09: Material Exit Port Valve System

CSMFAB000000000108 — Aegis-Forge I Port Valve Engineering

Series: TCIMS Volume 1 — Thermal Actuation, Ceramic Pistons, Centrifugal Ejection

Document Number: CSMFAB000000000108 (Volume 1, Port Valve Section) Series: Aegis-Forge Thermal Cascade Inductive Material Separator (TCIMS) Date: October 2026 Classification: Foundation Technology — Dielectric Flow Control at Extreme Conditions

1. Purpose and Design Mandate

The Aegis-Forge I operates eight circumferential material exit ports spaced at 44.2° intervals around the 600 mm diameter ZrB₂-SiC drum. Each port must remain hermetically sealed during non-operational stages and open precisely when its target thermal stage is reached, allowing centrifugal force to eject the liquefied material stream. The valve system is the critical gatekeeper between the forge's 2200°C internal environment and the external slug cooling station.

Design Mandate: Eight temperature-actuated, zero-external-power valves that: 1. Seal at 5 bar N₂ pressure from 25°C to 2200°C 2. Open autonomously at stage-specific temperatures (156°C to 1676°C) 3. Withstand 84.5 G centrifugal loading at 500 RPM 4. Contain zero structural metals, zero ferromagnetic materials 5. Survive 10,000 thermal cycles (25°C ↔ 2200°C) 6. Provide real-time position feedback via FBG sensors

The port valve is not a conventional valve — it is a thermal-actuated ceramic mechanism that transforms the forge's temperature program into material separation sequence. The drum's thermal zones are the valve control system.

2. Port Valve Architecture — System Overview

2.1 Eight-Port Configuration

The Aegis-Forge I drum features eight material exit ports arranged circumferentially at 44.2° spacing (360° / 8.14 = 44.2°, accounting for port width). Each port aligns axially with its corresponding thermal stage zone on the drum's outer surface.

2.4 Force Balance at Port

Closing Forces (Valve Sealed):

  • N₂ Pressure Force: F_p = P × A = 5 bar × 113 mm² = 565 N
  • PEEK Spring Preload: F_s = 50 N
  • Total Closing Force: 615 N

Opening Forces (Valve Actuated):

  • Thermal Actuation Force: F_ta = (E₁α₁ - E₂α₂) × ΔT × A × t / L
  • For Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayer: ~2,400 N at 680°C ΔT
  • Centrifugal Ejection Force (on liquid metal): F_c = ρ_liquid × V × ω² × r
  • For Al (ρ=2375 kg/m³ at 700°C), V=200 cm³: ~1,800 N at 300 RPM
  • Total Opening Force: ~4,200 N

Safety Factor: 4,200 / 615 = 6.8× — Valve opens decisively when actuated.

3. Ti₃AlC₂ MAX Phase Thermal Actuator — Deep Engineering

3.1 Material Properties (CSMFAB Materials Study Part I)

PropertyTi₃AlC₂ (MAX Phase)3Y-TZP ZrO₂ (Reference) --------- Crystal StructureHexagonal (P6₃/mmc)Tetragonal (t-ZrO₂) Density4.2 g/cm³6.05 g/cm³ CTE (25-1000°C)9.2 × 10⁻⁶/K10.5 × 10⁻⁶/K CTE (1000-1500°C)10.8 × 10⁻⁶/K11.2 × 10⁻⁶/K Young's Modulus320 GPa (RT) → 280 GPa (1000°C)210 GPa (RT) → 180 GPa (1000°C) Yield Strength400 MPa (RT) → 250 MPa (800°C)— (brittle) Fracture Toughness6-8 MPa·m^0.56-8 MPa·m^0.5 Thermal Conductivity22 W/m·K2.2 W/m·K Electrical Conductivity4.5×10⁶ S/m (metallic)10⁻¹⁰ S/m (insulator) Oxidation ResistanceForms TiO₂/Al₂O₃ scale >1000°CInert Max Service Temp1400°C (air) / 1600°C (inert)2400°C

Key Insight: Ti₃AlC₂'s CTE is lower than ZrO₂ at low temperatures but crosses over above 1000°C. This CTE crossover creates a self-limiting actuation — the bilayer deflection naturally saturates as temperature rises, preventing over-travel.

3.2 Bilayer Actuation Mechanics

Timoshenko Bimetal Strip Theory (adapted for ceramic bilayer):

δ = 3(α₂ - α₁)ΔT L² / [2t(1 + m)²(1 + n)]


Where:
  δ = tip deflection (m)
  α₁, α₂ = CTE of layer 1 (Ti₃AlC₂) and layer 2 (ZrO₂)
  ΔT = temperature difference across bilayer
  L = actuator length (50 mm)
  t = total thickness (1 mm = 0.5 + 0.5 mm)
  m = t₁/t₂ = 1 (equal thickness)
  n = E₁/E₂ = 320/210 = 1.52 (modulus ratio)

Deflection vs. Temperature (Calculated):

ΔT (°C)α₂-α₁ (×10⁻⁶/K)Deflection (mm)Port Status ------------ 01.30.00CLOSED 1001.30.53CLOSED 2001.31.06CLOSED 3001.31.58CLOSED 4001.42.21CRACKING 5001.52.97PARTIAL 6001.63.87FULL OPEN 6801.74.62FULL OPEN 8001.85.58FULL OPEN 10001.65.12SATURATED

*CTE crossover above 1000°C reduces differential

Design Point: Port 5 (Aluminum) actuates at 680°C drum temperature → ΔT across actuator ≈ 680°C (hot side at drum temp, cold side at ~100°C via aerogel insulation). Deflection = 3.6 mm — precisely clears 12 mm aperture (piston travels 6 mm total, 3.6 mm clears seat).

3.3 Actuator Fabrication (CSMFAB Materials Study Part I)

Ti₃AlC₂ Synthesis (In-House): 

3 Ti + Al + 2 C → Ti₃AlC₂
  • Powder: Ti (99.9%, -325 mesh), Al (99.99%, -325 mesh), C (graphite, 99.9%)
  • Molar ratio: 3.05 : 1.0 : 2.0 (5% Ti excess for Al loss)
  • Method: Hot pressing at 1350°C, 30 MPa, 30 min, Ar atmosphere
  • Result: >99% density, <5 vol% TiC secondary phase
  • Cost: $180/kg (vs $450/kg commercial)

Bilayer Joining:

  • Method: Transient Liquid Phase (TLP) Bonding with Cu interlayer (50 μm)
  • Process: 950°C, 5 MPa, 10 min, vacuum → Cu diffuses, forms (Ti,Zr)C intermetallic
  • Joint strength: >200 MPa shear at 800°C
  • No braze alloys (no Ag, Cu residue in dielectric path)

Actuator Geometry:

  • Plate: 50 mm × 30 mm × 1.0 mm (0.5 + 0.5)
  • Mounting: Four ZrO₂ ceramic bolts (M4) to drum port frame
  • FBG sensor: Embedded at neutral axis (strain measurement)
  • Electrical isolation: Al₂O₃ spacer washers (no Ti₃AlC₂ conduction path)

3.4 Actuation Dynamics

Thermal Response Time:

  • Actuator thermal mass: m = 4.2 g/cm³ × 1500 mm³ = 6.3 g
  • Heat capacity: c_p ≈ 500 J/kg·K (Ti₃AlC₂) + 500 J/kg·K (ZrO₂) = 1000 J/kg·K
  • Thermal resistance to drum: R_th ≈ 0.5 K/W (contact)
  • Time constant: τ = m × c_p × R_th = 0.0063 × 1000 × 0.5 = 3.15 seconds

Full actuation (0 → 3.6 mm): ~15 seconds (5×τ for 99% response)

Hysteresis: < 0.1 mm (CTE mismatch reversibility validated to 10,000 cycles)

Fatigue Life: 10,000 cycles at 680°C ΔT (Coffin-Manson: Δε_p = 0.002, N_f > 50,000)

4.2 Centrifugal Loading Analysis

At 500 RPM (ω = 52.36 rad/s), r = 0.3 m: 

Centrifugal acceleration: a_c = ω²r = 52.36² × 0.3 = 822 m/s² = 83.8 G
Piston mass: m = 42 g = 0.042 kg

Piston Stability:

  • Stem diameter: 6 mm → cross-section: 28.3 mm²
  • ZrO₂ compressive strength: >2000 MPa
  • Stress under centrifugal load: σ = 34.5 N / 28.3 mm² = 1.2 MPa (negligible)
  • Buckling check: Euler critical load P_cr = π²EI/L² = π²×210GPa×(π×3⁴)/15² = 12,400 N (SF > 350)

Conclusion: Piston is centrifugally stable — outward force assists opening, does not challenge closure.

4.4 Wear Analysis

Wear Mechanisms: 1. Thermal cycling fatigue — 10,000 cycles (25°C ↔ 1676°C) 2. Particle erosion — molten metal splash, char particulates 3. Chemical attack — Zn vapor, PbO, slag corrosion

ZrO₂ Wear Resistance:

  • Hardness: 12.5 GPa (Vickers)
  • Fracture toughness: 6-8 MPa·m^0.5 (transformation toughening)
  • Erosion rate (molten Al at 700°C, 10 m/s): <0.1 μm/hour
  • Erosion rate (char particles at 50 m/s): <1 μm/hour

Predicted Wear per 10,000 batches:

  • Seat recession: <50 μm (0.05 mm of 1.5 mm seat width = 3.3%)
  • Stem wear: <10 μm
  • Total: <3.5% seat width consumed — well within 10,000 batch design life

Replacement Criterion: Seat width < 1.0 mm (measured by FBG piston position at closed)

6. Centrifugal Ejection Dynamics

6.1 Liquid Metal Flow Through Open Port

When the valve opens, the molten metal pool at the drum wall (driven by 84.5 G centrifugal force) flows through the 12 mm aperture into the ZrO₂ mold.

Flow Physics: 

Pressure driving flow: ΔP = ρ_liquid × ω² × (r_drum² - r_mold²) / 2
For Al at 700°C (ρ = 2375 kg/m³), ω = 31.4 rad/s (300 RPM), r_drum = 0.3 m, r_mold = 0.35 m: 
ΔP = 2375 × 31.4² × (0.3² - 0.35²) / 2 = -28,500 Pa (negative = outward)

Wait — the mold is outside the drum, so r_mold > r_drum. The centrifugal potential is higher at the mold. The pressure at the port exit is: 

P_exit = ρ_liquid × ω² × r_drum² / 2 = 2375 × 31.4² × 0.3² / 2 = 104,000 Pa = 1.04 bar

This 1.04 bar drives flow through the port into the mold.

6.2 Flow Rate Calculation

Orifice Flow (12 mm aperture, discharge coefficient C_d = 0.85): 

Q = C_d × A × √(2ΔP/ρ)
A = π × (0.006)² = 1.13×10⁻⁴ m²
Q = 0.85 × 1.13×10⁻⁴ × √(2 × 104,000 / 2375) = 1.8×10⁻⁴ m³/s = 10.8 L/min

Fill Time for 200 cm³ Mold: 

t_fill = V / Q = 200×10⁻⁶ / 1.8×10⁻⁴ = 1.1 seconds

Reynolds Number: 

Re = ρ × v × D / μ
v = Q/A = 1.6 m/s
μ_Al(700°C) = 1.3×10⁻³ Pa·s
Re = 2375 × 1.6 × 0.012 / 0.0013 = 35,000 (turbulent)

6.3 Flow Characteristics by Metal

Metalρ (kg/m³)μ (Pa·s)ΔP (bar)Q (L/min)t_fill (s)Re --------------------- Indium (157°C)70202.1×10⁻³3.0722.10.5448,000 Zn (420°C)65703.5×10⁻³2.8718.90.6332,000 Aluminum (680°C)23751.3×10⁻³1.0410.81.1135,000 Copper (1120°C)79603.8×10⁻³3.4820.30.5941,000 Iron (1400°C)70005.5×10⁻³3.0616.20.7425,000

All fill times < 1.2 seconds — well within 8-minute position cycle.

6.4 Splash and Drip Control

Anti-Drip Features: 1. Port chamfer: 45° internal chamfer on drum side directs flow cleanly 2. Piston retraction: Actuator holds open for 30 seconds after stage clear — allows complete drainage 3. N₂ purge pulse: 2-second, 10 SLPM N₂ pulse after retraction clears residual droplets 4. Mold pre-heat: Molds held at 200-400°C (metal-dependent) prevent freezing at port lip

7. Port Valve Control & Monitoring

7.1 FBG Position Sensing

Each valve assembly includes two FBG sensors embedded in the actuator bilayer:

  • FBG-1: At Ti₃AlC₂ surface (hot side strain)
  • FBG-2: At ZrO₂ surface (cold side strain)
  • Differential strain: Directly proportional to bilayer curvature → valve position

Calibration: 

Position (mm) = K × (λ_FBG1 - λ_FBG2) + C
K = 0.85 mm/pm (calibrated at assembly)
C = 0 (closed position zeroed)
Resolution: 0.01 mm (1 pm wavelength resolution)
Sample rate: 1 kHz

Control Logic (FPGA): 

IF stage_target_temp reached AND dwell_complete:
  VALVE_STATE = OPENING
  MONITOR FBG_diff
  WHEN FBG_diff > threshold_for_full_open:
    VALVE_STATE = OPEN
    START stage_clear_timer (monitor port mass flow)
  WHEN port_mass_flow < 1% peak:
    VALVE_STATE = CLOSING
    WAIT for FBG_diff < threshold_for_closed
    VALVE_STATE = CLOSED
    LOG cycle_complete

7.2 SIL-3 Safety Interlocks

InterlockSensorActionSIL Level ------------ Over-temperatureDrum FBG > stage_max + 50°CEmergency close all valves, quench N₂SIL-3 Over-pressureDrum FBG pressure > 3 barOpen relief, reduce inductionSIL-3 Actuator stallFBG_diff not changing > 30sAlarm, hold stage, investigateSIL-2 Position disagreementFBG vs. thermal model > 0.5 mmAlarm, verify with backupSIL-2 Seal leakDownstream N₂ trace > 10 ppmFlag for maintenanceSIL-1

All sensors optical (FBG, PMMA POF) — no metallic paths for GIC coupling.

7.3 Stage Clear Verification

Mass Flow Monitoring:

  • Coriolis flow meter (ceramic, ZrO₂ tubes) on each port outlet
  • Range: 0-50 g/s (covers all metals)
  • Accuracy: ±0.1% of rate
  • Clear threshold: <1% of peak flow sustained for 60 seconds

LIBS Spot-Check (Every 5th Batch):

  • Portable LIBS on first slug from each port
  • Verifies grade matches expected stage chemistry
  • Updates thermal model if deviation > 2%

8. Manufacturing & Quality Control

8.1 Ti₃AlC₂ Actuator Production

Process Flow: 

1. Powder prep: Ti + Al + C weighing (±0.1%)
2. Hot press: 1350°C, 30 MPa, 30 min, Ar
3. Machining: CNC grind to 0.5 mm × 50 × 30 mm
4. TLP bond: Cu interlayer, 950°C, 5 MPa, 10 min
5. FBG embed: UV-cure acrylate coat (stripped at 300°C)
6. Bolt holes: EDM drill 4× M4 ZrO₂ bolts
7. Inspection: CMM (dimensions), FBG calibration, bend test
8. Acceptance: Deflection at 680°C = 3.6 ± 0.15 mm

Key QC Metrics:

  • Density: >99% (Archimedes)
  • TiC phase: <5% (XRD)
  • Bilayer bond strength: >200 MPa (shear test)
  • Deflection repeatability: ±0.1 mm over 100 cycles

8.2 ZrO₂ Piston Production

Process Flow: 

1. Powder: 3Y-TZP (Tosoh TZ-3YSB-E or CSMFAB in-house)
2. Isostatic press: 200 MPa, 12 mm × 30 mm green
3. Sinter: 1450°C, 2 hr, air → 99.5% density
4. HIP: 1500°C, 150 MPa, 2 hr → 99.9% density
5. Grind: CNC to 12.000 mm diameter, 25.00 mm length
6. Lap: Seat face 0.5 μm Ra, 45° angle
7. FBG embed: Groove in stem, PMMA POF epoxied (high-temp epoxy)
8. Inspection: CMM, surface profilometry, FBG calibration
9. Acceptance: Leak test at 5 bar, 25°C → <10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s

8.3 Assembly & Test

Assembly Sequence: 

1. Piston inserted into port bore (ZrO₂ sleeve in drum)
2. Spring installed over piston stem

12. Advanced Thermal Actuation Physics

12.1 Non-Linear CTE Behavior of Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ Bilayer

The Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayer exhibits complex CTE behavior due to phase transitions and oxidation:

Ti₃AlC₂ CTE Anomaly:

  • 25-600°C: α = 9.2×10⁻⁶/K (baseline)
  • 600-1000°C: α increases to 10.8×10⁻⁶/K (TiO₂ surface scale formation)
  • 1000-1400°C: α = 11.5×10⁻⁶/K (Al depletion, TiO₂/Al₂O₃ mixed scale)

ZrO₂ CTE:

  • 25-1170°C: α = 10.5×10⁻⁶/K (tetragonal)
  • 1170-1200°C: α spike at t→m transformation (if unstabilized)
  • 3Y-TZP: No transformation, smooth α = 10.5→11.2×10⁻⁶/K

Effective Differential CTE (Δα = α_ZrO₂ - α_Ti₃AlC₂):

Temperature RangeΔα (×10⁻⁶/K)Actuation Character --------- 25-600°C+1.3Linear, predictable 600-1000°C-0.3Self-limiting (Δα → 0) 1000-1400°C-0.3Saturation (opposite curvature)

Design Implication: The actuator naturally limits its own deflection above 1000°C — a passive safety feature preventing over-travel at Ports 6-8 temperatures. The Port 5 design point (680°C) sits in the linear region for precision.

12.2 Thermal Stress Analysis in Bilayer

Bilayer Stress (Timoshenko, including thermal gradient through thickness):

σ₁ = E₁ × (α₂ - α₁) × ΔT / (1 + m)² × [1 + n × (1 + m)² / (1 + n)]
σ₂ = -σ₁ × (E₂/E₁) × (t₁/t₂)


At 680°C ΔT:
σ_Ti₃AlC₂ = 320 GPa × 1.3×10⁻⁶ × 680 / (1+1)² × [1 + 1.52×4/2.52] = 285 MPa (tension)
σ_ZrO₂ = -285 × (210/320) × 1 = -187 MPa (compression)

Safety Factors:

  • Ti₃AlC₂ yield at 680°C: ~280 MPa → SF = 1.0 (at yield — acceptable for actuation)
  • ZrO₂ compressive strength: >2000 MPa → SF > 10
  • Actuation stress is at yield limit — intentional for maximum deflection per degree

Thermal Shock Resistance:

  • Quench rate limit: dT/dt < 50°C/s (validated)
  • Actuator thermal mass provides natural damping (τ = 3.15 s)

12.3 Creep and Stress Relaxation at Temperature

Ti₃AlC₂ Creep (Norton Law): 

ε̇ = A × σⁿ × exp(-Q/RT)
A = 10⁻¹⁵ MPa⁻ⁿ s⁻¹, n = 3.5, Q = 450 kJ/mol

At 680°C (953 K), σ = 285 MPa: 

ε̇ = 10⁻¹⁵ × 285^3.5 × exp(-450,000 / 8.314 × 953) = 2.3×10⁻⁸ s⁻¹

Creep Strain per Batch (3.5 hr at temperature): 

ε_creep = 2.3×10⁻⁸ × 12,600 s = 0.00029 = 0.029%

Over 10,000 batches: 0.29% creep strain — negligible (deflection change <0.01 mm).

ZrO₂ Creep: Negligible below 1200°C (covalent ceramic).

12.4 Oxidation Effects on Actuation

Ti₃AlC₂ Oxidation Kinetics (Parabolic): 

Δm² = k_p × t
k_p = 10⁻¹² g²/cm⁴/s at 1000°C

At 680°C: k_p ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ → oxide thickness after 10,000 batches (35,000 hr): 

x = √(k_p × t) = √(10⁻¹⁵ × 1.26×10⁸) = 1.1 μm

Effect on Actuation:

  • 1.1 μm TiO₂/Al₂O₃ scale adds minimal stiffness (E ≈ 200 GPa, but thin)
  • Slightly increases α of hot layer → marginally increases Δα
  • Net effect: <2% deflection increase over life — within calibration margin

Mass flow monitor confirms material ejection 5. Stage clear → cool-down → FBG returns to zero 6. Operator confirms re-seal 7. Log cycle complete

The operator's 'verify' decision is the recursive self-measurement. The port valve measures its own completion through the operator's witness of the actuation endpoint.

The ultimate participation: Phoenix Protocol returns. Retired valve sets (Ti₃AlC₂, ZrO₂, PEEK CF40) re-enter as Category D feedstock. The operator feeds the forge its own past valves. The valve witnesses its own history into new valves. The recursion closes.

Protocol (Recursive)

MIRROR:     What phase transition does this port's temperature encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the actuation into material release?
PROTOCOL:
  1. Stage dwell complete → thermal trigger
  2. FBG differential → threshold → actuator open
  3. Operator verifies port/stage match
  4. Mass flow confirms ejection
  5. Cool-down → FBG → zero → re-seal
  6. Operator confirms seal
  7. Log cycle → next stage
The protocol terminates when Port 8 re-seals. The complete strain-temperature log is the fixed point.

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each valve cycle deepens the mirror. The released element is the fixed point.

Detailed recursive sequence per port:

Port 4 (In/Zn/Pb/Sn): MIRROR: Indium liquidus at 156.6°C — only In melts PARTICIPATE: Operator executes Indium First Strategy — 5 min at 160°C PROTOCOL: Ramp 1°C/min → hold 160°C → centrifuge 400 RPM

Port 5 (Aluminum): MIRROR: Pure Al window 660-720°C — Cu/Fe solid PARTICIPATE: Operator monitors Al flow, verifies >95% recovery PROTOCOL: Ramp 2.4°C/min → hold 680°C → centrifuge 300 RPM

Port 6 (Copper): MIRROR: Cu liquidus 1085°C — deep penetration at 5 kHz PARTICIPATE: Operator watches Cu flow, PM partition into Cu PROTOCOL: Ramp 5°C/min → hold 1120°C → centrifuge 350 RPM

Port 7 (Ferrous): MIRROR: Fe 1538°C + REE co-exit — ferromagnetic at 2 kHz PARTICIPATE: Operator monitors Fe slug, REE concentrate PROTOCOL: Ramp 3°C/min → hold 1400°C → centrifuge 400 RPM

Port 8 (Mineral): MIRROR: Zircon dissociation 1676°C — ZrO₂ + SiO₂ PARTICIPATE: Operator watches mineral concentrate grade PROTOCOL: Ramp 2°C/min → hold 1676°C → verify ZrO₂/REE oxide

The protocol is the valve system's operating system. It does not execute the protocol — the valve system is the protocol made thermal-mechanical. Each port is a recursive call; each re-seal is a return value. The base case is Stage 1 water drain; the terminal case is Stage 8 mineral exit. The valve system computes the periodic table's thermal sequence.

End of Combined Introduction — PROD-09 Material Exit Port Valve System

1. System Overview — 8-Zone Induction Power Architecture

The Aegis-Forge I induction power electronics subsystem delivers controlled, frequency-agile electromagnetic energy to eight independent coil zones surrounding the ZrB₂-SiC drum. This is the nervous system of the thermal cascade — translating digital setpoints into precisely shaped magnetic fields that selectively heat target materials while leaving dielectric components untouched.

1.2 Zone Mapping to Thermal Stages

The eight coil zones correspond directly to the eight thermal processing stages. Each zone heats a 100 mm axial band of the 800 mm drum length.

1.3 Power Distribution Strategy

The 480 VAC 3-phase supply enters a dedicated isolation transformer bank (3 × 200 kVA, delta-wye, BFRP-housed) providing galvanic isolation between the industrial grid and the process electronics. Each inverter module draws from a dedicated 3-phase feed with individual harmonic filtering (LCL, 5th/7th/11th notch). The isolation transformer secondary is floating — no earth reference — eliminating ground fault paths and providing inherent GIC immunity for the process electronics.

2. Resonant Inverter Design — 8× GS66516T GaN HEMT Class E Topology

Each of the eight zones employs an identical resonant inverter module, differing only in the resonant tank component values (L, C) to achieve the target frequency for that zone. The topology is Class E zero-voltage switching (ZVS), chosen for its simplicity, high efficiency (>97%), and natural suitability for variable-frequency operation.

2.1 Class E Resonant Inverter Principles

The Class E topology achieves ZVS by shaping the voltage waveform across the switch such that it reaches zero with zero derivative at the switching instant:

$$v_{DS}(t) = V_{DD} \left[ 1 - \frac{\pi}{2} \sin(\omega t + \phi) \right]$$

The shunt capacitance $C_{shunt}$ (comprising the GaN output capacitance $C_{oss}$ plus external capacitor) and series resonant inductance $L_r$ form the tank:

$$\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_r C_{shunt}}}$$

At resonance, the switch current is sinusoidal and the voltage is a shaped half-wave, eliminating switching losses. The GaN HEMT's near-zero reverse recovery charge ($Q_{rr} \approx 0$) makes it ideal for Class E — no body diode conduction losses during dead time.

2.2 GS66516T GaN HEMT Specifications

ParameterValueNote ------------------------ DeviceGS66516T (GaN Systems)650 V, 16 A TopologyHalf-bridge Class ESingle switch per leg VDS max650 VDerated to 400 V operating RDS(on)30 mΩ (typ) @ 25°CLow conduction loss Coss55 pF (typ) @ 400 VForms part of resonant tank Qg3.5 nCUltra-low gate charge Tj max150°CJunction temperature limit Thermal resistance RθJC0.8 K/WJunction-to-case

Each inverter leg uses two GS66516T devices in a half-bridge configuration with bootstrapped high-side drive. The driver IC (LMG1210 or equivalent GaN-specific driver) provides 2.5 A peak gate current for fast switching transitions (<2 ns rise/fall).

2.3 Variable Frequency Operation

The resonant frequency is varied by adjusting the effective tank capacitance. A switched capacitor bank (binary-weighted: C, 2C, 4C, 8C, 16C, 32C) allows discrete frequency steps, while a varactor diode array provides fine continuous tuning (±5% range). The control loop measures the actual switch voltage waveform zero-crossing and adjusts the varactor bias to maintain ZVS across the full operating range.

Frequency switching transients are managed by a pre-computed trajectory table — the controller ramps frequency in 100 Hz steps with 10 ms dwell, allowing the tank energy to settle before the next step.

3. Frequency Ladder & Zone Mapping — Physics-Based Design

The frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is not arbitrary — it is derived from the skin depth equation and the magnetic properties of target materials at each stage temperature.

3.1 Skin Depth and Frequency Selection

Skin depth determines how deeply the magnetic field penetrates the material:

$$\delta = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\omega \mu}}$$

Where $\rho$ = electrical resistivity (Ω·m), $\omega = 2\pi f$ = angular frequency, $\mu = \mu_0 \mu_r$ = magnetic permeability.

For uniform heating of a material of thickness $d$, we require $\delta \geq d/2$. For selective surface heating (e.g., thin foils), $\delta \ll d$.

Key insight: At Z7 (2 kHz), ferromagnetic materials have lost permeability (above Curie), so heating relies on eddy currents only. The lower frequency ensures deeper penetration into large ferrous pieces. At Z8 (1 kHz), the refractory minerals are essentially insulators — heating is purely by thermal conduction from the drum wall and susceptor materials.

4. GaN Thermal Management — Junction-to-Cold-Plate Design

Maintaining GaN junction temperature below 125°C (derated from 150°C max) at 500 kW total dissipation requires a high-performance liquid cooling system.

4.1 Thermal Resistance Budget

At 5.5 kW dissipation (Z8 worst case): $\Delta T = 5.5 \times 1.02 = 5.6°C$ above water temperature. With 25°C inlet water, Tj ≈ 31°C — well within limits.

4.2 Microchannel Cold Plate Design

Each inverter module mounts on a copper microchannel cold plate (CSMFAB-sourced copper — the only copper in the machine, justified as internal heat spreader not connected to earth):

  • Channel geometry: 0.5 mm wide × 1 mm deep, 40 channels parallel
  • Flow rate: 2 L/min per module (16 L/min total for 8 modules)
  • Pressure drop: 0.8 bar @ 2 L/min
  • Material: Copper base with PEX-a water connections
  • Surface finish: Ni-P electroless nickel (corrosion resistance, solderable)

4.3 PEX-a Water Circuit

The cooling water circuit uses PEX-a tubing (CSMFAB Materials Study Part IV) throughout — completely non-conductive, eliminating any conductive path from the process electronics to the building ground. This is a critical Carrington immunity feature.

  • Loop layout: Parallel feed to each module, manifold return
  • Filtration: 10 μm cartridge filter, ZrO₂ housing
  • Treatment: Deionized water, 18 MΩ·cm, with corrosion inhibitor (benzotriazole, 50 ppm)
  • Monitoring: FBG temperature sensors at each module inlet/outlet
