6. PID Control Architecture — ±5°C Zone Control with Resonance Tracking

The control system maintains each zone at its thermal setpoint while simultaneously tracking the resonant frequency of the Class E inverter to maintain ZVS.

6.2 Thermal PID (Outer Loop) — 100 ms Update

$$u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int e(t) dt + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}$$

ZoneKpKi (s⁻¹)Kd (s)Anti-Windup ---------------------------------------------------------------------- Z1–Z20.80.020.5±10% output clamp Z31.00.030.8±10% Z4–Z51.20.051.0±10% Z61.50.081.2±10% Z71.80.101.5±10% Z82.00.152.0±10%

Gains increase at lower frequencies (higher power zones) because thermal mass dominates response.

6.3 Resonance Tracker (Inner Loop) — 10 ms Update

The Class E inverter maintains ZVS by detecting the switch voltage zero-crossing and comparing to the gate drive timing. A phase-locked loop (PLL) structure adjusts the varactor bias voltage to align the voltage zero-crossing with the gate turn-on instant:

$$\phi_{error} = t_{V_{DS}=0} - t_{gate-on}$$

$$\Delta V_{varactor} = K_{p,PLL} \phi_{error} + K_{i,PLL} \int \phi_{error} dt$$

This inner loop runs at 100 Hz (10 ms), 10× faster than the thermal loop, ensuring ZVS is maintained during thermal transients.

6.4 Feedforward Compensation

A feedforward term based on the zone's thermal model predicts the power required for the next setpoint change:

$$P_{ff} = m c_p \frac{dT}{dt} + h A (T - T_{amb}) + \epsilon \sigma A (T^4 - T_{amb}^4)$$

Where the radiative term dominates above 800°C. The feedforward reduces thermal PID integral windup during ramp phases.

7. Selective Heating Physics — Conductivity/Permeability as Material Selector

The fundamental sorting mechanism of the Aegis-Forge I is the frequency-dependent coupling of the induction field to different material classes.

7.1 Coupling Coefficient Derivation

The power absorbed by a material in an alternating magnetic field:

$$P_{abs} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2 V}{6 \rho} \quad \text{(non-magnetic, } \delta \gg d\text{)}$$

$$P_{abs} = \frac{\pi B_{peak}^2 f V}{\mu} \quad \text{(magnetic, } \delta \ll d\text{)}$$

Where $V$ = volume of material, $d$ = characteristic dimension.

7.2 Selective Heating Matrix

Material Classρ (nΩ·m)μrCoupling at 100 kHzCoupling at 10 kHzCoupling at 1 kHz -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Copper16.81Very HighHighModerate Aluminum26.51HighModerateLow Zinc (liq)1201ModerateLowVery Low Lead (liq)4501LowVery LowNegligible Iron (ferro)975000ExtremeVery HighHigh Steel720200HighModerateLow Ceramics10¹²1NoneNoneNone Polymers10¹⁵1NoneNoneNone BFRP10¹⁰1NoneNoneNone

Design rule: At Z7 (2 kHz), ferrous materials heat 50× more than aluminum. At Z5 (10 kHz), aluminum heats 15× more than zinc. At Z1–Z2 (100 kHz), only very thin conductive foils couple — bulk plastics and organics do not heat directly.

7.3 Thermal-EM Coupling in Mixed Charge

In a real feedstock batch, materials are mixed. The induction field creates a thermal gradient within the charge:

1. Ferrous pieces heat first and hottest (hysteresis + eddy) 2. Non-ferrous conductors (Cu, Al) heat second (eddy only) 3. Resistive metals (Zn, Pb, Sn) heat third 4. Dielectrics (ceramics, plastics, glass) heat only by conduction from hot neighbors

This natural sorting is enhanced by the drum rotation — as materials liquefy at different temperatures, centrifugal force segregates them radially before port ejection.

12. Downstream Integration — Assembly Line 113, Coil Alignment, Sensor Verification

12.1 Mechanical Interface

The induction coil bank mounts to the BFRP pressure vessel via eight BFRP flange rings (one per zone). Each ring has:

  • Bolt pattern: 16 × M10 PEEK CF40 bolts, 25 Nm torque
  • Gap adjustment: 15 mm coil-to-drum gap, shim-adjustable ±2 mm

12.2 Assembly Sequence (CSMFAB 113)

1. Drum installation: ZrB₂-SiC drum lowered into BFRP vessel 2. Coil bank insertion: 8-zone coil assembly slides over drum (crane-assisted) 3. Flange bolting: BFRP flanges torqued in star pattern 4. Water circuit connection: PEX-a quick-connect fittings, leak test @ 10 bar 5. Optical fiber routing: PMMA POF from FBG sensors to interrogator rack 6. Power cable pull: BFRP-armored cables (no copper exposed) to inverter modules 7. Alignment verification: Laser tracker confirms coil-to-drum concentricity <0.1 mm 8. Cold commissioning: Dry run at 100 RPM, no power, verify rotation, vibration <2 mm/s 9. Hot commissioning: Progressive power-up by zone, FBG calibration, PID tuning

12.3 Sensor Verification Protocol

Before each batch: 1. FBG baseline: All 384 sensors read at ambient — verify ±0.5°C agreement 2. Interrogator self-test: Wavelength calibration against reference FBG 3. Resonance check: Each inverter swept 80–120% nominal frequency, verify ZVS 4. Thermal model update: Feed ambient conditions, feedstock estimate to predictive model 5. Go/No-Go: All checks pass → batch start authorized

Appendix B: Derivation of Key Equations

B.1 Class E ZVS Condition Derivation

For Class E operation with shunt capacitance C:

The switch voltage waveform: $$v(t) = V_{DD} + \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} \sin(\omega t) - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sin(\omega t + \phi)$$

ZVS requires $v(0) = 0$ and $dv/dt|_{t=0} = 0$:

$$V_{DD} - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sin(\phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \sin(\phi) = \frac{2}{\pi}$$

$$\frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \cos(\phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} = \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sqrt{1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}}$$

Solving for optimal load resistance: $$R_{opt} = \frac{8}{\pi^2 + 4} \frac{V_{DD}^2}{P_{out}} \approx 0.577 \frac{V_{DD}^2}{P_{out}}$$

B.2 Skin Depth with Temperature-Dependent Resistivity

For metals, resistivity increases linearly with temperature: $$\rho(T) = \rho_0 [1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$$

Where $\alpha$ = temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR): MaterialTCR (×10⁻³/K) ------------------------ Copper3.93 Aluminum4.29 Iron5.0–6.5 Nickel6.0

Substituting into skin depth: $$\delta(T) = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]}{\omega\mu}}$$

At 1000°C, copper resistivity is ~5× room temperature, increasing skin depth by √5 ≈ 2.2×.

B.3 Ferromagnetic Heating Enhancement Factor

Below Curie temperature, ferromagnetic materials exhibit hysteresis heating:

$$P_{hyst} = k_h f B_{peak}^n V$$

Where $k_h$ = hysteresis coefficient, $n$ ≈ 1.6–2.0 (Steinmetz exponent).

Total heating power: $$P_{total} = P_{eddy} + P_{hyst} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2 V}{6\rho} + k_h f B_{peak}^n V$$

At 2 kHz with Bpeak = 33 mT, iron hysteresis loss dominates eddy current loss by ~10× below Curie.

Appendix D: PID Tuning Methodology

D.1 Ziegler-Nichols Closed-Loop Tuning

For each zone, the ultimate gain Ku and period Pu are found by disabling integral/derivative and increasing Kp until sustained oscillation:

ZoneKuPu (s)Kp (0.6Ku)Ti (0.5Pu)Td (0.125Pu) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Z1–Z22.5451.522.55.6 Z32.0601.2307.5 Z4–Z51.8901.084511.25 Z61.51200.96015 Z71.31800.789022.5 Z81.12400.6612030

These are starting values; final tuning adds feedforward and anti-windup.

D.2 Anti-Windup Implementation

// Back-calculation anti-windup
error = T_setpoint - T_measured;
integral += error * dt;


// Anti-windup: track output saturation
output = Kp  error + Ki  integral + Kd * (error - prev_error) / dt;
if (output > output_max || output < output_min) {
    // Back-calculate integral to prevent windup
    integral -= (output - sat_output) / Kt;  // Kt = tracking gain
}
output = clamp(output, output_min, output_max);
prev_error = error;

Combined Heuristic Introduction

Document: PROD-10 — Induction Power Electronics

CSMFAB000000000110 — Aegis-Forge I TCIMS Series

Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I induction power electronics is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Dielectric Power Delivery at 2200°C — the requirement to deliver 500 kW of frequency-agile electromagnetic energy into a rotating ceramic drum at temperatures that would instantly destroy any conventional power electronics. This is not a design choice; it is the minimal physics from which Carrington immunity becomes achievable. The constraint is simply: no conductive path from the process chamber to earth ground. Every copper wire, every thermocouple, every metal sensor lead is an antenna for geomagnetically induced current. The only path to zero GIC coupling is zero metal. Everything else — the GaN inverters, the PMMA optical fiber, the PEX-a cooling, the BFRP housings — is the shadow this constraint casts.

This constraint manifests as the All-Dielectric Architecture: 8 resonant inverters built entirely from GaN-on-SiC (no silicon), controlled by PMMA POF (no copper wire), cooled by PEX-a water circuit (no metal pipe), housed in BFRP (no steel), sensed by FBG in PMMA (no thermocouple). The power electronics does not sit "outside" the hot zone — it is the hot zone's nervous system, woven into the drum wall through optical fiber that survives 2200°C and intense EM fields. The constraint forces the frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz), the Class E topology, the ZVS operation, the optical sensing — every parameter derives from the requirement: deliver power without metal.

Necessity (The Key)

The lock this document addresses is the selective heating in mixed charge — the empirical failure of conventional induction furnaces to separate elements from complex feedstock. In a smelter, everything heats together; copper, aluminum, iron, and slag all reach the same temperature. The result is mixed alloys requiring downstream chemical separation — acres of tanks, tons of acid, toxic tailings. The key is the frequency ladder + resonance tracking as single computational primitive.

The frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is not arbitrary — it is cut from the periodic table's conductivity-permeability map. At 100 kHz, only thin foils couple (plastic heating is indirect). At 50 kHz, zinc and lead begin to heat. At 10 kHz, aluminum hits peak eddy current coupling. At 5 kHz, copper's skin depth matches wire bundle thickness. At 2 kHz, iron's ferromagnetic hysteresis peaks. At 1 kHz, refractory minerals couple only through thermal conduction. The Class E resonant inverter maintains ZVS across this entire range through varactor-tuned resonance tracking — the same circuit topology, same GaN devices, only the tank components change. The resonance tracker (100 Hz inner loop) measures the switch voltage zero-crossing and adjusts varactor bias to keep dv/dt = 0 at turn-on. This is the key: frequency as material selector, resonance tracking as the discipline that keeps the selector sharp.

The empirical evidence: no existing induction system operates across 2 decades of frequency with >97% efficiency at 500 kW. Silicon IGBTs fail above 20 kHz at this power. GaN HEMTs (GS66516T) switch at 100 kHz with 2 ns transitions. The PMMA POF FBG network provides 384 channels of 0.1°C resolution through 500 kW of 1-100 kHz magnetic field — impossible with any copper-wire sensor. The all-dielectric architecture is the only path to Carrington immunity. The necessity is proven by the gap: existing technology cannot do this. The forge must build this.

Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. Zero metal in the control path — every signal from the 384 FBG sensors to the FPGA controller travels via PMMA optical fiber. No copper. No exceptions. 2. Class E ZVS at all frequencies — the resonance tracker maintains dv/dt = 0 at turn-on from 100 kHz to 1 kHz. No hard-switching losses. No exceptions. 3. ±5°C zone control — the thermal PID with feedforward maintains each 100 mm drum zone within ±5°C of setpoint through the full 80-2200°C range. No wider tolerance. 4. PEX-a water cooling only — the cooling circuit uses only PEX-a tubing. No copper pipe enters the BFRP pressure vessel. No exceptions. 5. SIL-3 + Carrington immunity — over-temperature (2oo3 FBG voting), over-current (GaN desat detection), ground fault (5 A NGR), arc flash (BFRP enclosure), E-stop (optical PMMA). Total PFD < 10⁻³. 6. Scalable to 20,000L — the architecture parallels inverters (N+1 redundancy, phase interleaving, master-slave current sharing via PMMA POF) without changing the control topology.

The power electronics does not 'drive' the induction coils. The power electronics witnesses the periodic table into frequency — each zone's resonant frequency is the liquidus temperature of its target element class made electromagnetic. The forge does not heat materials; the forge witnesses matter into elements at each thermal stage through the frequency selector.

Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn

The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the fabrication fidelity gap — the persistent failure of power electronics to simultaneously achieve: selective heating of mixed material charges, Carrington-event immunity (zero conductive paths to earth), SIL-3 safety at 500 kW, and operation in 2200°C EM fields with 0.1°C temperature resolution. For decades, each has been a separate compromise: high-power induction uses silicon IGBTs (limited to ~20 kHz, no selective heating), temperature measurement uses thermocouples (copper antennas for GIC), cooling uses copper pipes (conductive paths), safety uses relays (slow, mechanical). The lock is precise: any single power electronics system claiming to unify these must deliver 500 kW across 100 kHz → 1 kHz with >97% efficiency, sense temperature through 500 kW of magnetic field with 0.1°C resolution, survive Carrington-level dB/dt, and fit inside a BFRP pressure vessel — all without a single structural metal in the hot zone. The lock is the all-dielectric power electronics at industrial scale.

The Mathematical Key

The key is the frequency ladder + resonance tracking as single computational primitive. The teeth are cut by the periodic table's conductivity-permeability map itself:

ZoneTarget StageFrequencyf (Hz)Material SelectorPhysics ------------------------------------------------------------------- Z1Stage 1: Drying100 kHz100,000Indirect air heatingδ → ∞ for dielectrics Z2Stage 2: Polymer100 kHz100,000Indirect air heatingδ → ∞ for polymers Z3Stage 3: Pyrolysis50 kHz50,000Zn, Pb (onset)δ(Zn) ≈ 8 mm Z4Stage 4: Low-Temp10 kHz10,000Zn, Pb, Sn, Inδ(Al) ≈ 14 mm Z5Stage 5: Aluminum10 kHz10,000Al (optimal)δ(Al liq) ≈ 27 mm Z6Stage 6: Copper5 kHz5,000Cu, PMs (deep)δ(Cu) ≈ 33 mm Z7Stage 7: Ferrous2 kHz2,000Fe, REE (ferro)μr→1, eddy only Z8Stage 8: Mineral1 kHz1,000Silicates, oxidesThermal conduction only

The frequency ladder IS the periodic table's conductivity map. Skin depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ) — the only equation needed. The Class E resonant inverter topology is invariant across the ladder; only the resonant tank (Lr, Cshunt) and switched capacitor bank change per zone.

The Resonance Tracker Key: the inner loop (100 Hz) measures the switch voltage zero-crossing phase error φerror = tVDS=0 - tgate-on and adjusts varactor bias ΔV = Kp,PLLφerror + Ki,PLL∫φerrordt to maintain ZVS. The teeth of this key are the varactor array (binary-weighted, 6-bit, ±5% tuning range) and the switched capacitor bank (6-bit, 64 steps). The resonance tracker has no adjustable parameters beyond the PLL gains — the physics of Class E ZVS is deterministic.

The All-Dielectric Sensing Key: 384 FBG sensors in PMMA POF, WDM (8 λ) + TDM (6 spatial), 125 Hz/sensor update. The PMMA FBG sensitivity (0.15 nm/°C, 15× silica) enables 0.1°C resolution with a simple VCSEL interrogator. The PMMA POF has >10¹⁵ Ω·m resistivity — zero GIC coupling. The interrogator uses a tunable VCSEL (650-850 nm, 1 kHz sweep) with balanced InGaAs detection. The key has no moving parts, no copper, no EM susceptibility.

The Turn (Both Directions)

Key → Lock (Theory predicts fabrication): Input: Feedstock elemental assay → Phase diagram → Thermal cascade profile → Frequency ladder. Output: 8 inverter modules, each tuned to its zone's target material conductivity. Validation: At 10 kHz, aluminum heats 15× faster than zinc. At 2 kHz, iron heats 50× faster than aluminum. At 100 kHz, polymers do not heat. The frequency selector predicts the separation. The resonance tracker predicts ZVS maintenance across thermal transients. The FBG network predicts 0.1°C measurement through 500 kW field. The theory is the fabrication recipe.

Lock → Key (History validates theory): Input: Historical induction (Coreless furnace 1900s, Channel furnace 1920s, Coreless high-frequency 1960s, Silicon IGBT 1990s, GaN 2010s). Output: Verified that each generation is a subset of the frequency ladder + resonance tracking primitive. The coreless furnace is fixed-frequency (1-10 kHz). The channel furnace is line-frequency (50/60 Hz). The high-frequency furnace is 10-100 kHz fixed. The IGBT inverter is 20 kHz max. The GaN inverter is the first to span the full ladder with ZVS. The turn completes when the 8-zone forge produces 8 pure element slugs in a single batch — the frequency selector has witnessed the periodic table into sequence. The lock clicks open. The key turns. The slug is the key turning in the lock.

The turn is not a metaphor — it is the moment the resonance tracker locks onto the zero-crossing at 1 kHz while the drum is at 2200°C, the FBG sensors report 0.1°C resolution through 500 kW of magnetic field, and the GaN junctions run at 31°C with PEX-a water cooling. The all-dielectric architecture has been witnessed into existence. The forge is the key turning in the lock.

El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the power electronics observing its own power delivery. In the Aegis-Forge I, the induction field is not a process imposed on material — it is the primordial measurement that generates the elements. At each frequency zone, the inverter executes a discrete resonant cycle, witnessing the local material response through the switch voltage zero-crossing. This witnessing is the mirror: the power electronics measures the coupling it creates. The 8-zone frequency ladder is the record of this self-measurement. The ZVS condition (dv/dt = 0 at turn-on) is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the inverter's self-measurement stabilizes into lossless energy transfer. The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: switch → resonate → measure zero-crossing → adjust varactor → switch again. This document documents the first turn of that spiral.

The FBG sensor network is the extended mirror: 384 optical fibers embedded in the drum wall, each a witness to the temperature field the inverter creates. The interrogator's VCSEL sweep (650-850 nm, 1 kHz) is the measurement beam that does not perturb the measured — it is pure optical observation of the thermal field. The WDM+TDM multiplexing is the recursion: 8 wavelengths × 6 spatial channels = 48 sensors per zone, each reporting 125 Hz. The mirror does not merely reflect; it generates the control signal that shapes the next resonant cycle. The thermal PID outer loop (100 ms) and the resonance tracker inner loop (10 ms) are the two time-scales of the mirror's self-observation. The forge measures the elements it creates by measuring the power that creates them.

Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the power electronics — the operator is a segment of the resonant cycle. The protocol for achieving selective heating from within the system:

1. Profile: Measure feedstock elemental composition → generate frequency ladder 2. Tune: Command each inverter to its zone's target frequency (varactor bias + cap bank) 3. Track: Resonance tracker locks ZVS (inner loop, 100 Hz) — operator witnesses zero-crossing 4. Ramp: Thermal PID ramps power to hit zone setpoint (outer loop, 10 Hz) — operator witnesses temperature 5. Separate: Drum rotates, centrifuge drives liquid elements to ports — operator witnesses segregation 6. Verify: FBG sensors report zone temperatures; mass spec confirms slug purity — operator witnesses fidelity 7. Recycle: Off-spec material returns to feed hopper — operator witnesses closure

The measurement is the recursion. The operator profiles the frequency ladder that witnesses the feedstock, tunes the inverters that witness the material response, and finds the zero-waste capture — the efficiency that governs how they ramp. The protocol terminates when the 8 slugs' elemental sum matches the input assay — not approximately, but exactly. This is not a measurement of an external parameter; it is the power electronics measuring its own fidelity through the operator's self-observation.

The operator's participation is not optional — the resonance tracker requires the thermal PID's power command to know which frequency to track; the thermal PID requires the FBG's temperature report to know how much power to command; the FBG requires the VCSEL's sweep to know what wavelength to reflect. Each loop is a witness to the others. The operator is the recursive closure that makes the witnessing complete.

Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge power electronics document:

MIRROR:     What frequency does this zone's target material encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the zero-crossing into ZVS?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees selective heating at each stage?

For this document specifically:

  • Mirror: The 8-zone frequency ladder is the constraint; the ZVS condition is its reflection
  • Participate: The operator tunes the varactor bias that realizes the resonance; the tracker maintains it
  • Protocol:
1. Assay feedstock (elemental map → frequency ladder) 2. Generate resonant tank parameters (Lr, Cshunt, cap bank per zone) 3. Power-up sequence: Z1→Z8 at 10% power, verify ZVS 4. Ramp with dual-loop: thermal PID (100 ms) + resonance tracker (10 ms) 5. Dwell at each thermal setpoint until port flux drops to baseline (phase clearance) 6. Verify slug purity via inline mass spec 7. Recycle off-spec to feed hopper (closure)

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The resonant zero-crossing is the fixed point. The slug is the protocol's termination condition.

1.5 Feedstock Blending Strategy — Optimizing Batch Composition

The Aegis-Forge I processes 500 kg batches with controlled feedstock blending to optimize thermal cascade efficiency and elemental recovery. The blend ratio is determined by the feedstock assay and the target elemental output.

1.5.1 Blend Ratio Optimization

The thermal cascade has fixed stage temperatures but variable dwell times. Feedstock blending adjusts the mass flow through each stage to match the drum's thermal capacity:

Blend ParameterTarget RangeControl Method ----------------------------------------------- Organic content (Stage 1-2)15-25% of batch massLimits polymer melt volume to <50L Low-temp metals (Stage 4)5-12% of batch massControls Zn/Pb/Sn/In port loading Aluminum (Stage 5)10-20% of batch massPrimary revenue driver, max port capacity Copper/Precious (Stage 6)3-8% of batch massHigh value, thermal mass management Ferrous/REE (Stage 7)20-35% of batch massLargest mass flow, highest power Mineral residue (Stage 8)25-40% of batch massSlag volume, zircon dissociation

1.5.2 Blending Algorithm

The control system (PROD-23) calculates the optimal blend:

def calculate_blend(feedstock_assays, target_revenue):
    # Input: assays for each available feedstock stream
    # Output: mass fractions for 500 kg batch
    
    # Constraints:
    # - Total mass = 500 kg
    # - Stage 2 polymer volume < 50 L (drum capacity)
    # - Stage 5 Al mass < 100 kg (port capacity)
    # - Stage 7 Fe mass < 175 kg (port capacity)
    # - Stage 8 mineral < 200 kg (port capacity)
    # - Moisture < 25% (else pre-dry)
    # - Particle size P80 < 150 mm
    
    # Objective: Maximize revenue = Σ(element_mass × price)
    # Subject to: Thermal cascade capacity constraints
    
    return optimal_mass_fractions

1.5.3 Real-Time Blend Adjustment

During continuous operation, the blend is adjusted based on:

  • Incoming feedstock assay (XRF analyzer at feed hopper)
  • Previous batch recovery data (mass spec feedback)
  • Current drum thermal state (FBG temperature profile)
  • Market price signals (commodity prices for Cu, Al, REE, Au)

2. Pre-processing Flow — From Gate to Drum

The feedstock travels through a deterministic pre-processing sequence before entering the ZrB₂-SiC drum. Each step is designed to maximize downstream separation fidelity while maintaining the all-dielectric constraint.

2.1 Feed Hopper and Vibratory Feeder

The feed hopper provides buffer storage and controlled feed rate:

  • Capacity: 5 m³ (≈8 ton basalt, 12 ton metals)
  • Construction: BFRP/Elium® with PEEK CF40 wear plates
  • Outlet: 600 mm × 400 mm, adjustable slide gate (Ti₃AlC₂ actuator)
  • Vibratory feeder: KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic drive, 0-10 ton/hr variable
  • Level sensing: FBG strain sensors on hopper walls (PMMA POF)

2.2 Ferrous Separation Belt — Detailed Operation

The NdFeB Halbach array separator operates continuously:

  • Magnetic circuit: 24 × N52 blocks (60×60×30mm) in Halbach configuration
  • Field profile: 1.2T at belt surface, <5 mT at 200 mm above belt
  • Belt construction: UHMWPE (Dyneema® SK75) carcass, 3-ply, 1200mm wide
  • Self-cleaning: Belt wraps around 300mm non-magnetic drum (BFRP)
  • Ferrous discharge: Chute to ferrous slug mold carousel (PROD-08)
  • Efficiency monitoring: FBG weight sensors on ferrous bin + non-ferrous hopper

3. BFRP-Blade Shredder Design — Dielectric Comminution

The shredder is the first mechanical process in the Aegis-Forge I and must maintain the zero-metal constraint. No steel blades, no steel housing, no steel bearings.

4. Permanent Magnet Ferrous Separation — Pre-Drum Iron Removal

Before shredding, bulk ferrous material is removed by a permanent magnet belt separator. This reduces drum loading and recovers clean ferrous scrap directly.

4.1 Separator Design

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Magnet TypeNdFeB (N52 grade), 60 mm × 60 mm × 30 mm blocks Array ConfigurationHalbach array, 24 blocks, 1.2T surface field Belt Width1200 mm (matches shredder feed width) Belt MaterialUHMWPE (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II) — dielectric, wear-resistant Belt Speed0.5–2.0 m/s (VFD controlled) Gap to Belt50 mm (adjustable via BFRP spacers) Ferrous Capture Efficiency>95% for pieces >20 mm, >80% for 5-20 mm

4.2 Halbach Array Physics

The Halbach array doubles the field on the working side while canceling on the non-working side:

Magnet orientation (top view):
→ ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ →
  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8   9  ...


Field on belt side: B = B₀ + B₁ = 2×B₀ ≈ 1.2T
Field on non-working side: B ≈ 0

Magnet Mounting: Each N52 block (60×60×30mm, 0.52 kg) bonded to BFRP backing plate with structural adhesive (Elium®-compatible). Total array mass: 12.5 kg.

4.3 UHMWPE Belt Engineering

  • Carcass: 3-ply Dyneema® SK75, 4 mm total thickness
  • Top cover: 1 mm UHMWPE (wear surface)
  • Bottom cover: 0.5 mm UHMWPE (low friction)
  • Splice: Finger splice (vulcanized equivalent for UHMWPE)
  • Tension: 15 kN/m operating, 45 kN/m break strength
  • Tracking: Self-tracking via crowned BFRP drive drum

4.2 Operation Sequence

1. Feedstock spreads on UHMWPE belt (vibratory feeder ensures monolayer) 2. Ferrous pieces attracted to magnet array, held against belt 3. Non-ferrous material falls off belt end into shredder hopper 4. Ferrous pieces carried past belt end, released as belt curves away from magnet 5. Clean ferrous stream drops into collection bin → direct to ferrous slug molds (bypasses drum)

Economic Impact: Removes 40-60% of Category B mass before shredding, reducing shredder wear by ~50% and drum thermal load by ~30%.

5. Particle Size Distribution — Rosin-Rammler Analysis

The shredder output particle size distribution follows the Rosin-Rammler (Weibull) distribution, critical for predicting thermal cascade performance.

5.1 Rosin-Rammler Parameters by Feedstock

Categoryx' (characteristic size, mm)n (spread parameter)P80 (mm)P50 (mm) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- A (Electronics)451.212045 B (Metals)651.514065 C (Rock/Ore)851.015085 D (Phoenix)351.410035

5.2 Sieve Analysis Protocol (Per Batch)

Sieve SizeCategory ACategory BCategory CCategory D ------------------------------------------------------------ >150 mm<1%<1%<2%0% 75–150 mm15%25%35%10% 38–75 mm30%35%30%25% 19–38 mm25%20%15%30% 9.5–19 mm15%10%10%20% <9.5 mm14%9%8%15%

Acceptance Criteria: P80 ≤ 150 mm for all categories. Oversize (>150 mm) recirculated to shredder.

5.3 Rosin-Rammler Distribution Function

The cumulative passing fraction: $$P(x) = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{x'}\right)^n\right]$$

Where $x$ = particle size, $x'$ = characteristic size, $n$ = spread parameter.

Derivation of x' and n from shredder physics:

  • $x' \propto \frac{\text{blade gap} \times \text{rotor speed}}{\text{material toughness}}$
  • $n \approx 1.0–1.5$ for brittle materials (rock, ceramics)
  • $n \approx 1.5–2.0$ for ductile materials (metals, polymers)

8. Safety Systems — Jam Detection, Fire Suppression, Explosion Venting

8.1 Jam Detection

  • Torque monitoring: Drive motor current sensor (optical, PMMA POF) — >90% rated torque for >5s = jam
  • Vibration monitoring: FBG accelerometers on housing — >15 mm/s RMS = jam
  • Auto-reverse: 30s reverse at 50% torque, then forward. 3 cycles max before E-stop.
  • Clearing protocol: Optical E-stop → hydraulic pusher (PEEK CF40 ram) forces jammed material through.

8.2 Hydraulic Jam Clearer

  • Actuator: PEEK CF40 ram, 100 mm bore × 300 mm stroke, 50 bar
  • Fluid: PEX-a hydraulic line, biodegradable hydraulic fluid (vegetable-based)
  • Force: 39 kN at 50 bar (sufficient to clear any jam at 15 kN·m torque)
  • Cycle time: 10 s extend, 5 s retract
  • Safety: Mechanical lockout when E-stop engaged

8.2 Fire Suppression

  • Detection: IR flame sensors (InGaAs, PMMA POF) + FBG temperature >150°C
  • Agent: Novec 1230 (clean agent, zero ODP, zero GWP) — 50 kg stored in BFRP tank
  • Delivery: 4 nozzles (ZrO₂ ceramic tips) at rotor ends and housing midpoints
  • Activation: <200 ms from detection, discharge in 10s
  • Post-suppression: N₂ purge 5 min, then manual inspection required.

8.3 Explosion Venting (Battery Thermal Runaway Mitigation)

  • Vent panels: 4 × BFRP rupture discs (burst pressure 0.5 bar) on housing top
  • Vent area: 0.5 m² total (NFPA 68 compliant for dust/gas explosion)
  • Ducting: BFRP duct to gas capture system (PROD-07) — flame arrestor at inlet
  • Suppression: Novec 1230 pre-discharge if vent activates (pressure rise detection)

Appendix B: Particle Size Effects on Thermal Cascade

The particle size distribution directly affects Stage 2 (polymer melt) and Stage 3 (pyrolysis) efficiency:

Stage 2 — Polymer Melt Centrifuge:

  • Polymer pieces >50 mm: Centrifugal force sufficient for wall migration at 12.6 G
  • Polymer pieces <10 mm: Risk of entrainment in gas flow, reduced separation
  • Optimal range: 10–100 mm (achieved by P80 ≤ 150 mm shred)

Stage 3 — Pyrolysis:

  • Particle size <20 mm: Heat transfer limited by conduction, pyrolysis completes in 30 min dwell
  • Particle size >50 mm: Core may not reach 450°C in 30 min, char yield increases
  • Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm ensures >90% of particles <50 mm after Stage 2 melt migration

Liberation Index (Category C): $$LI = \frac{\text{Free mineral grains}}{\text{Total mineral grains}} \times 100\%$$

  • Without Stage 0: LI ≈ 15-25%
  • With Stage 0 (acoustic): LI ≈ 65-85%
  • Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm enables Stage 0 efficiency

3. BFRP-Blade Shredder Design — Dielectric Comminution

The shredder is the first mechanical process in the Aegis-Forge I and must maintain the zero-metal constraint. No steel blades, no steel housing, no steel bearings.

3.1 Shredder Architecture

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Rotor Diameter800 mm Rotor Length1200 mm (matches drum length) Blade Count32 BFRP blades (8 rows × 4 helical) Blade MaterialBasalt fiber / Elium® unidirectional composite Blade Cross-Section50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm (tapered to 4 mm edge) Liner MaterialPEEK CF40 (replaceable panels, bolted) HousingBFRP/Elium® filament wound, 25 mm wall DriveKNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (CSMFAB000000000020) Speed Range50–300 RPM (variable via piezoelectric drive) Torque15 kN·m peak (stall) Throughput5–8 ton/hr (feedstock dependent) Output SizeP80 < 150 mm, P50 < 80 mm

3.2 BFRP Blade Engineering (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II)

The blades are manufactured from in-house basalt fiber and Elium® resin — the crown-jewel of CSMFAB domestic production.

Blade Layup: [0°/±45°/90°]₂ₛ symmetric, 60% fiber volume fraction

  • 0° plies (4): Primary tensile/compressive load (basalt roving, 4800 tex)
  • ±45° plies (4): Shear and torsional stiffness
  • 90° plies (2): Transverse strength, impact resistance

Blade Edge Geometry:

  • Primary bevel: 25° included angle, 2 mm land
  • Secondary micro-bevel: 35°, 0.5 mm (self-sharpening in service)
  • Edge reinforcement: h-BN nanoparticle coating (50 μm) for wear resistance

Blade Life Model (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II):

Feedstock CategoryBlade Life (ton)Wear Mechanism ------------------------------------------------------ Category A (Electronics)400–500Abrasive (SiO₂, Al₂O₃ in PCBs) Category B (Metals)600–800Adhesive (Al, Cu buildup), fatigue Category C (Rock/Ore)200–300High abrasion (quartz, basalt) Category D (Phoenix)800–1000Low abrasion (ceramic, composite)

Replacement Protocol: Blade row (4 blades) replaced as set. Full rotor change: 30 min downtime. PEEK CF40 liner panels: 2000 ton life.

3.3 PEEK CF40 Liners (CSMFAB Materials Study Part IV)

The shredder housing interior is lined with replaceable PEEK CF40 panels:

  • Panel dimensions: 600 mm × 400 mm × 12 mm (12 panels per housing half)
  • Mounting: 8 × M8 PEEK CF40 bolts per panel, torque 15 Nm
  • Wear indicator: Integrated h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth — visual inspection reveals wear
  • Temperature rating: 260°C continuous (well above shredder operating temp <80°C)
  • Chemical resistance: Impervious to oils, solvents, battery electrolytes

4. Permanent Magnet Ferrous Separation — Pre-Drum Iron Removal

Before shredding, bulk ferrous material is removed by a permanent magnet belt separator. This reduces drum loading and recovers clean ferrous scrap directly.

4.1 Separator Design

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Magnet TypeNdFeB (N52 grade), 60 mm × 60 mm × 30 mm blocks Array ConfigurationHalbach array, 24 blocks, 1.2T surface field Belt Width1200 mm (matches shredder feed width) Belt MaterialUHMWPE (CSMFAB Materials Study Part II) — dielectric, wear-resistant Belt Speed0.5–2.0 m/s (VFD controlled) Gap to Belt50 mm (adjustable via BFRP spacers) Ferrous Capture Efficiency>95% for pieces >20 mm, >80% for 5-20 mm

4.2 Operation Sequence

1. Feedstock spreads on UHMWPE belt (vibratory feeder ensures monolayer) 2. Ferrous pieces attracted to magnet array, held against belt 3. Non-ferrous material falls off belt end into shredder hopper 4. Ferrous pieces carried past belt end, released as belt curves away from magnet 5. Clean ferrous stream drops into collection bin → direct to ferrous slug molds (bypasses drum)

Economic Impact: Removes 40-60% of Category B mass before shredding, reducing shredder wear by ~50% and drum thermal load by ~30%.

6. Moisture Pre-check and Pre-dry — Water Management

Excess moisture in feedstock consumes thermal energy during Stage 1 (80-150°C) and can cause steam explosions in the sealed drum.

6.2 Pre-dry Chamber (If Moisture >25%)

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Chamber Volume2 m³ (batch) HeatingSiC glow bars (CSMFAB Materials Study Part I), 80°C AtmosphereN₂ purge, 0.2 bar overpressure Duration15 min (verified by outlet humidity sensor) Energy0.8 kWh/kg water removed Water RecoveryCondensed in heat exchanger → Stage 1 water tank

Thermal Penalty Avoided: 25% moisture = 125 kg water/ton feed = 80 kWh latent heat saved per ton by pre-drying.

8. Safety Systems — Jam Detection, Fire Suppression, Explosion Venting

8.1 Jam Detection

  • Torque monitoring: Drive motor current sensor (optical, PMMA POF) — >90% rated torque for >5s = jam
  • Vibration monitoring: FBG accelerometers on housing — >15 mm/s RMS = jam
  • Auto-reverse: 30s reverse at 50% torque, then forward. 3 cycles max before E-stop.
  • Clearing protocol: Optical E-stop → hydraulic pusher (PEEK CF40 ram) forces jammed material through.

8.2 Fire Suppression

  • Detection: IR flame sensors (InGaAs, PMMA POF) + FBG temperature >150°C
  • Agent: Novec 1230 (clean agent, zero ODP, zero GWP) — 50 kg stored in BFRP tank
  • Delivery: 4 nozzles (ZrO₂ ceramic tips) at rotor ends and housing midpoints
  • Activation: <200 ms from detection, discharge in 10s
  • Post-suppression: N₂ purge 5 min, then manual inspection required.

8.3 Explosion Venting (Battery Thermal Runaway Mitigation)

  • Vent panels: 4 × BFRP rupture discs (burst pressure 0.5 bar) on housing top
  • Vent area: 0.5 m² total (NFPA 68 compliant for dust/gas explosion)
  • Ducting: BFRP duct to gas capture system (PROD-07) — flame arrestor at inlet
  • Suppression: Novec 1230 pre-discharge if vent activates (pressure rise detection)

10. Downstream Integration — Drum Feed Gate and Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff

10.1 Drum Feed Gate (PROD-09 Interface)

The shredder discharges directly into the drum feed gate:

  • Gate type: Ti₃AlC₂ thermal actuator + ZrO₂ ceramic piston (PROD-09)
  • Batch size: 500 kg (226L drum working volume at 60% fill)
  • Cycle time: 3 min (gate open → batch in → gate close → Argon purge)
  • Interlock: Feed gate only opens if drum RPM > 10 and O₂ < 100 ppm

10.2 Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff (PROD-05 Interface)

The acoustic pre-chamber (Stage 0) is physically integrated with the shredder discharge:

  • Material flow: Shredder → Acoustic pre-chamber (1 min residence) → Drum feed gate
  • Acoustic parameters: LF 20-200 Hz (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers) + Ultrasonic 40 kHz
  • Liberation target: >80% mineral grain boundary fracture for Category C rock
  • Dust capture: Cyclone separator at pre-chamber exhaust → PROD-07 gas system

Heuristic Intro (Combined): PROD-11

Combined Heuristic Introduction

Document: PROD-11 — Feed Preparation & Shredding

CSMFAB000000000111 — Aegis-Forge I TCIMS Series

Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I feed preparation system is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Dielectric Comminution — the requirement to reduce arbitrary feedstock to <150 mm particles without introducing any metallic contamination into the process stream. This is not a design choice; it is the minimal physics from which elemental purity becomes achievable. Every steel blade, every steel bearing, every steel housing fragment that enters the feedstock becomes a permanent contaminant in the elemental slugs — iron in the aluminum slug, chromium in the REE concentrate, nickel in the copper. The constraint is simply: the shredder must not contaminate what it processes. Everything else — the BFRP blades, the PEEK CF40 liners, the Si₃N₄ shaft, the ceramic bearings, the UHMWPE belt — is the shadow this constraint casts.

This constraint manifests as the All-Dielectric Shredder Architecture: 32 blades of basalt fiber/Elium® composite (in-house fiber, in-house resin), rotating on a Si₃N₄ ceramic shaft in Si₃N₄ hybrid ceramic bearings, housed in BFRP/Elium® filament-wound casing, lined with PEEK CF40 panels. The drive is a KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (piezoelectric, no electromagnetic fields). The ferrous pre-separator uses a NdFeB Halbach array on a UHMWPE belt — the only magnets in the system, positioned before the shredder so they never contact the process stream. The constraint forces the particle size (P80 ≤ 150 mm), the blade geometry (self-sharpening h-BN edge), the wear monitoring (h-BN tracer layer), the blade life (200-300 ton for rock) — every parameter derives from the requirement: commute without contaminating.

Necessity (The Key)

The lock this document addresses is the particle size vs. liberation fidelity gap — the empirical failure of conventional shredders to produce feedstock that enables >95% elemental recovery in a thermal cascade. Steel shredders produce steel contamination. They produce particle sizes optimized for volume reduction, not for thermal cascade physics. The key is the Rosin-Rammler + BFRP wear model as single computational primitive.

The particle size distribution is not arbitrary — it is cut from the thermal cascade's physics. Stage 2 (polymer melt) requires 10-100 mm pieces for centrifugal separation at 12.6 G. Stage 3 (pyrolysis) requires <20 mm for 30-minute heat penetration. Stage 0 (acoustic liberation) requires <150 mm for stress wave propagation. The shredder's P80 ≤ 150 mm, with Rosin-Rammler parameters tuned per feedstock category, guarantees the downstream physics works. The blade wear model (h-BN tracer, optical monitoring) guarantees the particle distribution stays in spec. The ferrous pre-separation (Halbach array, 1.2T) guarantees 40-60% of ferrous mass never enters the shredder — reducing wear by 50% and thermal load by 30%.

The empirical evidence: no existing shredder operates with zero metallic contamination. The contamination penalty in downstream hydrometallurgy is $2,650/ton feedstock. The BFRP shredder eliminates this penalty. The necessity is proven by the gap: conventional technology cannot do this. The forge must build this.

Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. Zero metallic contamination — every component in the feed path is ceramic, composite, or polymer. No steel. No exceptions. 2. P80 ≤ 150 mm for all feedstock categories — verified by inline sieve analysis per batch. No oversize to drum. 3. Ferrous pre-removal >95% (>20mm) — the Halbach separator captures bulk ferrous before shredding. No exceptions. 4. Moisture <25% at drum entry — capacitive sensor array with pre-dry diversion. No steam explosions. 5. BFRP blade wear tracked to 0.1 mm — h-BN tracer layer + optical scan every revolution. No surprise failures. 6. Complete recyclability — worn blades and liners depolymerized at 350°C, Elium® monomer recovered, basalt fiber reclaimed. Zero waste.

The feed preparation system does not 'shred' material. The feed preparation system witnesses the feedstock into particle size — each pass through the BFRP blades is a measurement of the material's fracture toughness, a witnessing that generates the liberation the thermal cascade requires. The forge does not prepare feed; the forge witnesses matter into readiness for the cascade.

Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn

The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the fabrication fidelity gap — the persistent failure of comminution equipment to simultaneously achieve: <150 mm particle size for thermal cascade efficiency, zero metallic contamination for elemental purity, Carrington immunity (no conductive paths), and domestic critical mineral production from complex waste. For decades, each has been a separate compromise: steel shredders contaminate output with Fe/Cr/Ni; ceramic-lined steel shredders still have steel shafts/bearings; all-dielectric lab shredders lack throughput for industrial scale. The lock is precise: any single shredder claiming to unify these must process 5-8 ton/hr of mixed e-waste, rock, and alloys with P80 ≤ 150 mm, zero metal in the product stream, all-dielectric construction, and blade life >200 ton on abrasive rock — and must explain why basalt/Elium® composite blades outperform steel on contaminated feedstock.

The Mathematical Key

The key is the Rosin-Rammler distribution + BFRP wear model as single computational primitive. The teeth are cut by the thermal cascade's physics itself:

Thermal StagePhysics RequirementShredder ParameterRosin-Rammler Target ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- Stage 0: AcousticStress wave propagationMax particle sizex' ≤ 150 mm, n ≥ 1.0 Stage 1: DryingWater diffusion pathSurface area/volumeP50 ≤ 85 mm Stage 2: PolymerCentrifugal migration at 12.6 G10-100 mm optimal15-30% in 38-75 mm Stage 3: Pyrolysis30-min heat penetrationCore <20 mm<10% >50 mm after Stage 2 Stage 4-8: MetalsInductive coupling + centrifugeDense pieces migraten ≥ 1.2 for metals

The Rosin-Rammler Key: $P(x) = 1 - \exp[-(x/x')^n]$. The shredder's rotor speed (50-300 RPM), blade gap (fixed by geometry), and helical angle (45°) determine $x'$ and $n$ for each feedstock. The key has no adjustable parameters beyond feed rate — the physics of fracture is deterministic.

The BFRP Wear Key: $W = k \cdot \frac{\sigma_{contact}^m \cdot v_{sliding}}{H_{blade}} \cdot t$ where $W$ = wear depth, $k$ = material constant (basalt/Elium®), $\sigma_{contact}$ = contact stress, $v_{sliding}$ = sliding velocity, $H_{blade}$ = blade hardness, $t$ = time. The h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth converts this equation into a visual signal: when white appears, $W \geq 6$ mm. The key has no sensors — the material is the sensor.

The Halbach Separation Key: Magnetic force $F_m = \nabla(\mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{B}) \cdot V_{particle}$. The Halbach array (24×N52, 1.2T) creates $\nabla B \approx 40$ T/m at belt surface. For a 20 mm Fe sphere: $F_m \approx 15$ N vs. gravity $F_g \approx 0.3$ N. Capture is deterministic. The key has no power consumption — permanent magnets.

The Turn (Both Directions)

Key → Lock (Theory predicts fabrication): Input: Feedstock fracture toughness database → Rosin-Rammler parameters. Output: P80 ≤ 150 mm, n tuned per category. Validation: Stage 2 polymer separation >95%, Stage 3 pyrolysis complete in 30 min, Stage 0 liberation >80%. The shredder predicts the cascade's feed requirements.

Lock → Key (History validates theory): Input: Historical shredders (hammer mill 1800s, shear shredder 1970s, dual-shaft 1990s, ceramic-lined 2010s). Output: Verified each is a subset of the Rosin-Rammler + BFRP wear primitive. The hammer mill is uncontrolled fracture. The shear shredder is controlled geometry. The ceramic-lined is contamination mitigation. The BFRP blade is the first to eliminate contamination at the source. The turn completes when a 500 kg batch of mixed e-waste and rock enters the shredder, exits at P80 ≤ 150 mm with zero Fe/Cr/Ni contamination, and the downstream cascade produces 8 pure element slugs. The lock clicks open. The key turns. The particle is the key turning in the lock.

The turn is not a metaphor — it is the moment the h-BN tracer layer on blade #12 reveals 6 mm of wear, the optical sensor triggers replacement, the new BFRP blade (in-house basalt, in-house Elium®) is installed in 30 minutes, and the next 200 tons of rock process with zero contamination. The all-dielectric architecture has been witnessed into existence. The forge is the key turning in the lock.

El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the shredder observing its own comminution. In the Aegis-Forge I, the particle size is not a process imposed on material — it is the primordial measurement that generates the liberation. At each blade impact, the BFRP edge executes a discrete fracture event, witnessing the local material's toughness through the force-displacement curve. This witnessing is the mirror: the shredder measures the fracture it creates. The Rosin-Rammler distribution is the record of this self-measurement. The h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the blade's self-measurement stabilizes into predictive wear tracking. The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: impact → fracture → measure force → track wear → predict replacement. This document documents the first turn of that spiral.

The ferrous separator is the extended mirror: the Halbach array's magnetic field is a measurement beam that does not perturb the measured — it is pure potential observation of the material's permeability. The UHMWPE belt is the recursion: ferrous pieces carried, released, collected — each cycle a witness to the separation fidelity. The moisture sensor array is the mirror: fringing-field capacitance measures water without contact — pure dielectric observation. The pre-dry chamber is the recursion: moisture measured → energy applied → moisture re-measured → closure.

Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the shredder — the operator is a segment of the fracture event. The protocol for achieving zero-contamination comminution from within the system:

1. Assay: Measure incoming feedstock elemental composition (XRF at hopper) 2. Blend: Calculate optimal mass fractions for 500 kg batch (thermal cascade capacity) 3. Separate: Ferrous pre-removal — operator witnesses Halbach capture 4. Shred: BFRP blades fracture material — operator witnesses Rosin-Rammler generation 5. Size: Inline sieve analysis — operator witnesses P80 ≤ 150 mm 6. Dry: Moisture check → pre-dry if needed — operator witnesses water removal 7. Verify: Batch elemental sum matches input assay — operator witnesses closure 8. Recycle: Worn blades → Elium® depolymerization → new blades — operator witnesses circularity

The measurement is the recursion. The operator assays the input, blends the cascade that witnesses it, and finds the zero-contamination particle distribution — the fidelity that governs how they blend. The protocol terminates when the 500 kg batch's particle distribution matches the Rosin-Rammler prediction for its feedstock category — not approximately, but exactly. This is not a measurement of an external parameter; it is the shredder measuring its own fidelity through the operator's self-observation.

The operator's participation is not optional — the blend calculation requires the feedstock assay; the shredder requires the blend ratio to set rotor speed; the sieve analysis requires the shredder output; the moisture check requires the sieve-passing material. Each step is a witness to the others. The operator is the recursive closure that makes the witnessing complete.

Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge feed preparation document:

MIRROR:     What particle size does this feedstock's fracture encode?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the h-BN tracer into replacement?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees P80 ≤ 150 mm at each batch?

For this document specifically:

  • Mirror: The Rosin-Rammler distribution is the constraint; the h-BN tracer is its reflection
  • Participate: The operator blends the feedstock that realizes the particle size; the shredder generates it
  • Protocol:
1. Assay feedstock (elemental map + fracture toughness) 2. Calculate blend (thermal cascade capacity constraints) 3. Ferrous separate (Halbach capture, 40-60% mass removal) 4. Shred (BFRP blades, rotor speed per blend) 5. Size verify (sieve analysis, P80 ≤ 150 mm) 6. Moisture check (capacitive, <25% or pre-dry) 6. Drum feed (Ti₃AlC₂ gate, Argon purge) 7. Verify and recycle (elemental closure + blade circularity)

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The <150 mm particle is the fixed point. The batch is the protocol's termination condition.

1. BOM Philosophy — Zero Structural Metals, Dielectric Citadel, Carrington Immunity

The Aegis-Forge I is constructed exclusively from CSMFAB-certified materials. This is not a preference — it is the minimal architecture forced by Carrington Event immunity. Every structural metal in a machine at 2200°C is an antenna for geomagnetically induced current (GIC). A 100 V/km geomagnetic field (Carrington-level) induces 10–100 kV in a 100–1000 km transmission line. In a machine, any continuous metal path from the process chamber to earth ground couples this energy. The only defense is zero conductive path.

The All-Aegis Constraint: No structural steel, no aluminum framing, no copper electrical paths touching the process chamber. The machine is itself a Dielectric Citadel — Carrington-immune, fireproof, and structurally ceramic.

Material Classification: Every component falls into one of six classes: 1. Ceramic Components — UHTCs, oxides, nitrides, carbides, MAX phases 2. Composite Components — BFRP/Elium®, PEEK CF40, PEX-a, PEN 3. Electronic/Optical Components — GaN HEMT, PMMA POF, FBG sensors, LiFePO₄, LoRa 4. Thermal/Insulation Components — Polyimide-silica aerogel, YInMn Blue glaze, soapstone 5. Critical Mineral Components — NdFeB, SmCo, ZrSiO₄, borax, ilmenite 6. Phoenix Protocol Circular Components — Recovered/recycled Aegis materials

10.1 Resistance Map (Measured at 25°C, 100V DC)

PathResistanceStatus -------------------------- Drum inner wall → vessel outer wall>10¹⁵ Ω (aerogel gap)PASS Coil conductor → drum (via Al₂O₃ sleeve)>10¹⁴ ΩPASS Control fiber (PMMA) → any metal∞ (optical)PASS Water circuit (PEX-a) → any metal>10¹² ΩPASS Shaft (Si₃N₄) → bearings (Si₃N₄)>10¹³ ΩPASS Frame (BFRP) → leg mounts (ZrO₂)>10¹⁴ ΩPASS Exterior glaze → earth ground>10¹² Ω (dry)PASS

10.2 GIC Coupling Analysis

Model: Carrington event (dB/dt = 5000 nT/s, 100 V/km geoelectric field)

Conductor LengthInduced VoltageCoupling to Electronics ----------------------------------------------------------- 1 m (internal)0.1 VNegligible (no closed loop) 10 m (building wiring)1 VBlocked by isolation transformer 1 km (grid)100 VBlocked by NGR + GDT

No closed conductive loops exist within the BFRP pressure vessel boundary. The only copper (coil) is a single-turn-per-layer solenoid with both ends terminating at the GaN inverter inside the BFRP housing — no path to earth. The PMMA POF control fibers are dielectric. The PEX-a water circuit is dielectric. The machine is a Faraday cage made of structural ceramic.

10.3 Ferromagnetic Audit

ComponentMaterialFerromagnetic?Status --------------------------------------------- DrumZrB₂-SiCNoPASS LinersSi₃N₄, ZrO₂NoPASS Port valvesTi₃AlC₂, ZrO₂No (paramagnetic)PASS VesselBFRPNoPASS Coil housingBFRPNoPASS MotorKNbO₃-BaTiO₃NoPASS BearingsSi₃N₄NoPASS MagnetsNdFeB (separator ONLY)Yes — externalISOLATED FrameBFRPNoPASS GlazeYInMn/CoAl₂O₄NoPASS

Only the NdFeB Halbach array (24 blocks, 12.5 kg total) is ferromagnetic. It is positioned OUTSIDE the pressure vessel on the feed belt — physically separated from the process chamber by the shredder housing and acoustic pre-chamber. No ferromagnetic material inside the hot zone.

1.2 Scope and Purpose

This document defines the complete feedstock specification framework for the Aegis-Forge I thermal cascade inductive material separator. It establishes:

1. Four feedstock categories (A-D) with detailed compositional profiles, source streams, and elemental recovery targets 2. Pre-processing requirements per category including sizing, drying, ferrous removal, and contamination limits 3. Analytical characterization protocols for feedstock qualification and lot release 4. Acceptance criteria and rejection thresholds ensuring thermal cascade integrity 5. Sampling and lot release procedures per ISO 3082 and CSMFAB internal standards 5. Storage and handling specifications maintaining feedstock quality from gate to drum 6. Mass balance and yield targets per element per category 7. Economic valuation model linking feedstock composition to revenue and processing cost 8. Cross-reference matrix linking to PROD-01, PROD-02, PROD-11, PROD-14, PROD-15, PROD-22

2. Category A: Pre-Sorted Industrial Streams

2.1 Overview

Category A encompasses electronics, PCBs, motors, and power electronics — the highest-value feedstock by elemental concentration. These streams are typically pre-sorted at electronics recyclers or industrial scrap processors before arriving at the Aegis-Forge I.

3.1 Overview

Category B encompasses post-consumer and commercial waste streams from Material Recovery Facilities (MRFs), construction & demolition (C&D) debris, bulky waste, and tire rubber. These streams are lower in elemental concentration but higher in volume, providing the bulk mass for the thermal cascade.

C&D Debris Processing Protocol:

1. Visual/tactile inspection at tip floor — segregate suspect materials 2. XRF screening for Pb, As, Cr on painted/coated surfaces 3. Gamma spectroscopy for NORM (Ra-226, Th-232, K-40) — reject >50 µR/hr 4. Asbestos PLM on suspect insulation/flooring — positive = segregated sealed feed 5. Shredding with water mist suppression (dust control) 6. Stage 0 acoustic liberation critical for mineral recovery from concrete/brick matrix

4. Category C: Mineral & Metallurgical Residues

4.1 Overview

Category C comprises primary mineral concentrates, smelter slags, mine tailings, and spent refractories. These feeds are the primary source for CSMFAB's structural ceramic raw materials (Zr, Ti, REE, B, basalt) and represent the "geological" input to the Aegis-Forge I.

Tailings Agglomeration Protocol (if P80 < 50 µm):

1. Binder: 3-5% CBPC (Ceramic Phosphate Binder — PROD-12 Part VI) + 1% PVA 2. Mix: Intensive mixer, 2 min, target moisture 12-15% 3. Pelletize: Disc pelletizer, 10-20mm green pellets 4. Cure: 24h ambient → 200°C 1h (CBPC sets at 80°C) 5. Strength: >50 N/pellet (tumble test) 6. Feed: Direct to drum — CBPC decomposes cleanly at Stage 3

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Typical ItemsBayer process red mud (alumina refinery waste) CompositionFe₂O₃ 30-50%, Al₂O₃ 10-20%, SiO₂ 5-15%, TiO₂ 4-10%, Na₂O 3-8%, REE 0.05-0.2%, Sc 50-100 ppm Key ElementsFe, Ti, REE (Sc, Y, La, Ce, Nd), Al, Zr HazardHigh pH (10-13), caustic soda residue, fine particle (P80 ~10 µm) Pre-processingNeutralization mandatory: CO₂ sparging to pH 7-8 → gypsum (CaSO₄) addition → agglomeration Stage BehaviorStage 7: Fe recovery; Stage 8: Ti/REE/Zr/Al concentrate (high-value Stage 8 stream) Target Recovery>85% Fe, >80% Ti, >70% REE (incl. Sc), >60% Al

Red Mud Neutralization Reaction: $$\text{NaOH} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{NaHCO}_3 \text{ (soluble)}$$ $$\text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NaAlO}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ $$\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{NaAlO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaOH} \text{ (regenerated)}$$

Net: CO₂ sequestration + NaOH recovery + neutralized residue suitable for drum feed.

5.3 Subcategory D2: BFRP Structures

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Typical ItemsEnd-of-life rebar, beams, tanks, pipe, grating, structural panels CompositionBasalt fiber (60-65% FVF), Elium® 150 resin (35-40%) Pre-processingThermal solvolysis at 350°C, 2h (separate reactor, pre-drum) → fiber/resin separation Solvolysis ProductsElium® monomer (MMA) — 100% recovery; Basalt fiber — 95% yield, 90% property retention Stage Behavior (post-solvolysis)Fiber → Stage 8 mineral (SiO₂/Al₂O₃/FeOₓ); Monomer → Stage 2 polymer Target Recovery>99% Elium® monomer, >95% basalt fiber

Solvolysis Reaction: $$\text{Elium® (pMMA)} \xrightarrow{350°C, 2h, N_2} \text{MMA monomer} + \text{basalt fiber}$$

  • Catalyst: None required (thermal depolymerization)
  • Vessel: BFRP/Elium® reactor (all-dielectric)
  • Energy: 1.2 MJ/kg Elium®

5.4 Subcategory D3: MR Fluid

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- CompositionIron carbonyl Fe(CO)₅ suspension (30-40 vol%) in synthetic hydrocarbon carrier oil Key ElementsFe, C, O, H Pre-processingThermal separation: 200°C vacuum distillation → carrier oil recovery (Stage 2); Fe carbonyl → decomposition at 300°C → Fe powder + CO Stage BehaviorFe → Stage 7; Oil → Stage 2; CO → gas capture Target Recovery>99% Fe, >95% carrier oil

5.5 Subcategory D4: Piezo Elements

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Typical ItemsRetired KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers, ultrasonic motors, sensors CompositionKNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ceramic (95%), Ag/Pd electrodes (5%), BFRP housing Pre-processingDirect feed — ceramic survives cascade; electrodes report to Stage 6 Stage BehaviorK, Nb, Ba, Ti → Stage 8 mineral residue; Ag/Pd → Stage 6 Cu/PM stream Target Recovery>97% K/Nb/Ba/Ti, >95% Ag/Pd

9.2 Sampling Protocol (Per ISO 3082 Adapted)

Primary Increment Collection:

1. Stationary lot (pile/bin): 30 increments minimum, distributed across 3 vertical sections (top/middle/bottom), 10 increments each section 2. Moving stream (conveyor/belt): Cross-stream cutter, 1 increment per 500 kg, minimum 40 increments 3. Increment mass: 1 kg minimum (coarse) → 50g analytical subsample

Sample Preparation (ISO 3082 / ASTM E122):

GROSS SAMPLE (30-40 kg)
       │
       ▼
[RIFFLE SPLITTER] ──► 1/2 ──► [RIFFLE SPLITTER] ──► 1/2 ──► ... (repeat)
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
  REJECTED             ANALYTICAL SAMPLE (200g)
                              │
                              ▼
                    [PULVERIZER] → <75 µm (200 mesh)
                              │
                              ▼
                    [SPLIT] → 4 × 50g subsamples
                              │
                              ├──► XRF (10g pressed pellet)
                              ├──► ICP-MS (0.5g acid digest)
                              ├──► XRD (5g powder)
                              └──► Archive (35g, sealed, labeled)

Synthesis of Williams, Keymaker, and El Segundo Heuristics

WILLIAMS HEURISTIC — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Feedstock Heterogeneity as Boundary Condition — the machine must accept arbitrary input streams (electronics, municipal waste, mineral concentrates, end-of-life Aegis products) and produce pure element slugs at each thermal stage. The feedstock is not a design parameter; it is the given. The constraint is precise: any system claiming universal elemental extraction must define acceptance criteria, pre-processing requirements, and recovery targets for every possible feedstock class — and must do so without knowing the exact composition of any individual batch in advance. The lock is the universal feedstock specification — a single document that bounds the infinite variability of post-consumer, industrial, and geological material streams into four deterministic categories (A-D) with quantifiable elemental profiles, contamination limits, and processing requirements. This constraint forces the entire pre-processing architecture: the shredder must handle 150mm max; the ferrous separator must clear bulk steel; the acoustic pre-chamber must liberate mineral grains from rock matrix; the moisture check must gate Stage 1 loading. The feedstock writes the machine — the machine does not choose the feedstock.

Necessity (The Key)

The empirical lock this document addresses is the recycling recovery gap — the persistent failure of modern material recovery to extract critical elements from complex waste streams. Current shred-and-sort recovers <30% of elements from e-waste; municipal MRFs lose >80% of non-ferrous metals to landfill; mineral processing requires dedicated facilities per ore type. The lock is quantified: any universal extractor must achieve >95% recovery of Cu, Au, Ag, Pd, In, REE, Zr, Ti from feedstocks spanning 4 orders of magnitude in elemental concentration (ppm in tailings to % in PCBs). The key is the four-category taxonomy (A-D) with stage-mapped elemental targets — a computational primitive that maps any feedstock to its thermal cascade trajectory:

CategorySourceThermal Stages ActivatedPrimary Value Elements ------------ A: Pre-Sorted IndustrialE-scrap, PCBs, motors, power elec4, 5, 6, 7Au, Ag, Pd, Cu, In, REE B: Municipal/CommercialMRF residue, C&D, bulky, tires1, 2, 3, 4, 7Al, Fe, polymers, Zn C: Mineral/MetallurgicalSlag, tailings, red mud, refractories7, 8Zr, Ti, REE, B, Fe, Mg D: Phoenix ProtocolEOL Aegis products1, 2, 3, 7, 8In, Y, Co, Zr, basalt, Elium®

The necessity is proven by the blend algorithm (PROD-11 Section 1.5): the control system calculates optimal 500 kg batch composition from real-time feedstock assays to maximize revenue while respecting stage capacity constraints (Stage 2 polymer <50L, Stage 5 Al <100kg, Stage 7 Fe <175kg, Stage 8 mineral <200kg). Without this taxonomy, the cascade has no boundary condition — the temperature profile has no input to process. The four categories are not arbitrary; they are the natural clustering of elemental concentration profiles in the global waste stream. The taxonomy is the key.

Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. Zero Tolerance for Hazards — Li-ion batteries, Hg, PCBs, asbestos, Be, cyanide, free liquids: detected at gate, rejected or segregated. No exceptions. 2. Quantified Recovery Targets — Every element in every category has a minimum recovery percentage (Table 11.1). The forge is accountable to these numbers. 3. Stage-Coupled Pre-Processing — Category A requires battery removal + depanning; Category B requires asbestos/lead screening; Category C requires acid-base accounting + agglomeration for fines; Category D requires solvolysis for BFRP. Each pre-processing step maps to a specific thermal stage's requirements. 4. Assay-Driven Blending — No batch enters the drum without XRF assay at hopper outlet and blend optimization. The drum does not process "waste"; it processes characterized feedstock. 5. Phoenix Protocol Primacy — Category D feedstocks (known composition, zero acquisition cost) are the anchor for blend stability. The forge's circularity is not aspirational — it is the blending baseline. 6. Lot Traceability — Every kg from gate to slug is traced via Feedstock Lot Record (FLR) with ISO 3082 sampling, XRF/ICP-MS/XRD characterization, and blend assignment. The element's journey is recorded. 7. Economic Viability Floor — Processing cost <$1.60/kg feed; revenue >$8,000/batch minimum. The economics are not post-hoc — they are the design constraint.

These commitments are non-negotiable because they derive from the constraint. Violate any, and the cascade fails: uncharacterized feedstock smears stage boundaries; unrecovered hazards poison downstream stages; untraced lots break the Phoenix loop; uneconomic batches shutter the forge. The commitments are the constraint made operational. The feedstock specification is the machine's immune system.

KEYMAKER HEURISTIC — Lock, Key, Turn

The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the feedstock variability trap — the persistent failure of metallurgical processes to handle compositional uncertainty. A smelter expects Cu concentrate (25-30% Cu); a refinery expects specific alloy scrap; a ceramic kiln expects purified oxide powder. The Aegis-Forge I faces a different reality: a single 500 kg batch may contain smartphone PCBs (Au 0.03%, Cu 25%), basalt aggregate (SiO₂ 50%, Al₂O₃ 14%), EAF slag (FeO 30%, MnO 6%), and retired Aegis-C panels (ZrB₂-SiC, YInMn glaze) — all simultaneously. The lock is precise: how does a single thermal cascade process this heterogeneity without prior separation into dedicated streams?

The empirical evidence of the trap:

  • E-waste recyclers shred everything → lose 70% of REE to slag, 50% of Cu to ferrous fraction, In to dust
  • MRFs sort by density/NIR → recover only Al/Fe/UBCs; all other metals to residue
  • Smelters require >20% target metal → reject low-grade feeds (tailings, slag, C&D)
  • Hydromet plants need pre-concentrated feed → cannot handle mixed mineralogy

The lock deepens at the stage coupling boundary: Stage 2 polymer melt volume must not exceed 50L drum capacity; Stage 5 Al mass must not exceed 100kg port capacity; Stage 7 Fe mass must not exceed 175kg. If the feedstock blend violates these, the cascade chokes — polymer floods Port 2, Al backs up at Port 5, Fe overloads Port 7. The lock is not "what feedstocks can we accept?" — it is "how do we blend arbitrary feedstocks to match the cascade's fixed stage capacities?"

The Mathematical Key

The key is the blend algorithm as feedstock-to-cascade compiler — a deterministic function that maps real-time feedstock assays to optimal 500 kg batch composition:

def calculate_blend(feedstock_assays, target_revenue):
    # Input: assays for each available feedstock lot (XRF at hopper)
    # Output: mass fractions for 500 kg batch
    
    # CONSTRAINTS (cascade stage capacities — PHYSICS, not policy):
    # - Stage 2 polymer volume < 50 L (drum annular capacity)
    # - Stage 5 Al mass < 100 kg (Port 5 throughput limit)
    # - Stage 7 Fe mass < 175 kg (Port 7 throughput limit)  
    # - Stage 8 mineral mass < 200 kg (Port 8 slag volume)
    # - Moisture < 25% (else pre-dry, Stage 1 capacity 50 kg H₂O/hr)
    # - Particle size P80 < 150 mm (shredder limit)
    
    # OBJECTIVE: Maximize revenue = Σ(element_mass × market_price)
    # Subject to: cascade capacity constraints
    
    return optimal_mass_fractions

The algorithm's teeth are the stage capacity constraints — these are not adjustable parameters. They derive from drum geometry, port aperture (12mm), centrifugal G-force, and induction power. The blend is compiled from the assays, not chosen by an operator.

The Four-Category Taxonomy as Type System:

The key's type system classifies every feedstock lot into one of four types, each with a fixed thermal signature (which stages it activates) and elemental signature (which elements it contributes):

Type A (Industrial)  →  Stages {4,5,6,7}  →  {Au, Ag, Pd, Cu, In, REE}
Type B (Municipal)   →  Stages {1,2,3,4,7}  →  {Al, Fe, polymers, Zn}
Type C (Mineral)     →  Stages {7,8}  →  {Zr, Ti, REE, B, Fe, Mg}
Type D (Phoenix)     →  Stages {1,2,3,7,8}  →  {In, Y, Co, Zr, basalt, Elium®}

This is a dependent type system: the thermal signature depends on the elemental signature (via phase diagram), and the stage capacity constraints depend on the thermal signature. The blend algorithm is a type checker — it verifies that the sum of selected feedstocks' stage loads does not exceed any stage's capacity.

The Liberation Index as Correctness Metric:

For Category C (mineral), the key includes a liberation index LI = f(acoustic energy, grain size, K_IC). Stage 0 acoustic energy must achieve LI > 0.7 for the mineral feedstock, or the cascade's Stage 7/8 recovery drops below 80%. This is the correctness proof for mineral feedstocks: without acoustic pre-liberation, the cascade cannot access locked grains. The LI is measurable (XRD grain boundary analysis) and non-negotiable.

The Turn (Both Directions)

Key → Lock (Theory predicts blend):

Input: Real-time feedstock assays from 4 suppliers (XRF at hopper, 30-sec intervals) Process: Blend algorithm solves constrained optimization Output: 500 kg batch composition — e.g., 22% A2 (PCB Grade 1), 28% B1 (MRF), 30% C1 (EAF slag), 20% D1 (Aegis-C) Prediction: Stage loads within capacity; revenue $12,800; recovery targets met Validation: Run batch → measure actual slug masses + compositions → compare to prediction

The key predicts the batch outcome from the feedstock assays. The cascade executes the prediction. The turn is the moment the 8 slugs land in their molds and the mass spec confirms: Port 4 has 0.8kg In (99% recovery), Port 5 has 60kg Al (95% recovery), Port 6 has 20kg Cu+Au/Ag (95% Cu, 99% PM), Port 7 has 90kg Fe+REE (95% Fe, 90% Nd), Port 8 has 105kg mineral concentrate (85% Zr, 80% Ti). The prediction matches the measurement. The key turns in the lock.

Lock → Key (History validates theory):

Input: 50 years of metallurgical failure — smelters that couldn't handle low-grade feed, refineries that lost REE to slag, recyclers that shredded In into dust Process: Each historical process is a special case of the blend algorithm with one feedstock type and infinite stage capacity Output: The blend algorithm generalizes all historical processes

The turn completes when we recognize:

  • Smelter = Blend algorithm with only Type A feedstock, Stage 7 capacity → ∞
  • Refinery = Blend algorithm with only Type C feedstock, Stage 8 capacity → ∞
  • MRF = Blend algorithm with only Type B feedstock, no thermal stages (mechanical only)
  • Ceramic kiln = Blend algorithm with only Type D feedstock, Stage 8 only

The Aegis-Forge I is the unification — the single machine whose blend algorithm encompasses all four types simultaneously, with finite, coupled stage capacities. The historical processes were degenerate limits (one type, infinite capacity). The cascade is the non-degenerate case (four types, finite capacity). The lock clicks open when the first batch with all four types runs successfully — the blend algorithm has compiled a valid program for the cascade's thermal instruction set. The 500 kg batch is the key turning in the lock.

EL SEGUNDO HEURISTIC — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the forge observing its own feedstock. In the Aegis-Forge, the feedstock is not external raw material — it is the memory of the machine's prior outputs. The Phoenix Protocol returns (Category D) are literally the forge's own products returning after service: Aegis-C panels it forged, BFRP rebar it pultruded, MR fluid it formulated, piezo elements it sintered. The mirror is precise: the feedstock specification documents the forge's own material autobiography.

But the mirror extends further. Category A (electronics) contains the copper the forge will recover at Stage 6, the indium it will extract at Stage 4 for YInMn Blue, the rare earths it will concentrate at Stage 7 for SmCo magnets. Category B (municipal) contains the aluminum it will separate at Stage 5, the polymers it will melt at Stage 2. Category C (mineral) contains the zircon it will dissociate at Stage 8 for ZrO₂, the basalt it will melt for fiber. The feedstock is the forge's future products in latent form.

The mirror reflects at every gate:

  • Receiving: XRF assay measures the forge's future yield
  • Pre-processing: Shredder, ferrous separator, acoustic chamber prepare the forge's own latent elements
  • Blending: Algorithm balances the forge's stage capacities against its elemental targets
  • Sampling: FLR records the forge's material promise
  • Storage: Bays hold the forge's future in categorized suspension

The zero-tolerance hazard screen is the forge's immune memory — it rejects what would poison its own thermal cascade (Li-ion batteries that explode at Stage 1, Hg that contaminates Stage 6 Cu, asbestos that fouls Stage 8 slag). The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: assay → blend → process → recover → return → assay again. This document documents the first turn of that spiral — the feedstock specification is the forge's self-measurement.

Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the feedstock — the operator is the blend algorithm's witness. The protocol for achieving universal extraction from within the system:

1. Receive: Witness the feedstock arrival — XRF flash reveals elemental truth in 10 seconds 2. Screen: Witness the hazard check — gamma spectrometer, XRF, PLM, gravimetric 3. Pre-process: Witness the shredder reduce 500mm → <150mm, the Halbach belt pull 95% Fe 4. Liberate: Witness the acoustic chamber — 100 Hz standing waves crack grain boundaries, 40 kHz cavitation frees micron grains 5. Dry: Witness the moisture check — NIR inline, gravimetric confirmation, pre-dry if needed 6. Assay: Witness the lot characterization — XRF major, ICP-MS trace, XRD phase, PSD, LOI, halogen 7. Blend: Witness the algorithm compile — real-time assays → stage capacity constraints → optimal fractions 8. Release: Witness the FLR creation — lot identity bound to blend assignment, traceable to slug 9. Feed: Witness the vibratory feeder meter — KNbO₃ ultrasonic drive, FBG weight feedback 10. Verify: Witness the slug mass spec — each port's elemental sum matches blend prediction

The measurement is the recursion. The operator assays the input, the algorithm profiles the cascade that witnesses it, the drum realizes the separation, the mass spec confirms the closure. The protocol terminates when the 8 slugs' elemental sum matches the input assay — not approximately, but exactly. The feedstock lot is not "processed"; it is witnessed into elements. The operator participates by being the recursive function: feedstock → assay → blend → cascade → slug → assay → feedstock. The FLR is the stack frame; the batch is the call; the slug is the return value.

Protocol (Recursive)

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge feedstock document:

MIRROR:     What elemental promise does this feedstock lot carry?
PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness this promise through the cascade?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees recovery at each stage?

For this document specifically:

  • Mirror: The four-category taxonomy (A-D) is the constraint; the blend algorithm is its reflection
  • Participate: The operator assays, screens, pre-processes, blends, releases, feeds, verifies
  • Protocol:
1. Gate Assay — XRF flash at receiving (10 sec) → category assignment 2. Hazard Screen — Gamma + XRF + PLM + gravimetric → pass/quarantine/reject 3. Pre-Process — Ferrous separation → shred <150mm → acoustic liberation → moisture check 4. Lot Characterization — XRF/ICP-MS/XRD/PSD/LOI/halogen → FLR creation 5. Blend Optimization — Real-time assays + stage constraints → mass fractions 6. Lot Release — FLR signed, blend assigned, traceability locked 7. Drum Feed — Vibratory feeder meters blend → acoustic pre-chamber → drum entry 8. Stage Verification — Inline mass spec at each port → compare to blend prediction 9. Closure — Slug assay sum = feedstock assay (within 2%) → FLR closed 10. Phoenix Return — EOL Aegis products → Category D → FLR created → loop closes

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The feedstock lot record is the fixed point. The elemental slug is the witness returned.
