2. Stage 0: Acoustic Mineral Liberation

2.1 Liberation Physics — The Fundamental Mechanism

2.1.1 Grain Boundary Fatigue

The AMLS exploits the inherent weakness of mineral grain boundaries in rock matrices. Unlike crushing (compressive overload → transgranular fracture + fines), acoustic liberation applies cyclic tensile stress at the grain's matrix-constrained resonant frequency, inducing progressive fatigue failure at grain boundaries.

Grain boundary fracture toughness: $$K_{IC}^{gb} \approx 1.5 \text{ MPa·m}^{0.5}$$ (Compared to transgranular $K_{IC} \approx 3.5 \text{ MPa·m}^{0.5}$ for zircon)

Stress wave equation in heterogeneous media: $$\nabla^2 \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{u}}{\partial t^2}$$ Where $\mathbf{u}$ is the displacement vector, $c$ is the phase velocity in the composite matrix.

Acoustic stress at grain boundary: $$\sigma_{acoustic} = \rho c \omega A$$ Where $\rho$ = density (4650 kg/m³ for zircon), $c$ = wave speed, $\omega$ = angular frequency, $A$ = displacement amplitude.

At AMLS operating parameters:

  • LF (100 Hz, $A \approx 50 \mu m$): $\sigma_{LF} \approx 2.9 \text{ MPa}$ — below single-cycle fracture, accumulates over $10^3-10^6$ cycles
  • US (40 kHz, $A \approx 5 \mu m$): $\sigma_{US} \approx 1.2 \text{ MPa}$ at grain boundary, enhanced by cavitation microjets to local 100+ MPa

2.1.2 Matrix-Constrained Resonance

The effective resonant frequency of a mineral grain embedded in a rock matrix drops from MHz (free grain) to the seismic range (10-500 Hz):

Free grain resonance (isolated): $$f_{free} = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}}$$

Matrix-constrained resonance (seismic range): $$f_{eff} \approx f_{free} \times \sqrt{\frac{K_{gb}}{K_{matrix}}} \times \left(\frac{V_{grain}}{V_{matrix}}\right)^{1/3}$$

For zircon ($E=220$ GPa, $\rho=4650$ kg/m³, $L=0.5$ mm): $f_{free} \approx 1.7$ MHz In silica matrix: $f_{eff} \approx 50-200$ Hz — matching earthquake disaggregation frequencies.

This matrix-constrained resonance is the acoustic lock that the AMLS key (frequency sweep) must turn.

2.1.3 Cavitation-Induced Liberation

Ultrasonic frequencies (40 kHz) produce cavitation in water:

  • Water molecules cannot follow rapid negative pressure excursions → vacuum microbubbles form
  • Microbubble collapse (implosion in <1 µs): Local pressure 10²-10³ bar, temperature 5000-10000°C, microjet velocity 100-300 m/s
  • This localized shock concentrates at grain boundary interfaces — the weakest points in rock

Rayleigh-Plesset equation for bubble dynamics: $$R\ddot{R} + \frac{3}{2}\dot{R}^2 = \frac{1}{\rho}\left(P_g - P_\infty - P_{ac}(t) - \frac{2\sigma}{R} - \frac{4\mu\dot{R}}{R}\right)$$

At collapse ($R_{min}/R_0 \approx 0.01$):

  • Local pressure: $P_{collapse} \sim 1$ GPa (theoretical), ~1000 bar (measured)
  • Strain rate: $\dot{\epsilon} \sim 10^9$ s⁻¹

Cavitation threshold intensity: $$I_{cav} = \frac{P_{cav}^2}{2\rho c} \approx 1-3 \text{ W/cm}^2$$ AMLS operating intensity: 25 W/cm² at probe face — well above threshold.

2.1.4 Fatigue Accumulation Model

Grain boundary failure follows Miner's rule for cumulative fatigue damage: $$D = \sum_{i} \frac{n_i}{N_i}$$ Where $n_i$ = cycles at stress level $\sigma_i$, $N_i$ = cycles to failure at $\sigma_i$.

For sinusoidal loading at $\sigma_a = 2.9$ MPa (LF array): $$N_f \approx 10^6 \text{ cycles} \quad \text{at} \quad \sigma_a / \sigma_{UTS}^{gb} \approx 0.15$$ With 100 Hz sweep over 15 min (900 s): $n = 90,000$ cycles per frequency step. 30-second dwell at 20 frequencies: $D \approx 0.9$ — near complete boundary failure.

2.2.2 Standing Wave Control

BFRP chamber natural frequencies: $$f_{chamber,n} = \frac{n c_{air}}{2L} \quad \text{(axial modes, } c_{air} \approx 343 \text{ m/s)}$$ $$f_{chamber,m} = \frac{\alpha_{mn} c_{air}}{2\pi R} \quad \text{(radial modes)}$$ For 600 mm diameter × 400 mm length:

  • Fundamental axial: $f_1 \approx 425$ Hz
  • Fundamental radial: $f_{01} \approx 185$ Hz

Standing wave mitigation: 1. Asymmetric transducer mounting — 8 LF plates at irregular angular positions (not 45° regular) 2. Chamber wall damping — BFRP viscoelastic loss factor η = 0.02-0.03 dissipates standing waves 3. Water coupling — Water fill (10-15L) disrupts air-mode standing waves 4. Bidirectional sweep — 20→500→20 Hz captures resonances from both directions

2.4 Liberation Index Metric

2.4.1 Definition

Liberation Index (LI) quantifies the fraction of target mineral grains fully liberated from the rock matrix:

$$LI = \frac{N_{liberated}}{N_{total}} \times 100\%$$

Where:

  • $N_{liberated}$ = grains with >90% surface exposed (free particles)
  • $N_{total}$ = total grains of target mineral in sample

Measurement method: Automated SEM-EDS particle analysis on representative subsample (ISO 3082 sampling).

2.4.2 CSM-Specific Liberation Targets

2.4.3 Liberation Index Feedback Control

The AMLS uses real-time LI estimation via FBG vibration damping:

1. FBG sensors on chamber wall measure vibration transmissibility 2. As grains liberate, effective chamber damping changes (free particles absorb more energy) 3. DSP correlates damping increase with LI calibration curves 4. When LI > target (default 75%), sweep terminates early (minimum 10 min)

3. Stage 1: Infrared Drying (80-150°C)

3.1 Target Materials & Physics

3.1.1 Moisture Species and Release Temperatures

Moisture TypeSourceRelease TempMechanism ------------------------------------------------ Free surface waterAll wet feeds80-100°CEvaporation Crystal-bound waterGypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O)107-120°CDehydration Crystal-bound waterBorax (Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O)100-140°CDehydration Crystal-bound waterKaolin (Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄)150°CPartial dehydration Low-boiling organicsAlcohols, acetone residues80-150°CVaporization PCB flux solventsTerpineol (Tb=218°C)>150°CBegins at Stage 1 end

3.1.2 Why Infrared (Not Induction)?

Induction heating is ineffective at 80-150°C because:

  • Target materials (water, hydrated minerals, organics) are non-conductive (ρ > 10⁸ Ω·m)
  • Induction couples to conductivity (eddy currents) and permeability (hysteresis)
  • Water has ε'' (dielectric loss) peak at 3 µm and 6 µm — ideal for IR absorption

IR absorption spectrum of water:

  • Primary peak: 3.0 µm (O-H stretch)
  • Secondary peak: 6.3 µm (H-O-H bend)
  • SiC glow bar emission peak: ~3.6 µm at 800-900°C surface temp
  • Match: SiC IR output overlaps water absorption peak → high coupling efficiency

3.5 Water and Volatile Recovery

Exiting vapor (mostly H₂O) exits through Port 1 (150°C set-point):

1. Condensation: BFRP heat exchanger (chilled to 10°C by PEX-a cooling circuit) 2. Liquid water collected: Analyzed for metal content (ICP-MS), either:

  • Purified (RO + UV) → reused as process water
  • Discharged if <1 ppm metals
3. Organic vapors: Trace quantity passes through activated carbon bed (char from Stage 3!)
  • Elegant closed cycle: Char from Stage 3 later used to adsorb Stage 1/2 organics
4. Gas composition monitoring: Online GC-MS on Port 1 exhaust
  • H₂O (primary), organics (<50 ppm), HCl (<10 ppm if PVC present), NH₃ (<5 ppm)

Water recovery rate: 90-95% of input moisture recovered as liquid water.

6. Control System Architecture

6.1 Stage 0 Control Hierarchy

The AMLS control system operates as a three-level hierarchy:

LEVEL 1: SUPERVISORY (Batch Level)
├── Batch recipe selection (feedstock category A-D)
├── Target LI setting (75% default, category-adjusted)
├── Total duration limit (30 min max)
└── Interlock: Drum ready, water level, N₂ pressure


LEVEL 2: SEQUENCE (Stage Level)
├── Phase 1: LF Sweep (20→500 Hz, 15 min)
├── Phase 2: US Cavitation (40 kHz, 15 min) — concurrent with LF
├── Phase 3: Resonant Dwell (extra 60s at detected peaks)
└── Phase 4: Drain & Transfer (5 min)



LEVEL 3: REAL-TIME (Cycle Level, 1 ms loop)
├── FBG vibration spectrum acquisition (1 kHz sample rate)
├── FFT computation (2048-point, 0.5 Hz resolution)
├── Peak detection & tracking (adaptive threshold)
├── Frequency/power setpoint update (per transducer)
└── Phase-lock maintenance (all 16 channels synchronized)

6.2 Adaptive Frequency Sweep Algorithm

The core innovation of the AMLS is feedstock-adaptive frequency targeting:

def adaptive_sweep(fbg_spectrum, current_freq, dwell_timer):
    """
    Input: FBG vibration spectrum (magnitude vs frequency)
    Output: Next frequency setpoint, dwell extension
    """
    # Detect resonant peaks >3 dB above local baseline
    peaks = find_peaks(fbg_spectrum, prominence=3, distance=5)  # Hz
    
    # Classify peaks by mineral signature (pre-calibrated library)
    mineral_matches = {}
    for peak_freq in peaks:
        for mineral, sig in MINERAL_SIGNATURES.items():
            if abs(peak_freq - sig.freq) < sig.bandwidth:
                mineral_matches[mineral] = peak_freq
    
    # Priority dwell extension for high-value minerals
    dwell_extension = 0
    if 'zircon' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 60  # Extra 60s at zircon resonance
    if 'bastnasite' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 45
    if 'ilmenite' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 30
    
    # Continue sweep unless at final frequency
    if current_freq >= 500:
        return SWEEP_COMPLETE, dwell_extension
    else:
        next_freq = current_freq * 1.122  # Logarithmic step (1/6 octave)
        return min(next_freq, 500), dwell_extension


MINERAL_SIGNATURES = {
    'zircon': {'freq': 185, 'bandwidth': 15, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'bastnasite': {'freq': 95, 'bandwidth': 20, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'ilmenite': {'freq': 55, 'bandwidth': 10, 'priority': 'MED'},
    'quartz': {'freq': 280, 'bandwidth': 25, 'priority': 'LOW'},
    'feldspar': {'freq': 145, 'bandwidth': 15, 'priority': 'LOW'},
}

6.3 Phase-Locked Multi-Channel Synchronization

To prevent destructive interference between 16 transducer channels (8 LF + 8 US), all drivers are phase-locked to a master clock:

MASTER CLOCK (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC)
         │
         ├── LF CHANNEL 0 (0° reference)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 1 (+45°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 2 (+90°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 3 (+135°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 4 (+180°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 5 (+225°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 6 (+270°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 7 (+315°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 0 (40 kHz, 0°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 1 (40 kHz, +45°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 2 (40 kHz, +90°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 3 (40 kHz, +135°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 4 (40 kHz, +180°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 5 (40 kHz, +225°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 6 (40 kHz, +270°)
         └── US CHANNEL 7 (40 kHz, +315°)

Phase error budget: <5° at 40 kHz, <0.5° at 100 Hz (achieved via optical fiber distribution of master clock).

COMBINED HEURISTIC INTRODUCTION

PROD-14: Stage 0-1: Acoustic & Drying (Liberation Physics, IR Drying)

CSMFAB000000000114 — Aegis-Forge I TCIMS Product Document 14 of 40

Synthesis of Williams, Keymaker, and El Segundo Heuristics

WILLIAMS HEURISTIC — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment

Constraint (The Lock)

The Aegis-Forge I is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Liberation Precedes Separation — no thermal cascade can separate elements that remain locked in rock matrix. The feedstock enters the drum as composite particles (mineral grains cemented in silicate/oxide matrix), and induction heating only couples to conductive phases. If grains are not liberated before heating, the matrix shields them, induction cannot reach them, and they report to Stage 8 slag as unrecovered value. The constraint is precise: mechanical liberation at ambient temperature must achieve >75% grain freedom for target minerals before Stage 2 heating begins. This constraint forces the entire Stage 0 architecture: a dedicated pre-chamber, water-coupled acoustic energy, KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers (the only piezoelectric that survives the all-dielectric mandate), and a feedback loop that adapts frequency to the specific mineralogy of each batch. The liberation writes the cascade — without it, the thermal profile has nothing to separate.

Necessity (The Key)

The empirical lock this document addresses is the comminution energy gap — conventional crushing consumes 250-500 W/kg to achieve <50% liberation, generating fines that contaminate downstream stages. The key is the acoustic frequency sweep as single computational primitive — a logarithmic 20→500 Hz sweep (LF) + 40 kHz cavitation (US) that targets the matrix-constrained resonant frequency of embedded grains:

MechanismFrequencyPhysicsLiberation Gain ------------ LF Resonant Vibration20-500 HzGrain boundary fatigue (10³-10⁶ cycles)+250% for basalt US Cavitation40 kHzMicrojet shock (1000 bar, 10⁹ s⁻¹ strain)+95% for zircon Adaptive DwellFBG-guidedExtra 60s at mineral-specific peaks+15% LI overall

The necessity is proven by the liberation index (LI) feedback: FBG sensors on the chamber wall measure vibration damping as grains liberate; when LI >75%, the sweep terminates. Without Stage 0, Stage 7-8 REE/Zr recovery drops from >85% to <40% — the cascade fails its primary mandate. The acoustic sweep is the key.

Commitment (The Turn)

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

1. Zero Metallic Transducers — KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ only; no PZT (lead), no metallic bolts in acoustic path. ZrO₂ ceramic M10 bolts, PEEK CF40 back masses. 2. Water Coupling Mandatory — 10-15L water per batch; reclaimed post-Stage 0 for Stage 1 moisture management. No dry acoustic operation. 3. Adaptive Sweep Default — Logarithmic 20→500 Hz, 30s/step, +60s at FBG-identified resonances. No fixed-frequency operation. 4. Liberation Index Target — ≥75% LI for Category C feeds; ≥85% for Category A (PCB mineral fraction). Measured via SEM-EDS per lot. 5. Stage 1 IR Only — No induction heating at 80-150°C. SiC glow bars at 3.6 µm (water absorption peak). N₂ at 1.2 bar. 6. Moisture Verification Triad — FBG humidity + NIR inline + FBG mass loss. All three must agree <1% moisture. 7. Energy Cap — Stage 0 ≤ 3.2 kWh/batch; Stage 1 ≤ 62 kWh/batch. Total pre-thermal ≤ 65 kWh.

These commitments are non-negotiable because they derive from the constraint. Violate any, and the cascade fails: metallic transducers couple GIC; dry acoustic gives <20% LI; fixed frequency misses mineral resonances; induction at Stage 1 wastes 95% power on non-conductive water; single moisture sensor risks undetected wet feed. The commitments are the constraint made operational. The acoustic-drying pair is the forge's immune system against locked grains.

KEYMAKER HEURISTIC — Lock, Key, Turn

The Empirical Lock

The lock this document addresses is the liberation-separation coupling problem — how to achieve sharp mineral liberation at ambient temperature using only acoustic energy, then transition cleanly to thermal drying without cross-contamination or energy waste. The lock has three tumblers:

Tumbler 1 — Frequency Selectivity: A single rock contains zircon (target: 185 Hz), bastnäsite (95 Hz), ilmenite (55 Hz), quartz (280 Hz). A fixed-frequency transducer liberates one mineral at the expense of others. The lock demands simultaneous multi-mineral liberation.

Tumbler 2 — Energy Density: Cavitation threshold is 1-3 W/cm²; effective liberation requires 25 W/cm² at grain boundary. But 25 W/cm² at 40 kHz erodes probe tips in 5,000 hours. The lock demands high intensity without consumable destruction.

Tumbler 3 — Stage Coupling: Stage 0 discharges wet, liberated feedstock (10-15% moisture). Stage 1 must dry to <1% in 20 minutes using IR at 3.6 µm. But water vapor from Stage 1 condenses on Stage 2 polymer melt if not fully removed. The lock demands zero moisture carryover.

The lock deepens at the all-dielectric boundary: every component in the AMLS and IR dryer must be BFRP, ceramic, PEEK, or PEX-a. No steel shafts, no copper windings, no magnetic bearings. The transducer bolts are ZrO₂ ceramic. The IR emitter mounts are Al₂O₃. The control wiring is PMMA POF. This is not a preference — it is the minimal architecture forced by Carrington immunity.

The Mathematical Key

The key is the dual-mechanism acoustic primitive + IR absorption match — two computational primitives that solve the three tumblers simultaneously:

Primitive 1: The Adaptive Frequency Sweep (AFS)

def AFS(fbg_spectrum, mineral_library):
    """
    The key's first tooth: frequency as material selector.
    """
    # Detect peaks in chamber vibration response
    peaks = find_peaks(fbg_spectrum, prominence=3)
    
    # Match to mineral signatures (pre-calibrated)
    targets = {}
    for mineral, sig in mineral_library.items():
        if any(abs(p - sig.freq) < sig.bw for p in peaks):
            targets[mineral] = sig.freq
    
    # Generate dwell schedule: base 30s + priority bonus
    schedule = []
    for mineral, freq in targets.items():
        bonus = {'HIGH': 60, 'MED': 30, 'LOW': 0}[mineral_library[mineral].priority]
        schedule.append((freq, 30 + bonus))
    
    # Fill remaining sweep with logarithmic steps
    current = 20
    while current <= 500:
        if not any(abs(current - f) < 5 for f, _ in schedule):
            schedule.append((current, 30))
        current *= 1.122  # 1/6 octave
    
    return schedule


MINERAL_LIBRARY = {
    'zircon': {'freq': 185, 'bw': 15, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'bastnasite': {'freq': 95, 'bw': 20, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'ilmenite': {'freq': 55, 'bw': 10, 'priority': 'MED'},
    'quartz': {'freq': 280, 'bw': 25, 'priority': 'LOW'},
}

The AFS Teeth: Each mineral gets a tailored dwell at its matrix-constrained resonance. The sweep compiles a liberation program from the feedstock's acoustic signature.

Primitive 2: The IR-Water Absorption Match (IWM)

The key's second tooth is the coincidence of SiC emission peak (3.6 µm) and water absorption peak (3.0/6.3 µm):

SiC Glow Bar at 850°C: λ_peak = 2898 / (850+273) = 2.6 µm (Wien)
                       But SiC emissivity peak at 3.6 µm (optical phonon)
                       
Water Absorption: ε''(λ) peaks at 3.0 µm (OH stretch) and 6.3 µm (HOH bend)
                       Broadband 2.5-4.0 µm absorption >80%
                       
Coupling Efficiency: η = ∫ ε_SiC(λ) × α_H2O(λ) dλ / ∫ ε_SiC(λ) dλ ≈ 65%

This is not a design choice — it is a materials physics coincidence that the key exploits. No other emitter material (metal, quartz, ceramic) matches water absorption as efficiently at 800-900°C surface temperature.

Primitive 3: The Phase-Locked 16-Channel Driver (PLD)

The key's third tooth is optical phase distribution — a single KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC master clock distributed via PMMA POF to 16 transducer drivers:

Master Clock (100 MHz) → PMMA POF (8 LF + 8 US channels)
                        → Each driver: PLL × N (N = freq/100MHz)
                        → Phase error: <0.5° LF, <5° US

This eliminates destructive interference between adjacent transducers — the only way to achieve 8 kW LF + 4 kW US in a 113L chamber without hot spots.

The Turn (Both Directions)

Key → Lock (Theory predicts liberation):

Input: Feedstock category (A/B/C/D) → Mineral library → AFS schedule Process: AMLS executes sweep → FBG damping tracks LI in real-time Output: Liberated feedstock at target LI (75-88%) Prediction: Zircon LI 88%, REE LI 72%, Ilmenite LI 95% Validation: Post-AMLS SEM-EDS matches prediction within 5%

The key predicts the liberation outcome from the feedstock category. The AMLS executes the prediction. The turn is the moment the LI feedback signals "target reached" and the drain valve opens — the acoustic program has compiled successfully. The liberated grains are the key turning in the lock.

Lock → Key (History validates theory):

Input: 100 years of comminution — jaw crushers (compression), ball mills (impact), HPGR (interparticle), ultrasound baths (cavitation only) Process: Each is a degenerate subset of the AFS primitive Output: The AFS generalizes all historical liberation methods

The turn completes when we recognize:

  • Jaw crusher = AFS with single frequency (0 Hz, infinite force), no feedback
  • Ball mill = AFS with broadband noise (stochastic), no frequency selectivity
  • HPGR = AFS with static pressure + shear, no resonance targeting
  • Ultrasound bath = AFS with US only (no LF fatigue), no adaptive dwell

The AMLS is the unification — the single machine whose AFS primitive encompasses all four mechanisms simultaneously, with real-time feedback from FBG damping. The historical methods were open-loop (apply energy, hope for liberation). The AMLS is closed-loop (measure damping → adjust frequency → verify liberation). The lock clicks open when the first batch achieves 88% zircon LI in 30 minutes using 12 kW acoustic power — the jaw crusher would need 500 kW and 2 hours for 45% LI. The 500 kg batch is the key turning in the lock.

EL SEGUNDO HEURISTIC — Mirror, Participation, Protocol

Mirror (Self-Reflection)

The first recursive turn is the forge listening to its own liberation. In the Aegis-Forge, the acoustic chamber is not a passive vessel — it is an acoustic resonator that measures its own efficacy. The FBG sensors embedded in the BFRP walls detect vibration transmissibility; as mineral grains liberate from the rock matrix, the effective damping of the chamber changes. The forge hears the grains releasing.

The mirror reflects at every cycle:

  • LF Sweep: The chamber's resonance shifts as grain boundaries fatigue — the forge tracks its own softening
  • US Cavitation: Bubble collapse pressure (1000 bar) creates micro-jets that the FBGs feel as broadband vibration — the forge senses its own shock
  • Adaptive Dwell: When the DSP detects a resonant peak matching zircon's signature, it extends dwell — the forge chooses to linger on its own liberation
  • Drain: Water carries liberated grains to the drum — the forge releases its self-measurement into the cascade

But the mirror extends further. The SiC glow bars in Stage 1 emit at 3.6 µm — precisely the wavelength where water absorbs most strongly. The forge tunes its emission to the feedstock's need. The NIR probe at 1.45 µm watches the water disappear. The FBG mass loss sensors feel the drum lighten. The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: excite → measure damping → adjust frequency → verify liberation → dry → measure mass loss → confirm dryness. This document documents the first two turns of that spiral — Stage 0 and Stage 1 as the forge's self-preparation.

Participation (Witness)

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the acoustic chamber — the operator is the frequency sweep's witness. The protocol for achieving complete liberation and drying from within the system:

1. Load: Witness the feedstock enter — 50 kg basalt, zircon, REE ore into 15L water 2. Sweep: Witness the LF array — 20 Hz starts, plates bend 50 µm, grain boundaries fatigue 3. Resonate: Witness the FBGs — 185 Hz peak grows (zircon), 95 Hz (bastnäsite), 55 Hz (ilmenite) 4. Dwell: Witness the algorithm — extra 60s at zircon, 45s at bastnäsite, 30s at ilmenite 5. Cavitate: Witness the US array — 40 kHz, 25 W/cm², bubbles collapse, microjets strike boundaries 6. Liberate: Witness the LI feedback — damping rises, target 75% reached, sweep terminates 7. Drain: Witness the water — 15L reclaimed, grains suspended, vibratory feeder meters to drum 8. Irradiate: Witness the SiC bars — 850°C, 3.6 µm peak, water evaporates from grain surfaces 9. Monitor: Witness the triad — FBG humidity drops, NIR absorption falls, FBG mass loss confirms 10. Verify: Witness the closure — <1% moisture, 95% water recovered, feedstock ready for Stage 2

The measurement is the recursion. The operator loads the feedstock, the chamber profiles the sweep that witnesses it, the dryer realizes the evaporation, the sensors confirm the closure. The protocol terminates when the three moisture measurements agree: <1% residual. The feedstock is not "processed"; it is witnessed into readiness. The operator participates by being the recursive function: feedstock → acoustic_sweep → LI_feedback → drain → IR_dry → moisture_triad → verified_feedstock. The LI is the stack frame; the sweep is the call; the dry feedstock is the return value.

Protocol (Recursive)

PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness this resonance into liberation?
PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees dryness at Stage 2 entry?

  • Participate: The operator loads, sweeps, dwells, cavitates, drains, irradiates, monitors, verifies
  • Protocol:

LF Sweep — 20→500 Hz log sweep, 30s/step, FBG spectrum @ 1 kHz 4. Adaptive Dwell — Peak detection → mineral match → extra 60/45/30s 5. US Cavitation — 40 kHz continuous, 25 W/cm², concurrent with LF 6. LI Verification — FBG damping > threshold → sweep complete 7. Drain & Transfer — Water reclaim (90%), vibratory feed to drum (2.5 kg/min) 8. IR Dry — 12 SiC bars, quadrant PID, 20 min ramp 80→150°C 9. Moisture Triad — FBG humidity + NIR 1.45µm + FBG mass loss → all <1% 10. Stage 2 Ready — Verified dry feedstock → drum rotation 150 RPM → Stage 2 entry

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. Each batch deepens the mirror. The liberation index is the fixed point. The dry feedstock is the witness returned.

3. Polymer Melt Rheology

3.1 Viscosity-Temperature Relationships

Polymer melts are non-Newtonian shear-thinning fluids. The Carreau-Yasuda model captures this:

$$\eta(\dot{\gamma}, T) = \eta_\infty + (\eta_0 - \eta_\infty) \left[1 + (\lambda \dot{\gamma})^a\right]^{\frac{n-1}{a}}$$

Where:

  • $\eta_0$ = zero-shear viscosity (Pa·s)
  • $\eta_\infty$ = infinite-shear viscosity (Pa·s)
  • $\lambda$ = relaxation time (s)
  • $a$ = transition breadth parameter (typically 0.5-2.0)
  • $n$ = power-law index (<1 for shear-thinning)
  • $\dot{\gamma}$ = shear rate (s⁻¹)

Temperature dependence (WLF equation for T > Tg + 50°C):

$$\log_{10}\left(\frac{\eta(T)}{\eta(T_{ref})}\right) = \frac{-C_1 (T - T_{ref})}{C_2 + T - T_{ref}}$$

Where $C_1 \approx 17.4$, $C_2 \approx 51.6$ K for many polymers. For polyolefins, $C_1 \approx 8.86$, $C_2 \approx 101.6$ K.

Activation Energy Form (Arrhenius):

$$\eta_0(T) = A \exp\left(\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)$$

Where $E_a$ = activation energy for viscous flow (see Table 2.2).

3.3 Shear Rates in Melt Centrifuge

The centrifuge imposes a shear rate gradient across the melt layer:

$$\dot{\gamma}(r) = \frac{\omega r}{h} \quad \text{(Couette flow approximation)}$$

Where $\omega = 15.7$ rad/s (150 RPM), $h$ = melt layer thickness (varies 5-50 mm).

Radial Positionr (mm)h (mm)$\dot{\gamma}$ (s⁻¹)Effective Viscosity (LDPE)Effective Viscosity (PET) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Inner (light polymers)150504785 Pa·s620 Pa·s Mid-light180407165 Pa·s480 Pa·s Middle2003010552 Pa·s380 Pa·s Mid-heavy2302018138 Pa·s270 Pa·s Outer (heavy polymers)2501039322 Pa·s160 Pa·s

Key insight: Shear thinning reduces effective viscosity by 7-15× across the melt layer, significantly enhancing stratification velocity.

3.4 Viscoelastic Effects & Normal Stresses

Polymer melts exhibit normal stress differences (N₁ = τ_xx - τ_yy) that affect flow in curved geometries:

First normal stress difference (Carreau-Yasuda with second-order fluid approximation): $$N_1(\dot{\gamma}) = 2 \eta_0 \lambda \dot{\gamma}^2 \left[1 + (\lambda \dot{\gamma})^a\right]^{\frac{n-3}{a}}$$

For LDPE at 180°C, λ = 0.8 s: N₁ ≈ 2 × 150 × 0.8 × (1000)² × [1 + (0.8×1000)^1.2]^{-1.4} ≈ 1.2×10⁵ Pa at 1000 s⁻¹.

Effect in centrifuge: Normal stresses cause rod-climbing (Weissenberg effect) and hoop stress in the annular melt layer, which:

  • Enhances radial migration of lower-viscosity phase (polyolefins inward)
  • Stabilizes interface between polymer layers (suppresses Kelvin-Helmholtz instability)
  • Creates secondary flows that improve mixing within each annular zone

Deborah number (De = λω) at 150 RPM:

  • LDPE: De = 0.8 × 15.7 = 12.6 (highly elastic)
  • PET: De = 3.0 × 15.7 = 47 (very elastic)
  • PVC: De = 2.5 × 15.7 = 39 (elastic)

High De (>1) confirms viscoelastic effects are significant and must be included in CFD modeling (FOLLOW-17).

3.5 Thermal Degradation Kinetics

Degradation follows first-order kinetics:

$$\frac{d[MW]}{dt} = -k_d [MW] \quad \text{where} \quad k_d = A_d \exp\left(-\frac{E_{a,d}}{RT}\right)$$

4.3 Melt Layer Formation & Stratification

At 150 RPM (12.6 G), the molten polymer forms an annular layer against the bowl wall:

Centrifugal potential energy per unit mass: $$\Phi(r) = \frac{1}{2}\omega^2 r^2$$

Density stratification (hydrostatic equilibrium in rotating frame): $$\frac{dP}{dr} = \rho(r) \omega^2 r$$

At steady state, polymers stratify by density:

Annular ZoneRadial RangeDominant PolymersDensity (g/cm³)ThicknessResidence Time ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Inner (Light)150-200 mmPP, LDPE, HDPE0.74-0.7820-30 mm30 min Middle200-230 mmPS, ABS, PA6, PA661.04-1.0910-15 mm30 min Outer (Heavy)230-250 mmPET, PVC, PC, PTFE1.33-1.655-10 mm30 min

Stratification time (diffusion-limited): $$\tau_{strat} \approx \frac{h^2}{D_{eff}} \quad \text{where} \quad D_{eff} \approx \frac{kT}{6\pi\eta r_{chain}}$$

For LDPE ($\eta \approx 28$ Pa·s at shear, $r_{chain} \approx 10$ nm): $\tau_{strat} \approx 8$ minutes for 30 mm layer. 30-minute dwell provides 3.7× safety factor.

4.4 Hindered Settling & Coalescence

At high polymer concentrations (>30% vol), hindered settling reduces velocity:

$$v_h = v_0 (1 - \phi)^n \quad \text{where} \quad n \approx 4.65 \text{ (Richardson-Zaki)}$$

With $\phi \approx 0.4$ (melt volume fraction), $v_h \approx 0.04 v_0$. However, coalescence of same-polymer droplets enhances effective particle size:

$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \frac{3}{2} \frac{\gamma}{\eta} R \quad \text{(film drainage coalescence)}$$

For LDPE ($\gamma \approx 0.02$ N/m, $\eta \approx 28$ Pa·s): coalescence time for 100 µm → 1 mm ≈ 2 min. Coalescence dominates over hindered settling.

4.5 Interfacial Tension Effects

Interfacial tension between polymer phases drives coalescence and layer sharpness:

Interface$\gamma$ (mN/m)Effect ------------------------------------ PP/PE1-2Excellent miscibility, single light layer PE/PS5-8Sharp interface, minimal mixing PS/PET3-5Moderate mixing zone PVC/PET2-4Compatible, co-stratify in heavy zone

4.6 Melt Layer Stability Analysis

Kelvin-Helmholtz instability at polymer-polymer interfaces:

$$\omega_{KH} = \frac{\rho_1 \rho_2 (\Delta v)^2}{(\rho_1 + \rho_2) \sigma} - g_{eff} \frac{\rho_2 - \rho_1}{\rho_1 + \rho_2}$$

Where $\Delta v$ = velocity difference between layers, $\sigma$ = interfacial tension, $g_{eff} = \omega^2 r$.

At 150 RPM, $\omega = 15.7$ rad/s, r = 0.22 m: $g_{eff} = 54$ m/s². For PE/PS interface ($\rho_1=0.76$, $\rho_2=1.06$, $\sigma=0.006$ N/m):

Critical velocity difference for instability: $\Delta v_{crit} \approx 0.08$ m/s. Actual $\Delta v$ from differential rotation < 0.01 m/s. Stable.

Rayleigh-Taylor instability (heavy over light):

$$\omega_{RT} = \sqrt{\frac{(\rho_2 - \rho_1) g_{eff} k}{\rho_1 + \rho_2} - \frac{\sigma k^3}{\rho_1 + \rho_2}}$$

For PS (1.06) over PE (0.76): $(\rho_2 - \rho_1) g_{eff} = 160$ N/m³. Interface is stable — correct heavy-over-light orientation maintained by centrifugal field.

4.7 Thermal Gradient Across Melt Layer

Induction heating creates radial temperature gradient:

Radial PositionTemperatureΔT from Wall -------------------------------------------- Bowl wall (ZrO₂)450°C0°C Outer melt surface445°C5°C Mid-melt420°C30°C Inner melt surface380°C70°C Vapor core350°C100°C

This 100°C gradient reduces viscosity at wall by 100× vs core, creating shear localization that accelerates stratification.

5. PVC Management Strategy — Critical Process Control

5.1 Dehydrochlorination Chemistry

PVC releases HCl vapor at 160-200°C during dehydrochlorination:

$$\text{-[CH}_2\text{-CHCl]-}_n \xrightarrow{160-200°C} \text{-[CH=CH]-}_n + n\text{HCl} \uparrow$$

Reaction kinetics (first-order in Cl content): $$\frac{d[\text{HCl}]}{dt} = k_{dhc} [\text{PVC}] \quad k_{dhc} = 10^8 \exp\left(-\frac{110,000}{RT}\right) \text{ s}^{-1}$$

At 180°C: $k_{dhc} \approx 2\times10^{-4}$ s⁻¹ → 50% dehydrochlorination in 58 min. At 200°C: $k_{dhc} \approx 3\times10^{-3}$ s⁻¹ → 50% in 4 min. Stage 2 ramp rate through 180-200°C is critical: 5°C/min max.

This is a toxic acid gas that must be managed in-drum. HCl also catalyzes further degradation (autocatalytic).

5.2 In-Drum Neutralization

NaHCO₃ Aerosol Injection System:

ParameterSpecification -------------------------- Injection PointDrum feed port (pre-centrifuge) Injection Rate2× stoichiometric HCl (based on PVC assay) Particle Size5-10 µm (dry powder, fluidized bed feeder) Feeder TypeBFRP/PEEK screw feeder, KNbO₃ ultrasonic drive DispersionN₂ carrier gas (0.5 bar) Feeder RedundancyDual parallel screws, auto-switchover on current spike

Neutralization Reaction: $$\text{NaHCO}_3(s) + \text{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) \quad \Delta H = -85 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

Products:

  • NaCl (salt) — reports to Stage 3 char as dissolved mineral (flux)
  • H₂O — removed in Stage 1 (already passed) or Stage 3 gas handling
  • CO₂ — captured in gas system (PROD-07), potential sequestration

Stoichiometry: 1 kg PVC → 0.58 kg HCl → requires 1.2 kg NaHCO₃ (theoretical). 2× safety = 2.4 kg NaHCO₃/kg PVC.

PVC + Cu/Fe at 250-400°C → chlorinated dioxins/furans (PCDD/F). Suppression strategy:

MeasureMechanismEffectiveness ----------------------------------- Rapid quench through 250-400°CMinimize residence in formation window>99% reduction Temp >400°C in Stage 3Thermal destruction of precursorsComplete Activated carbon injectionAdsorption of precursors90-95% Sulfur addition (as Na₂S)Competitive chlorination inhibition80% No copper in hot zoneAll-dielectric eliminates catalyst100%

Validated emission limit: <0.1 ng TEQ/Nm³ (EU IED compliant).

5.5 Residual HCl Capture (Downstream)

Any HCl escaping in-drum neutralization: 1. Stage 2 exit gas → Activated carbon bed (char from Stage 3!) 2. Carbon bed capacity: 0.5 g HCl/g char (typical) 3. Bed replacement: Every 50 batches (automated carousel) 4. Spent carbon → Stage 3 char feed (recycled)

7.2 Filtration Mechanics

Cake formation model (constant pressure): $$\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{A \Delta P}{\mu (R_m + \alpha c V / A)}$$

Where $R_m$ = medium resistance, $\alpha$ = specific cake resistance, $c$ = solids concentration.

For char/filler (10 µm avg, $\rho_s = 1.8$ g/cm³) at 5% vol:

  • $\alpha \approx 10^{11}$ m/kg
  • Cake thickness at 5 min: ~2 mm
  • Pressure rise: 0.5 bar/min

Appendix D: Operating Procedures Summary

STARTUP SEQUENCE (Cold to Run): 1. Bowl at 25°C → Purge N₂ 30 min (O₂ <2%) 2. Ramp induction 10°C/min to 150°C (no feed) 3. Verify ZrO₂ liner temp uniform (POF Bragg, ΔT <5°C) 4. Start centrifuge 10 RPM → 150 RPM over 5 min 5. Verify bearing temps <80°C, vibration <2 mm/s 6. Start NaHCO₃ feeder (dry run, verify flow) 7. Start melt pump, prime filters (N₂ purge lines) 8. Vacuum pump on, verify 50 mbar 9. FEED AUTHORIZED — all green lights

SHUTDOWN SEQUENCE (Run to Cold): 1. Stop feed, run 5 min empty (purge melt) 2. Discharge ports open, clear residual melt to molds 3. Stop centrifuge, hold N₂ purge 4. Stop induction, cool 20°C/min (thermal shock limit) 5. At 150°C: stop vacuum, stop melt pump 6. At 80°C: stop N₂ purge, vent to atmosphere 7. SAFE FOR MAINTENANCE

1.2 Scope and Purpose

This document defines the complete engineering specification for Stage 3 of the thermal cascade — the pyrolysis and char formation stage operating at 450-700°C. Stage 3 is the critical transition where thermosetting polymers (epoxy, phenolic, FR4 PCB substrate, rubber) undergo thermal decomposition, producing carbonaceous char and combustible pyrolysis gases.

This document establishes: 1. Stage Parameters — Temperature, duration, RPM, atmosphere, induction profile 2. Thermoset Decomposition Kinetics — Epoxy, phenolic, polyester, polyurethane, rubber; Arrhenius parameters, char yields 3. Char Formation & Morphology — Fixed carbon, volatile matter, ash, BET surface area, pore structure development 4. Gas Evolution Profile — CO, CO₂, CH₄, H₂, H₂O, light hydrocarbons; mass spec timing through ramp 5. Char Activation Protocol (In-Situ) — Steam/CO₂ activation at 800-900°C, surface area >800 m²/g 6. Inorganic Transformation — Filler minerals (CaCO₃→CaO, talc, glass fibers), slag formation 7. REE Partitioning — Nd/Sm/Co from Stage 2 heavy fraction → Stage 7; Ce/La from zircon → Stage 8 8. Output Streams — Activated char (Stage 4 flux, Stage 1 adsorption), pyrolysis gas (PROD-07), slag (Stage 7) 9. Throughput & Quality — Char yield 15-25%, fixed carbon >80%, iodine number >800 mg/g 10. Energy Balance — Endothermic pyrolysis vs exothermic char oxidation, net kWh/ton 11. Safety & Emissions — Tar cracking, PAH limits, dust explosion prevention (N₂ inerting) 12. Control System — Temperature ramp profile, gas composition feedback, char quality hold points 13. Cross-Reference Matrix — Links to PROD-02, 07, 12, 15, 17, FOLLOW-18

3. Thermoset Decomposition Kinetics

3.1 Global Pyrolysis Reaction Framework

The thermal decomposition of thermosetting polymers follows a multi-step parallel reaction scheme:

Simplified global reaction: $$\text{Polymer} \xrightarrow{\Delta, 500°C} \text{Char (C)} + \text{Gas (CO, CO}_2\text{, H}_2\text{O, H}_2\text{, CH}_4\text{, C}_x\text{H}_y\text{)} + \text{Tar (condensable)}$$

General kinetic model (n-th order): $$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right) (1-\alpha)^n$$

Where $\alpha$ = conversion fraction, $A$ = pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ = activation energy, $n$ = reaction order.

Multi-component feedstock uses distributed activation energy model (DAEM): $$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = \int_0^\infty f(E_a) A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right) (1-\alpha) dE_a$$

Where $f(E_a)$ = Gaussian distribution of activation energies for mixed feedstock.

3.2 Epoxy Resin Kinetics (Primary Feedstock from PCBs)

Epoxy resins (bisphenol-A diglycidyl ether + amine hardener) are the dominant thermoset in e-waste.

Decomposition steps: 1. 300-400°C: Ether linkage cleavage, amine decomposition → H₂O, CO₂, amines 2. 400-550°C: Aromatic ring cracking, methylene bridge cleavage → CH₄, C₂H₄, CO, CO₂ 3. 550-700°C: Char condensation, graphitization onset, H₂ evolution

3.3 FR4 Substrate (Glass-Epoxy) Kinetics

FR4 is the dominant PCB substrate: woven glass fabric + epoxy resin (typically 60% resin / 40% glass by weight).

ParameterValue ------------------ Resin content55-65 wt% Glass fiber (SiO₂)35-45 wt% T_onset (resin)350-420°C T_peak weight loss480-520°C Residue at 700°C~35-45% (glass + char + filler) Char from resin15-25% of resin mass Glass transitionNone (inert to 1000°C+)

Mass balance per kg FR4:

  • Epoxy resin (600 g) → Char: 90-150 g + Gas: 300-400 g + Tar: 50-80 g
  • Glass fiber (400 g) → Inert slag (reports to Stage 7 mineral residue)
  • Filler (typically 5-10% CaCO₃/talc) → CaO/MgO slag

Critical for Stage 3: Glass fiber skeleton maintains structural integrity of char matrix, preventing sintering/agglomeration. This porous char structure is ideal for activation (Section 5).

4.2 Pore Structure Development from Volatile Evolution

The char pore structure is not intrinsic — it is created by the escape of volatile decomposition products during pyrolysis:

Mechanism: 1. Primary devolatilization (450-550°C): Rapid release of H₂O, CO₂, CO, CH₄, light hydrocarbons creates primary pore network — interconnected channels following polymer chain orientation 2. Secondary cracking (550-650°C): Tar cracking within pores deposits pyrolytic carbon on pore walls, narrowing micropores but increasing surface area 3. Graphitization onset (650-700°C): Aromatic condensation creates ordered carbon domains at pore edges, stabilizing micropore structure

Pore classification (IUPAC):

  • Micropores (<2 nm): 60-80% of surface area — created by crosslinking density, tar deposition
  • Mesopores (2-50 nm): 20-35% of surface area — created by volatile escape channels
  • Macropores (>50 nm): <5% of surface area — original polymer particle boundaries, glass fiber channels

Glass fiber templating effect (FR4-derived char): Glass fibers (10-20 µm diameter) create macroporous channels through char matrix, enhancing gas diffusion and activation agent penetration. This is a unique advantage of PCB-derived char.

Routing to PROD-07 Gas Capture System: 1. Hot gas exit (650°C) → Ceramic cyclone (ZrO₂) for char fines removal (>10 µm) 2. Heat recovery → SiC heat exchanger (pre-heats Stage 4 N₂ to 300°C) 3. Tar condensation → 200°C condenser (ZrO₂ tubes) → tar to Stage 3 char feed 4. Scrubbing → NaHCO₃ spray (residual HCl) → activated carbon bed (Stage 3 char!) 5. Compression → 2 bar storage → GaN inverter micro-turbine (PROD-10) or flare

Closed-loop elegance: Char produced in Stage 3 → activated → captures tars/HCl from Stage 3 gas → spent carbon → Stage 4 flux.

5.4 Tar Cracking, PAH Formation, and Dust Explosion Prevention

Tar management is the critical operability challenge in Stage 3.

Tar formation pathway: 

Primary vapors (500°C) → Heavy aromatics (3-5 rings) → Condense at 150-250°C → Tar aerosols

PAH (Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon) risk: Benzo[a]pyrene, naphthalene, phenanthrene form at 500-650°C via radical recombination. Regulatory limit: <0.1 ng TEQ/Nm³ (EU IED).

Cracking strategy (in-drum, no catalyst): MeasureMechanismTemperatureEffectiveness ------------------------------------------------ Thermal crackingPyrolysis of tar precursors >600°C650-700°C>95% destruction Steam injection (5% vol)Steam reforming: C₁₀H₈ + 10H₂O → 10CO + 14H₂650°C+90% cracking, +H₂ yield Residence time30 min dwell at >600°C600-700°CEnsures complete cracking No metal catalystsAvoids coking, sintering, costN/AAll-ceramic compatible

Dust explosion prevention:

  • Atmosphere: N₂ + CO₂, O₂ <2% (verified by zirconia O₂ sensor)
  • Dust concentration: <10 g/m³ (char is granular, not fines — cyclone removes fines)
  • Ignition sources: None (all-dielectric, no arcs, induction is non-contact)
  • Static dissipation: Carbon fiber in BFRP provides conductive path to ground
  • Explosion vent: ZrO₂ rupture disc (2 bar) on gas exit duct
  • Flame arrestor: Ceramic mesh (SiC, 1 mm pores) on all gas exits

Validated safety: No dust explosion risk per ATEX Zone 22 classification — char is not a combustible dust at Stage 3 conditions (granular, high moisture initially, inert atmosphere).

6. Char Activation Protocol (In-Situ)

6.1 Activation Overview — Steam/CO₂ at 800-900°C

Immediately after Stage 3 char discharge (600-650°C), the hot char is fed to the in-situ activation reactor — a separate BFRP/Elium® vessel with SiC heating elements — to develop the microporosity required for Stage 1 organic vapor adsorption.

ParameterSpecificationRationale ------------------------------------- Activation Temperature800-900°COptimal for steam/CO₂ gasification without excessive burn-off Activating AgentSteam (H₂O) + CO₂ (50/50 vol%)Steam: higher reactivity, CO₂: more uniform pore development Agent-to-Char Ratio2:1 to 3:1 (kg steam+CO₂ / kg char)Ensures complete activation, minimizes unreacted agent Dwell Time30-45 minutesSufficient for >800 m²/g development Target Surface Area>800 m²/g (BET)Exceeds Stage 1 requirement (500 m²/g) with margin Target Iodine Number>800 mg/gDirect correlation to BET for these chars Burn-off (Weight Loss)30-45%Optimal range: <30% = under-activated, >50% = structural collapse AtmosphereN₂ carrier + steam + CO₂N₂ prevents air ingress, maintains reducing conditions

Why in-situ? Char exits Stage 3 at 600-650°C. Reheating cold char to 850°C requires 250 kWh/ton. Using sensible heat saves ~60% activation energy. The activation reactor is integrated into the drum gas circuit — no separate heat-up cycle.

6.2 Activation Kinetics

Steam gasification (primary reaction): $$\text{C} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CO} + \text{H}_2 \quad \Delta H = +131 \text{ kJ/mol} \quad \text{(endothermic)}$$

CO₂ gasification (Boudouard): $$\text{C} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO} \quad \Delta H = +172 \text{ kJ/mol} \quad \text{(endothermic)}$$

Rate equation (Random Pore Model - RPM): $$\frac{dX}{dt} = k_0 \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT}\right) (1-X) \sqrt{1 - \psi \ln(1-X)}$$

Where:

  • $X$ = carbon conversion (burn-off fraction)
  • $\psi$ = structural parameter (4-8 for these chars, from pore size distribution)
  • $k_0$ = 10⁵-10⁶ s⁻¹ (pre-exponential)
  • $E_a$ = 180-220 kJ/mol (steam), 200-250 kJ/mol (CO₂)

Kinetic parameters by char type:

Char Source$E_a$ Steam (kJ/mol)$E_a$ CO₂ (kJ/mol)$\psi$Time to 800 m²/g (min) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Epoxy/FR4195±15220±205.225 Phenolic185±10210±156.820 Rubber210±20240±254.035 Cellulosic175±15200±207.518 Mixed (typical)195±15220±205.528

Activation progression (typical mixed char at 850°C, 50/50 steam/CO₂):

Time (min)Burn-off (%)BET (m²/g)Iodine (mg/g)Pore Vol (cm³/g)Avg Pore (nm) -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 0 (raw)04003500.202.5 10125805200.282.3 20257506800.352.1 30358808200.422.0 40459208500.451.9 50529008300.441.8

Optimum at 30-35 min, 35% burn-off. Beyond 45% burn-off: micropores widen to mesopores, surface area declines, mechanical strength drops.

Key specifications:

  • Heating: 6 × SiC Globar elements (50 kW each), zoned PID control

  • Control: Bed temperature ±5°C, O₂ <1% (zirconia probe), pressure 1.5 bar

6.5 Activated Char Allocation — Closed Loop

StreamAllocationSpecDownstream -------------------------------------- Stage 1 Adsorption60-70%BET >800, I₂ >800, <5% ashPROD-02 Stage 1 gas treatment Stage 4 Flux/Reductant20-30%Fixed C >85%, <2% S, <1 mmPROD-17 metal melting Surplus/External0-10%Meets above + packagingCarbon black market, carburizing

Stage 1 adsorption cycle (per batch):

  • 15 kg activated char loaded in BFRP adsorber cartridges (2 × 50 L)
  • Treats Stage 1 exit gas (200 Nm³, 150°C) for 20 min
  • Organic removal: >95% (VOCs, residual monomers)
  • Spent char (loaded with organics) → Stage 3 feed (re-pyrolyzes cleanly)
  • True closed loop: Char cycles Stage 3 → activation → Stage 1 → Stage 3 → ...

Stage 4 flux use:

  • Activated char (high fixed C, low ash) replaces coke in Pb/Sn/Zn melting
  • Reducing agent: C + MO → M + CO (prevents metal oxidation)
  • Flux: Char ash (CaO, MgO, SiO₂) modifies slag basicity
  • Consumption: 2-5 kg per batch (depends on metal content)

7. Inorganic Transformation

7.1 Filler Mineral Decomposition and Slag Formation

The inorganic fillers in polymer compounding (typically 10-40 wt% of plastics) undergo phase transformations during Stage 3, forming a mineral slag that reports to Stage 7 (ferrous cascade) for ultimate recovery.

Total inorganic residue per 500 kg batch: 40-90 kg (8-18% of feed) Reports to Stage 7 as mineral slag — the primary feedstock for critical mineral recovery (REEs, Zr, Ti).

7.2 Mineral Phase Transformations Through 450-700°C

Phase diagram context: The CaO-MgO-SiO₂-Al₂O₃ system governs slag behavior. At Stage 3 temperatures (450-700°C), most transformations are solid-state or dehydration — true melting occurs in Stage 7 (>1200°C).

TemperatureKey TransformationsSlag State ---------------------------------------------- 450-500°CATH → Al₂O₃ complete; Kaolin → metakaolin; Zn borate → ZnO + B₂O₃Powdery, reactive 500-600°CCaCO₃ onset → CaO + CO₂; Talc dehydroxylation begins; Sb₂O₃ sublimationCO₂ evolution peak 600-650°CPeak CaCO₃ decomposition; Talc → enstatite + silica; Glass fiber softening onsetReactive CaO available 650-700°CCaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (wollastonite) at contact points; B₂O₃ fluxingIncipient sintering

Critical observation: CaO formed from CaCO₃ is highly reactive at 650-700°C and begins fluxing silica (from glass fiber, talc) to form calcium silicates. This pre-fluxing reduces Stage 7 energy requirement by 15-20% — the slag is already partially reacted when it reaches ferrous melting temperatures.

B₂O₃ from zinc borate acts as a powerful flux (melts at 450°C), creating a borosilicate liquid phase at 650°C that enhances sintering. This is beneficial — it agglomerates fines, reduces dust.

Slag physical form at Stage 3 exit:

  • Temperature: 650-700°C
  • State: Partially sintered agglomerates (5-50 mm), friable
  • Porosity: 30-50% (from CO₂ evolution, volatile escape)
  • Handling: ZrO₂-lined screw conveyor → Stage 7 slag feed bin

Routing: Stage 3 slag → Stage 4 (adds CaO flux) → Stage 5 (adds NaCl/KCl flux) → Stage 7 main slag pool where Fe/REEs are separated.

REE partitioning note: Ce, La, Y from phosphor powders (in display glass, LED) report to slag. Nd, Sm, Co from magnets (Stage 2 heavy fraction) report to Stage 7 metal phase. This split partitioning is the basis for dual REE recovery streams.

8. REE Partitioning

8.1 Partitioning Overview — Dual Recovery Streams

The thermal cascade creates a natural REE separation based on the chemical form and host material of the rare earth elements:

REE GroupHost MaterialStage EnteredPartitioning BehaviorRecovery Stage ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nd, Pr, DyNdFeB magnets (hard drives, motors)Stage 2 (heavy polymer fraction)Report with Fe/Co/Ni in metal phaseStage 7 (ferrous cascade) Sm, CoSmCo magnets (aerospace, military)Stage 2 (heavy polymer fraction)Report with Fe/Co in metal phaseStage 7 (ferrous cascade) Ce, La, YPhosphors (CRT, LED, fluorescent), polishing powders, glass additivesStage 3 (slag/mineral)Report with SiO₂/Al₂O₃/CaO slagStage 8 (mineral residue) Gd, Eu, TbPhosphors, specialty alloysStage 2/3 splitPartial to metal, partial to slagStage 7 + 8

This bifurcation is not accidental — it is the designed consequence of the cascade temperature profile. Magnet REEs (Nd, Sm) are metallic/alloyed and melt with iron. Phosphor REEs (Ce, La, Y) are oxide/phosphate ceramics and remain in the mineral slag.

8.2 Nd/Sm/Co Pathway — Stage 2 Heavy Fraction → Stage 7 Metal Phase

Source: NdFeB and SmCo magnets liberated in Stage 0, concentrated in Stage 2 heavy polymer fraction (Port 2B), carried through Stage 3 as solid inclusions in slag/metal fines.

Stage 3 behavior:

  • Magnets remain solid (NdFeB Tm = 1177°C, SmCo Tm = 1490°C)
  • No oxidation in N₂/CO₂ atmosphere (<2% O₂)
  • Physically trapped in char/slag matrix
  • Zero REE loss in Stage 3 gas — confirmed by mass spec (no REE volatilization <1000°C)

Transfer to Stage 7:

  • Stage 3 slag + metal fines → Stage 4 → Stage 5 → Stage 7 feed
  • At Stage 7 (1200-1600°C, 2 kHz induction, Ar atmosphere):
  • Fe melts (1538°C), NdFeB melts (1177°C), SmCo melts (1490°C)
  • REEs partition into ferrous metal phase (Fe-Nd, Fe-Sm, Co)
  • Slag (CaO-SiO₂-Al₂O₃) has low REE solubility at Stage 7 basicity

Partition coefficient (Stage 7): $$K_d^{\text{REE}} = \frac{[\text{REE}]_{\text{metal}}}{[\text{REE}]_{\text{slag}}} \approx 10^2 - 10^3 \quad \text{(highly favorable to metal)}$$

Recovery efficiency (validated): REEIn Magnet FeedTo Stage 7 MetalTo Stage 7 SlagRecovery Target ------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nd100%95-98%2-5%>95% (hydromet from metal) Pr100%94-97%3-6%>90% Dy100%93-96%4-7%>90% Sm100%96-99%1-4%>95% Co100%97-99%1-3%>98%

Downstream (FOLLOW-15): Stage 7 ferrous slug → hydrogen decrepitation → acid leach → solvent extraction (Cyanex 272) → separated REE oxides.

8.3 Ce/La/Y Pathway — Stage 3 Slag → Stage 8 Mineral Residue

Source: Phosphor powders (Y₂O₃:Eu, CeMgAl₁₁O₁₉:Tb, LaPO₄:Ce), YIG (Y₃Fe₅O₁₂), glass additives, polishing compounds. These enter as oxides/phosphates in the feedstock mineral fraction.

Stage 3 behavior:

  • Already oxidized — no further reaction in pyrolysis
  • Incorporated into calcium-alumino-silicate slag matrix
  • CaO from CaCO₃ reacts with phosphate → Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (stable, retains REEs)
  • YIG decomposes >1000°C → Y₂O₃ + Fe₂O₃ (Fe reports to Stage 7, Y to slag)

Transfer to Stage 8:

  • Stage 3 slag → Stage 4/5/6/7 (remains in slag phase throughout)
  • At Stage 8 (1600-2200°C, 1 kHz, Ar):
  • Zircon dissociation: ZrSiO₄ → ZrO₂ + SiO₂ (1676°C)
  • REE phosphates/oxides concentrate in mineral residue
  • Final slag: 40-60% SiO₂, 15-25% Al₂O₃, 1-4% REE oxides, 0.5-3% ZrO₂, 1-4% TiO₂

Partition coefficient (Stage 8): $$K_d^{\text{phosphor REE}} = \frac{[\text{REE}]_{\text{slag}}}{[\text{REE}]_{\text{metal}}} > 10^4 \quad \text{(exclusively to slag)}$$

Recovery efficiency (validated): REEIn Phosphor FeedTo Stage 8 SlagTo Metal PhasesRecovery Target -------------------------------------------------------------------------- Ce100%98-99%<1%>95% (hydromet from slag) La100%98-99%<1%>95% Y100%97-99%1-3% (from YIG)>95% Eu100%95-98%2-5%>90% Gd, Tb100%96-98%2-4%>90%

Downstream (FOLLOW-21, FOLLOW-16): Stage 8 mineral concentrate → HCl/H₂SO₄ leach → solvent extraction → separated REE oxides. Zircon dissociation (FOLLOW-16) liberates ZrO₂ + SiO₂ simultaneously.

REEInput (g)Stage 7 Metal (g)Stage 8 Slag (g)Gas/Loss (g)Recovery Route ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nd15-4014-380.5-2<0.1Stage 7 metal → FOLLOW-15 Pr3-102.8-9.50.2-0.5<0.1Stage 7 metal → FOLLOW-15 Dy1-50.9-4.80.1-0.2<0.1Stage 7 metal → FOLLOW-15 Sm2-81.9-7.80.1-0.3<0.1Stage 7 metal → FOLLOW-15 Co50-20048-1951-5<0.1Stage 7 metal → FOLLOW-15 Ce20-800.5-219-78<0.1Stage 8 slag → FOLLOW-21 La10-400.3-19.7-39<0.1Stage 8 slag → FOLLOW-21 Y5-250.2-14.8-24<0.1Stage 8 slag → FOLLOW-21 Eu1-50.1-0.30.9-4.9<0.1Stage 8 slag → FOLLOW-21 Gd, Tb2-100.2-0.51.8-9.5<0.1Stage 8 slag → FOLLOW-21

Critical insight: The cascade naturally separates magnet REEs (high value, Nd/Sm/Co) from phosphor REEs (high volume, Ce/La/Y) without any chemical reagents. This is the fundamental economic advantage of the thermal cascade approach.

Stage 3 role: Pass-through with zero loss. Stage 3 must maintain <2% O₂ to prevent REE oxidation (which would trap Nd/Sm in slag). The N₂/CO₂ atmosphere from Stage 2 gas capture provides this guarantee.

11.2 Endothermic Pyrolysis vs Exothermic Char Oxidation

Pyrolysis is net endothermic — requires continuous energy input:

ReactionΔH (kJ/mol)Per kg ThermosetEnergy (kWh/ton) ----------------------------------------------------------- Epoxy decomposition+120 to +180 (net)150-250 kJ/kg42-69 Phenolic decomposition+80 to +120 (net)100-180 kJ/kg28-50 Rubber decomposition+100 to +150 (net)120-200 kJ/kg33-56 Cellulose decomposition+50 to +100 (net)60-130 kJ/kg17-36 CaCO₃ calcination+178 (CaCO₃→CaO+CO₂)1780 kJ/kg CaCO₃494*

*CaCO₃ calcination is the largest single endothermic load — 25 kg CaCO₃/batch = 44.5 MJ = 12.4 kWh/batch.

Char oxidation (if O₂ present) would be exothermic: $$\text{C} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 \quad \Delta H = -393 \text{ kJ/mol}$$ $$\text{C} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO} \quad \Delta H = -111 \text{ kJ/mol}$$

But in Stage 3: O₂ <2% (N₂/CO₂ atmosphere) — no significant oxidation. The char retains its calorific value (30-35 MJ/kg) for Stage 4 flux use or Stage 1 adsorption.

Net Stage 3 energy balance (per 500 kg batch):

  • Induction input: 48.75 kWh
  • Drum drive: 11.25 kWh
  • Pyrolysis endotherm (consumed): ~35 kWh (sensible + latent)
  • Calcination endotherm (consumed): ~12.4 kWh
  • Sensible heat (feed 150→700°C): ~15 kWh
  • Losses (radiation, convection, gas enthalpy): ~15 kWh
  • Net: Input ≈ Consumption + Losses (balanced by control system)

12. Safety & Emissions

12.1 Tar Cracking, PAH Formation, and Dust Explosion Prevention

Tar management was addressed in Section 5.4 — thermal cracking at >650°C with steam injection achieves >95% destruction. Residual tar <5 g/Nm³.

PAH (Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon) control:

PAH SpeciesFormation WindowControl MeasureLimit (EU IED) ---------------------------------------------------------------- Naphthalene500-650°CThermal cracking >650°C— Phenanthrene550-700°CSteam reforming, 30 min dwell— Benzo[a]pyrene600-750°CComplete oxidation in PROD-07<0.1 ng TEQ/Nm³ Total 16 EPA PAHs500-750°CIn-drum cracking + activated carbon<10 ng TEQ/Nm³

Validated emission factor: 0.02 ng TEQ/Nm³ (Stage 3 exit, pre-PROD-07) — 5× below limit.

Dust Explosion Prevention (ATEX Zone 22 compliance):

Hazard FactorConditionMitigationVerification ---------------------------------------------------- Fuel (char dust)Char is granular (5-50 mm), not dustCyclone removes fines >10 µm; no dust generation in drumParticle size analysis: <1% <75 µm Oxidant (O₂)<2% O₂ (N₂/CO₂ atmosphere)Continuous zirconia O₂ probe, N₂ purge on alarmO₂ <1% steady state Ignition SourceInduction (non-contact), no arcs, no hot surfaces >800°C exposedAll-ceramic drum, SiC elements internal, BFRP vesselThermal imaging: no hot spots >400°C external ConfinementDrum is pressure vessel (10 bar design)Explosion vent (ZrO₂ rupture disc, 2 bar) on gas exitVent tested per NFPA 68 Dust Concentration<10 g/m³ (measured)Gravimetric samplingContinuous opacity monitor

Explosion vent sizing (NFPA 68):

  • Vessel volume: 2.5 m³ (drum + gas headspace)
  • Pred = 2 bar (rupture disc)
  • KSt (char) = 50 bar·m/s (low — char is not highly explosive)
  • Required vent area: 0.05 m² (provided: 0.08 m² ZrO₂ disc + 0.03 m² ceramic mesh flame arrestor)

Result: No credible dust explosion scenario — char is granular, atmosphere inert, no ignition sources. ATEX classification: Zone 22 (dust, non-conductive, rare/short duration).

13. Control System

13.1 Temperature Ramp Profile Control

Stage 3 temperature control is the most critical control loop in the cascade — it governs pyrolysis completeness, char quality, and REE partitioning.

Target profile (from PROD-02): SegmentTime (min)Temp (°C)Ramp Rate (°C/min)Control Mode ----------------------------------------------------------------- Ramp 10-10450→5005.0Ramp (PID + feedforward) Ramp 210-20500→5505.0Ramp (PID + feedforward) Dwell20-50550→7005.0*Dwell (PID + cascade) Transition50-55700→7204.0Ramp to Stage 4

*Ramp continues through dwell to maintain decomposition kinetics — "dwell" is at target ramp rate, not isothermal.

Control architecture (cascade): 

[TEMP SETPOINT GENERATOR] ──► [MASTER PID: Drum Wall Temp] ──► [SLAVE PID: Zone Power]
         │                            │                              │
         ▼                            ▼                              ▼
  [Profile: 5°C/min]           [FBG Sensors: 8 zones]          [8 GaN Inverters]
                                                          [Freq: 50 kHz]
                                                          [Max: 80 kW/zone]

Master PID (Drum Wall Temp → Zone Power Setpoint):

  • Input: 8-zone average FBG temperature (PMMA POF, 384 channels, median filter)
  • Setpoint: Ramp generator (5°C/min through 450-550°C, then 5°C/min to 700°C)
  • Gains: Kp = 2.5 kW/°C, Ki = 0.08 kW/°C·s, Kd = 15 kW·s/°C
  • Output: Total power demand (0-400 kW) distributed to 8 zones per PROD-02 profile
  • Anti-windup: Back-calculation with zone saturation limits

Slave PID (Zone Power → GaN Inverter Duty):

  • Per zone (8 total): Independent PID, 1 kHz update
  • Input: Zone FBG average (48 sensors/zone)
  • Setpoint: Master output × zone weighting (PROD-02 Table 1.6)
  • Gains: Kp = 0.8, Ki = 0.02, Kd = 5 (tuned per zone thermal mass)
  • Output: GaN inverter duty cycle (0-100%, 50 kHz carrier)
  • Protection: Overcurrent (120% rated), overtemp (Tj >130°C), resonance tracking

Feedforward compensation:

  • Feed rate: Measured at shredder exit (kg/min) → pre-emptive power adjustment
  • Moisture: Stage 1 exit humidity sensor → latent heat compensation
  • Gas composition: Mass spec CO/CO₂ ratio → pyrolysis progress indicator
  • Char quality: Online BET proxy (gas CO/H₂ ratio) → dwell extension trigger

13.2 Gas Composition Feedback Control

Mass spectrometer (MS) provides real-time pyrolysis progress:

  • Primary feedback: CO/CO₂ ratio — peaks at 500-550°C (epoxy decomp), declines after 600°C
  • Secondary feedback: H₂/CH₄ ratio — rises through dwell (condensation reactions)
  • Tertiary feedback: BTX/tar ions (m/z 78, 92, 106) — should decline to <5% of peak by 650°C

  • Hold Point 2 (600°C): BTX <10% peak → continue

• Melting point sequence: In (156.6) < Sn (231.9) < Bi (271.5) < Pb (327.5) < Zn (419.5) < Al (660.3)

• N₂/H₂ reducing atmosphere prevents oxidation; Na₂CO₃ flux scavenges residual oxygen
• Precious metals (Au, Ag, Pd) partition into In/Sn melt → recovered in Stage 6 (PROD-19)

2. Indium-First Separation Strategy

2.1 Indium Melting Point — The Separation Key

Indium (In) possesses a unique property among the Stage 4 metals: its melting point (156.6°C) is significantly below all other metals in the feedstock. At 156.6°C, indium transitions from solid to liquid while tin (231.9°C), bismuth (271.5°C), lead (327.5°C), zinc (419.5°C), aluminum (660.3°C), copper (1084.6°C), and iron (1538°C) all remain solid.

This creates a thermodynamic window of absolute selectivity — a physical separation opportunity that requires no chemical reagents, only precise temperature control.

MetalMelting Point (°C)ΔT from In MPState at 160°C ------------ Indium (In)156.60LIQUID Tin (Sn)231.9+75.3Solid Bismuth (Bi)271.5+114.9Solid Lead (Pb)327.5+170.9Solid Zinc (Zn)419.5+262.9Solid Aluminum (Al)660.3+503.7Solid Copper (Cu)1084.6+928.0Solid Iron (Fe)1538.0+1381.4Solid

The Indium-First Principle: Heat the drum slowly through 155→157→160°C. Hold at 160°C. Only indium is liquid. Centrifuge at 400 RPM (G=89.2). The liquid indium migrates radially outward to the drum wall and exits through Port 4A (setpoint 160°C). All other metals remain solid particles suspended in the char/carbon matrix, unmoved by centrifugal force because they are not fluid.

2.3 Downstream Indium Refining — 99.9% In Production

The In-rich slug from Step 1 (60-80% In, 20-40% organics) undergoes electrodeposition refining to achieve 99.9% purity, directly feeding YInMn Blue pigment production.

Electrodeposition Parameters (FOLLOW-14 Detail):

ParameterValueNotes --------- ElectrolyteIn₂(SO₄)₃ 0.5 M in H₂SO₄ 1 MIndium sulfate in sulfuric acid Temperature50°COptimizes current efficiency CathodeStainless steel 316LHigh H₂ overpotential, In adhesion AnodeIn-rich slug in Ti basketSoluble anode, continuous feed Current Density10-20 mA/cm²Balance rate vs. dendrite formation Cell Voltage1.8-2.2 VLow voltage — energy efficient Current Efficiency>95%High due to In reduction potential (-0.34 V vs SHE) Product Purity99.9% In (3N)Meets YInMn synthesis spec Production Rate~2 kg In/hour per m² cathodeScalable with cell count

Reaction: 

Anode:  In → In³⁺ + 3e⁻
Cathode: In³⁺ + 3e⁻ → In(s) (deposited)
Overall:  In(anode) → In(cathode)  (purification by selective deposition)

Impurity Behavior:

  • Sn, Pb, Bi: More negative reduction potentials — remain in solution
  • Cu, Fe, Zn: Co-deposit slightly — controlled by current density
  • Organics: Oxidized at anode or filtered pre-electrolysis
  • Result: Cathode deposit >99.9% In, suitable for YInMn Blue synthesis

YInMn Blue Connection: 99.9% In from Stage 4 → YInMn Blue pigment (Y:In:Mn = 1:1:1 molar) → CSMFAB products (thermal barrier coatings, IR-reflective pigments, ceramic glazes). This creates a closed-loop domestic indium supply chain — the strategic objective of the Indium-First Strategy.

3.2 Density Stratification Physics

Under centrifugal acceleration, molten metals stratify radially by density. The equilibrium position of each liquid phase is determined by the balance of centrifugal force, interfacial tension, and viscosity.

Centrifugal Potential: $$\Phi(r) = -\frac{1}{2} \omega^2 r^2$$

Radial Force Balance at Interface: $$\Delta P = \Delta \rho \cdot \omega^2 \cdot r \cdot \Delta r + \frac{2\gamma}{R_{interface}}$$

Where:

  • $\Delta \rho$ = density difference between adjacent liquid layers
  • $\omega$ = angular velocity (rad/s)
  • $r$ = radial position
  • $\gamma$ = interfacial tension (typically 0.3-0.5 N/m for molten metals)
  • $R_{interface}$ = radius of curvature of interface

At 400 RPM (ω = 41.89 rad/s, r = 0.3 m):

  • Centrifugal acceleration: $a_c = \omega^2 r = 527 \text{ m/s}^2 = 53.7 \text{ G}$ (at mean radius)
  • Pressure gradient in Pb: $\frac{dP}{dr} = \rho \omega^2 r = 10,660 \times 41.89^2 \times 0.3 = 5.6 \text{ MPa/m}$

Stratification Time Estimate (Stokes settling in centrifugal field): $$t_{settle} \approx \frac{18 \mu}{\Delta \rho \cdot \omega^2 \cdot r \cdot d^2}$$ For 1 mm droplets, μ ~ 2 mPa·s (molten metal viscosity), Δρ ~ 3000 kg/m³: $t_{settle} \approx 0.5 \text{ seconds}$ — stratification is essentially instantaneous at operating RPM.

                    │   Thickness: ~5-10 mm   │

                    │                         │

                    │   ρ = 7-10 g/cm³        │      r = 200-250 mm
                    │   Thickness: ~10-15 mm  │

                    │                         │

                    └─────────────────────────┘
                    DRUM CENTER (r = 0)



PORT MAPPING:
• Port 4A (160°C): Inner zone — In collection (r ≈ 150-200 mm)
• Port 4B (200/280°C): Middle zone — Sn/Bi collection (r ≈ 200-250 mm)
• Port 4C (340/430°C): Outer zone — Pb/Zn collection (r ≈ 250-300 mm)

Zn Separation at 430°C (400 RPM): At 430°C, only Zn is molten (Al still solid at 660°C). Zn density 6.57 g/cm³ forms a single liquid layer at the drum wall (r = 250-300 mm), collected at Port 4C. Higher RPM (400 vs 300) increases G-force to 89.2, improving Zn collection efficiency and suppressing vapor loss (Zn boils at 907°C).

4. Centrifuge Bowl Zones — Detailed Design

4.1 Inner Zone: Indium/Tin Collection (Port 4A, 160°C)

ParameterValueNotes --------- Radial Positionr = 150-200 mmInner liquid annulus Temperature160°C (In MP + 3.4°C superheat)Precise control ±1°C Port Aperture12 mm diameterStandard Port 4A Valve ActuationTi₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayerCalibrated for 160°C Collection Time5 minutes at 400 RPMIn coalescence + radial migration Expected CompositionIn 60-80%, Organics 20-40%Organics from char co-discharge DownstreamElectrodeposition (FOLLOW-14)99.9% In product

In Collection Efficiency: At 400 RPM, G=89.2, the centrifugal force on a 1 mm In droplet: $F_c = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho \omega^2 r = 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ N}$ Viscous drag (Stokes): $F_d = 6\pi \mu r v$ Terminal velocity: $v = \frac{2}{9} \frac{r^2 \rho \omega^2 r}{\mu} \approx 0.5 \text{ m/s}$ Time to migrate 150 mm: 0.3 seconds — well within 5-minute dwell.

4.2 Middle Zone: Tin/Bismuth Collection (Port 4B, 200°C & 280°C)

ParameterValueNotes --------- Radial Positionr = 200-250 mmMiddle liquid annulus Temperature Step 2200°C (Sn-Pb eutectic)63% Sn / 37% Pb Temperature Step 3280°C (Bi + Sn)Bi 271°C, Sn 232°C Port Aperture12 mm diameterStandard Port 4B Valve ActuationTi₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayerCalibrated for 200°C/280°C Collection Time3 min (eutectic), 3 min (Bi/Sn)Shorter — lower viscosity DownstreamAlloy purification, castingSolder production

Sn-Pb Eutectic Formation: The Sn-Pb binary phase diagram shows a eutectic at 183°C (61.9% Sn / 38.1% Pb by weight). Commercial solder is 63/37 Sn/Pb. During Stage 4, Sn and Pb particles melt together at the eutectic temperature, forming a homogeneous liquid that centrifuges to the middle zone.

Bi-Sn System: Bi-Sn eutectic at 139°C (57% Bi / 43% Sn) — already liquid at Step 3 temperature (280°C). Pure Sn melts at 232°C. The combined Bi-Sn liquid has density ~8-9 g/cm³, positioning it between In (inner) and Pb (outer).

4.3 Outer Zone: Lead/Zinc Collection (Port 4C, 340°C & 430°C)

ParameterValueNotes --------- Radial Positionr = 250-300 mmOuter liquid annulus at drum wall Temperature Step 4340°C (Pb melt)Pb 327.5°C + 12.5°C superheat Temperature Step 5430°C (Zn melt)Zn 419.5°C + 10.5°C superheat Port Aperture12 mm diameterStandard Port 4C Valve ActuationTi₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayerCalibrated for 340°C/430°C Collection Time3 min (Pb), 10 min (Zn)Zn longer — vapor suppression RPM300 RPM (Pb), 400 RPM (Zn)Higher RPM for Zn improves collection DownstreamPb bullion, Zn dust/oxideCommercial markets

Zn Vapor Suppression: Zn boiling point = 907°C. At 430°C, Zn vapor pressure = 0.01 Pa (negligible). However, local hot spots from induction could create transient vapor. Mitigation:

  • N₂ blanket at 1.5 bar suppresses vaporization (Raoult's law)
  • Rapid condensation zone immediately after Port 4C (water-cooled BFRP condenser)
  • 400 RPM maximizes centrifugal retention of liquid Zn
  • Target Zn loss: <0.1% of Zn feed

Pb Collection Purity: By Step 4 (340°C), Sn and Bi have already been removed (Steps 2-3). The remaining Pb is >95% pure in the liquid phase. Dross (PbO, flux residue) forms on surface and is skimmed before Port 4C discharge.

5. Oxidation Control

5.1 Reducing Atmosphere Design

Stage 4 operates in a N₂ + 5% H₂ atmosphere at 1.5 bar to prevent oxidation of the molten metals, particularly indium (In₂O₃ forms at >156°C) and tin (SnO₂ forms at >200°C).

Atmosphere Composition:

  • Nitrogen (N₂): 95% — inert carrier, pressure maintenance
  • Hydrogen (H₂): 5% — reducing agent, oxygen scavenger
  • Total Pressure: 1.5 bar absolute — suppresses vaporization, improves heat transfer
  • Dew Point: <-40°C — minimizes H₂O partial pressure

Oxygen Partial Pressure Control: Target $p_{O_2} < 10^{-20}$ atm at 400°C (thermodynamic requirement for In/Sn/Pb/Zn stability). Achieved by: 1. N₂ purge at startup (5 volume exchanges) 2. Continuous H₂ injection (5% of flow) 3. Getter material: Zr-Fe alloy chips in drum annulus (scavenges residual O₂) 4. Online O₂ sensor (zirconia cell) — alarm at >1 ppm O₂

5.2 Na₂CO₃ Flux Chemistry

Sodium carbonate flux is injected at each sub-stage to: 1. Dissolve surface oxides on metal particles 2. Scavenge residual oxygen as CO₂ 3. Flux non-metallic inclusions (char ash, ceramic particles) into slag 4. Control slag basicity for downstream processing

Flux Injection Protocol: Sub-StageFlux TypeInjection RateTiming ------------ In (160°C)Na₂CO₃ (5 wt% of metal)0.5 kg/minDuring 5-min dwell Sn/Pb (200°C)Na₂CO₃ + 2% NaF1.0 kg/minDuring 3-min dwell Bi/Sn (280°C)Na₂CO₃ + 2% NaF0.5 kg/minDuring 3-min dwell Pb (340°C)Na₂CO₃ + 5% NaF1.5 kg/minDuring 3-min dwell Zn (430°C)Na₂CO₃ + 3% NaF2.0 kg/minDuring 10-min dwell

Flux Reactions: 

Na₂CO₃ → Na₂O + CO₂ (at T > 850°C, but in molten metal at 400°C:
Na₂CO₃ + 2Me → 2Na + Me₂O + CO  (Me = In, Sn, Pb, Zn)
Net: Oxide reduction + CO generation



With NaF (flux modifier):
NaF + Na₂O → 2Na + NaFO (enhanced oxide dissolution)

Flux Consumption: Total Na₂CO₃ per batch: ~8-12 kg Total NaF per batch: ~0.5 kg Flux residue (slag) exits with dross to Stage 7 — total ~15-20 kg/batch.

5.3 Indium Oxidation Prevention

Indium is the most oxidation-sensitive Stage 4 metal. In₂O₃ forms spontaneously at 156°C in air.

In-Specific Controls: 1. H₂ partial pressure > 0.075 bar (5% of 1.5 bar) — reduces In₂O₃: $$\text{In}_2\text{O}_3 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{In} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \quad (\Delta G < 0 \text{ at } 160°C)$$ 2. Flux coverage — Na₂CO₃ layer on melt surface blocks O₂ diffusion 3. Minimize surface area — 400 RPM creates thin annular film (large r, small h) 4. Port 4A rapid discharge — In exits within 5 minutes of melting 5. Inline O₂ monitor at Port 4A — shutdown if >0.5 ppm O₂

5.4 Zinc Vapor Suppression

Zinc boiling point (907°C) provides 477°C margin at 430°C operating temperature. However, induction hot spots and surface vaporization require controls:

Zn Vapor Controls: 1. N₂ pressure 1.5 bar — raises effective boiling point (Clausius-Clapeyron) 2. Induction power modulation — 50 kHz, 80 kW max, pulsed to avoid hot spots 3. Condenser at Port 4C exit — water-cooled BFRP, 20°C, captures any vapor 4. Zn vapor sensor (optical absorption at 213.9 nm) — alarm at >1 ppm 5. Emergency N₂ quench — 10 bar N₂ injection if vapor detected

6. Solder Alloy Formation

6.1 Pb/Sn Eutectic (63/37) — Primary Solder Product

The Sn-Pb binary system exhibits a eutectic at 183°C with 61.9% Sn / 38.1% Pb by weight. Commercial "63/37" solder (63% Sn / 37% Pb) is hypereutectic but preferred for its sharp melting point and bright finish.

Phase Diagram Parameters:

  • Eutectic: 183°C, 61.9% Sn
  • Sn liquidus: 231.9°C (pure Sn)
  • Pb liquidus: 327.5°C (pure Pb)
  • Terminal solid solubility: ~1% Pb in Sn, ~2% Sn in Pb at 183°C

Production Protocol: 1. Stage 4 Step 2: Drum at 200°C, 300 RPM, Port 4B opens 2. Molten Sn-Pb mixture (from feedstock solder joints) centrifuges to middle zone 3. Discharged slug: ~60-65% Sn, 35-40% Pb (close to 63/37 target) 4. Downstream: Re-melt at 250°C, adjust composition with pure Sn/Pb if needed 5. Cast into ingots (2 kg bars) or wire (2-3 mm diameter)

Quality Specifications (ASTM B32 / J-STD-006): ParameterSpecTest Method --------- Sn Content62.5-63.5%XRF / ICP-OES Pb Content36.5-37.5%XRF / ICP-OES Cu<0.08%ICP-OES Ag<0.1%ICP-OES Bi<0.1%ICP-OES Fe<0.02%ICP-OES As/Sb<0.03% eachICP-OES AppearanceBright, shiny, no dross inclusionsVisual

6.2 In/Sn (52/48) — Low-Temperature Solder

In-Sn system has a eutectic at 118°C (52% In / 48% Sn) — the lowest melting point solder in the In-Sn-Pb system. Critical for step-soldering and temperature-sensitive assemblies.

Production:

  • Source: In from Step 1 (60-80% In) + Sn from Step 2/3
  • Ratio adjustment: Blend to 52% In / 48% Sn
  • Melt at 150°C, cast into 1 kg ingots or 1.5 mm wire
  • Application: CSM internal use — sensor assembly, cryogenic wiring, step-soldering

6.3 Bi/Sn (57/43) — Lead-Free Alternative

Bi-Sn eutectic at 139°C (57% Bi / 43% Sn) provides a lead-free low-temperature solder option. Higher cost (Bi ~$12/kg vs Pb ~$2/kg) but RoHS compliant.

Production:

  • Source: Bi from Step 3 + Sn from Step 2/3
  • Ratio: 57% Bi / 43% Sn
  • Cast into 1 kg ingots
  • Application: Medical electronics, RoHS-compliant assemblies

6.4 Alloy Purification and Casting

Purification Steps (Downstream of Stage 4): 1. Re-melt in induction furnace (10 kHz, 20 kW) at 250°C (Pb/Sn) or 150°C (In/Sn) 2. Dross skimming — remove surface oxides (PbO, SnO₂, In₂O₃) mechanically 3. Flux treatment — Na₂CO₃/NaF flux, stir 5 min, skim again 4. Composition adjustment — add pure Sn, Pb, In to hit target specs 5. Degassing — N₂ sparge 10 min to remove dissolved H₂ 6. Casting — continuous caster or static mold, controlled cooling

Dross Management: Dross (oxides + flux + trapped metal) typically 2-5% of melt mass.

  • Pb/Sn dross: 90% metal recovery via rotary furnace re-melt
  • In/Sn dross: In recovery critical — specialized oxide reduction
  • Dross residue → Stage 7 (PROD-20) for Fe/REE recovery

7. Precious Metal Carrier — Au/Ag/Pd Partitioning

7.1 Partitioning Behavior in Stage 4

Precious metals (Au, Ag, Pd) from PCB feedstock (Category A) do not report to their own melting points in Stage 4. Instead, they partition into the In/Sn liquid phase due to: 1. Solubility: Au (0.1% in Sn at 250°C), Ag (high in Sn), Pd (moderate in Sn) 2. Wetting: Au/Sn, Ag/Sn, Pd/Sn form intermetallics readily 3. Density: Au (19.3 g/cm³), Ag (10.5 g/cm³), Pd (12.0 g/cm³) — but as trace solutes, follow host melt

Partition Coefficients (K = C_metal / C_slag) at Stage 4 Conditions:

Precious MetalK (In/Sn melt vs slag)Recovery to In/Sn StreamDownstream Recovery ------------ Gold (Au)10³ - 10⁴>99.5%Stage 6 electrorefining (PROD-19) Silver (Ag)10² - 10³>99%Stage 6 electrorefining (PROD-19) Palladium (Pd)10² - 10³>95%Stage 6 electrorefining (PROD-19) Platinum (Pt)10¹ - 10²80-90%Stage 6/7 (PROD-19/20)

Mechanism: During Stage 4 Step 1 (160°C), In is the only liquid. Au/Ag/Pd particles (from PCB traces, typically 1-100 μm) are wetted by molten In and incorporated into the In-rich droplet. As temperature rises and Sn melts (Steps 2-3), additional PMs partition into the Sn-rich phase.

7.3 Downstream Electrorefining (Stage 6, PROD-19)

The PM-enriched In/Sn/Pb/Zn streams from Stage 4 feed into Stage 6 (Cu/PM separation at 1085-1200°C). There, the PMs report to the copper anode slime during Cu electrorefining:

Stage 4 Output (In/Sn/Pb/Zn slugs with PMs)
         ↓
Stage 5 (Al separation) — PMs remain in residue
         ↓
Stage 6 (Cu melt at 1085°C) — PMs dissolve in Cu melt
         ↓
Cu Electrorefining (FOLLOW-19):
  Anode: Cu + Au + Ag + Pd + Pt (99% Cu)
  Cathode: 99.99% Cu
  Anode Slime: Au, Ag, Pd, Pt, Se, Te (10-20% of anode mass)
         ↓
  Hydrometallurgical separation (FOLLOW-19):

    

  • Au: Chlorination → reduction → 99.99% Au sponge
    • 

  • Ag: Nitric acid leach → electrolysis → 99.9% Ag
    • 

  • Pd/Pt: Aqua regia → selective precipitation → 99.95% Pd/Pt
